Part 0

How to Actually Study This

Reading is the weakest thing you can do with this material, and it feels like the strongest. The four techniques the daily sessions are built on, and the exact protocol to follow.

Suggested time · 30 min

You already know how to read. The problem is that reading is the weakest thing you can do with this material, and it feels like the strongest.

This part is short. It explains the four techniques the daily sessions are built on, why they work, and the exact protocol to follow. Read it once properly — it changes the return on every other hour you spend.

0.1 The trap: fluency is not learning MUST KNOW

You reread the decorators section. The words look familiar. Everything makes sense. You feel ready.

Then in the interview someone says "walk me through writing a decorator that takes arguments" and nothing comes.

What happened is called the fluency illusion. Familiarity with text is not the same skill as retrieving information without the text in front of you. Rereading builds the first and barely touches the second — and because it feels smooth, it's the most over-used study method there is.

The interview only ever tests the second skill. So the study method has to train that one directly.

The rule this whole system is built on: if you can see the answer, you are not studying. You are reading. The moment of learning is the moment you try to produce the answer and can't quite.

What to stop doing: rereading, highlighting, copying code out, watching videos, "reviewing" notes. All of them feel productive. None of them make retrieval easier.

0.2 Active recall — the technique that does the work MUST KNOW

Active recall means retrieving information from memory before checking whether you were right.

The counter-intuitive part: the struggle is the mechanism, not a sign that it's going badly. Every time you successfully pull something out of memory, that memory gets stronger and easier to find next time. Reading the answer skips the part that does the work.

This has a name in the literature — the testing effect — and it holds across subjects, ages and materials. Testing yourself beats restudying by a wide margin, and the gap grows the longer you wait before the real test.

How to do it here, specifically

  1. Read the card question. Cover the answer.
  2. Say the answer out loud, in full sentences. Not "yeah, the GIL thing" — the actual explanation you'd give an interviewer.
  3. Then flip and compare.
  4. Grade yourself honestly on whether you produced it, not on whether you recognised it.

Saying it out loud matters more than it sounds. It forces complete sentences, exposes the gaps that silent nodding hides, and it is literally the skill being tested — you're not going to write your answer in the interview, you're going to say it.

The honesty problem. Everyone's first instinct is to flip early, read the answer, think "yes, I knew that", and grade Good. That is rereading with extra steps, and it will quietly waste your month. If you didn't say it out loud, you didn't know it.

0.3 Spaced repetition — reviewing at the right moment MUST KNOW

Memory decays on a curve. Left alone, you'll lose most of what you learn today within a week.

Each time you successfully recall something, two things happen: the decay slows down, and the curve gets flatter. So the efficient move is to review just before you would have forgotten — early enough to succeed, late enough to be difficult.

That's what expanding intervals do. A card you keep getting right goes 1 day → 3 → 8 → 20 → 50 → 125. A card you miss drops back to today.

Why this beats cramming: cramming produces a high score tomorrow and almost nothing in three weeks. Spacing the same total minutes across days produces dramatically better long-term retention. Since your interview is weeks away, not tomorrow, spacing is strictly better use of identical effort.

Why the intervals have to expand: reviewing everything daily is both exhausting and wasteful — you'd spend most of your time on cards you already know cold. Expanding intervals concentrate your minutes on the material that's actually at risk of being forgotten.

The four grades, and what they mean

Grade Use it when Next review
Again You couldn't produce it, or you got it wrong Later today
Hard You got there, but slowly or incompletely Short
Good You produced it correctly with normal effort Normal expansion
Easy Instant, complete, no hesitation Long jump

Grade honestly. Inflating grades doesn't make you know more; it just removes the card from your rotation while the gap is still there. Under-grading is the safer error.

0.4 Elaboration — how you actually understand something MUST KNOW

Recall gets facts to stick. It doesn't, on its own, produce understanding. For that you need elaboration: connecting the new thing to things you already know, and being able to explain why it is the way it is.

Three prompts, and they're the ones this handbook is written around:

"Why does this exist?" Every tool solves a problem someone had. If you can't say what breaks without it, you don't understand it yet. Decorators exist because cross-cutting concerns would otherwise be copy-pasted into twenty functions.

"When would this be the wrong choice?" Knowing the limits is what distinguishes understanding from memorisation — and it's exactly what interviewers probe with follow-ups. Anything you can only praise, you don't understand.

"What does this remind me of?" Python's late-binding closures and JavaScript's var in a loop are the same bug. Java's StringBuilder and Python's "".join() solve the same O(n²) problem. Connections make things far harder to forget than isolated facts.

The teach-back test

Take one concept from today and explain it out loud as if to a competent developer who's never met it. No notes.

Where you stall, hedge, or go vague — that's the gap. Go back and read only that part, then explain again. It takes four minutes and it finds the holes reading never will.

Every session in this handbook ends with one teach-back prompt for exactly this reason.

0.5 Interleaving — mix, don't block SHOULD KNOW

The instinct is to do twenty sliding-window problems in a row. It feels efficient and produces fast, confident practice.

It also means that after the second problem you've stopped choosing the pattern — you already know it's sliding window, so you only practise the execution, never the recognition. In the interview nobody tells you which pattern it is, and recognition is the part that actually fails.

Mixing topics within a session feels harder and performs worse in the moment. It also produces substantially better transfer to unfamiliar problems. That's a real trade you're making: comfort now versus capability later.

The review queue in this handbook shuffles topics for exactly this reason. Don't sort it.

0.6 The daily protocol MUST KNOW

About 35 minutes. Same shape every day.

Phase Minutes What you do
1. Review first 5–8 Clear the due cards before new material, while you're fresh. This is the non-negotiable part
2. Read 15–20 The day's sections. Read for the why and the when not, not for coverage
3. Do 8–10 The practice task. Write the code, say the answer, do the drill
4. Teach back 2–3 One concept, out loud, no notes

Review comes first. If you read first, you'll run out of time and skip the review — and the review is the part that works. Protect it by doing it first.

Two Pomodoros covers a day. Use the timer in the bottom corner: one 25-minute block for review plus reading, a five-minute break, one more for practice and teach-back. The break is not optional — spacing within a session helps too, and the timer stops you drifting into a two-hour session on day three and skipping day four.

If you have ten minutes and nothing else, do the review cards. A day of only recall is worth far more than a day of only reading.

0.7 When a card won't stick SHOULD KNOW

Some cards you'll miss five, six, seven times. These are called leeches, and they eat a disproportionate share of your time. The handbook flags them for you.

Three fixes, in order:

The card is doing too much. "Explain the GIL" is not one fact, it's five. Break it into separate questions: what it is, why it exists, what it means for threads, what it means for processes.

You memorised words you don't understand. Go back to the section and read the why. A fact with no mechanism behind it has nothing to hang on. This is the most common cause by far.

You have no hook. Attach it to something concrete — a bug you've hit, a line in your own project, a comparison with a language you know. Facts with a connection are much harder to lose.

0.8 Six mistakes that waste the month MUST KNOW

  1. Flipping the card before really trying. The most common one and the most costly. Sit in the discomfort for a few seconds.
  2. Answering in your head instead of out loud. Silent answers are always more complete than spoken ones — that's the illusion.
  3. Grading generously. "I basically knew that" is a Hard at best, usually an Again.
  4. Skipping review to read more. Reading feels like progress. Retrieval is progress.
  5. Blocking one topic all week. Feels efficient, kills recognition. Follow the plan's mixed order.
  6. Cramming after falling behind. If you miss three days, don't do three days at once. Do today's review plus one day's reading and let the schedule catch up. The system is designed to absorb gaps.

0.9 What good looks like

By week three you should be able to look at a card question and produce a complete spoken answer in under fifteen seconds, most of the time. Not recognise it. Produce it.

That's the same motion as an interviewer asking a question and you answering. Which is the whole point: you haven't been studying the material, you've been rehearsing the performance.

How to Use This Handbook

What to study, in what order, and what to skip. Read this first — it is the map for everything else.

Suggested time · 15 min

Your single study resource for one month. Read this page first — it tells you what to study, in what order, and what to skip.

How this handbook is built

Every topic follows the same shape so you can skim or go deep:

WHAT → WHY → PROBLEM IT SOLVES → HOW → WHEN → WHEN NOT → CODE → INTERVIEW → FOLLOW-UP → COMMON MISTAKES → ENGINEER'S PERSPECTIVE

Not every topic gets all eleven. Small topics get four. Big ones get all of them.

Priority labels

Label Meaning Time budget
MUST KNOW MUST KNOW You will be asked this. Not knowing it fails the round. 60% of your time
SHOULD KNOW SHOULD KNOW Comes up often. Separates "passed" from "strong hire". 30%
NICE TO KNOW NICE TO KNOW Occasional. Skip if short on time. 10%

If you are ever unsure what to do next: do the MUST KNOW items in the order below.

Contents

Part Topic Priority Est. study time
1 How Full Stack SDE interviews actually work; communication framework MUST 1.5 h (read twice)
2 Python — fundamentals to advanced, plus "logic you must write without help" MUST 20 h
3 JavaScript — closures, this, event loop, async, output questions MUST 8 h
4 React — hooks, re-renders, memoisation, architecture MUST 10 h
5 Web, HTTP and REST APIs — auth, JWT, CORS, caching, idempotency MUST 5 h
6 Backend development with Python — layering, FastAPI, transactions SHOULD 8 h
7 SQL — joins, window functions, indexes, the ten classic problems MUST 8 h
8 DSA — patterns, recognition signals, curated 45-problem set MUST 30 h
9 System design — framework plus eight case studies SHOULD 10 h
10 Project interview preparation MUST 3 h

12 Software engineering principles — SOLID, coupling, useful patterns SHOULD 2 h
13 Follow-up trees and question bank SHOULD rolling
14 How to answer like a real engineer MUST 1 h
15 The 30-day preparation plan — —
16 The 7-day plan — —
17 The one-day emergency revision — —
18 Cheat sheets — —
19 Mock interview mode — four full mocks MUST 6 h

The three shortest paths

One month: follow the Part 15 plan exactly. Don't improvise.

One week: Part 16. You will skip system design depth, Redux internals, and DP beyond the base patterns.

One day: Part 17. Read it once in the morning, once at night. Nothing else.

The one thing that matters most

Interviewers are not checking whether you know the answer. They are checking whether they'd want to debug a production incident with you at 2am.

That means, in every round:

  1. Restate the problem before solving it.
  2. Say the brute force out loud, then say why it's not good enough.
  3. Name the trade-off you're making, not just the choice.
  4. Say "I don't know, here's how I'd find out" instead of guessing confidently.

A candidate who solves 80% of the problem while narrating clearly beats one who silently solves 100%. This is not motivational fluff — it is the actual scoring rubric at most companies.

Part 1

How Full Stack SDE Interviews Actually Work

The pipeline, the rubric interviewers actually score against, and a communication framework you can use in every round.

Suggested time · 1.5 h

MUST KNOW MUST KNOW. Read this before you study anything technical, and again the night before your interview.

1. The actual pipeline

Resume screen
      |
Online assessment / DSA screen
      |
Coding round 1  -- DSA + Python
      |
Coding round 2  -- practical / debugging / API
      |
Frontend round  -- JS + React
      |
Backend + SQL round
      |
System design
      |
Project deep-dive
      |
Hiring manager / behavioural

Not every company runs all nine. Typical shapes:

Company type Rounds you'll actually get
Startup (10–100 people) 1 DSA screen, 1 practical build/debug, 1 project deep-dive, 1 founder chat
Mid-size product company OA → 2 DSA → 1 frontend → 1 backend/SQL → 1 design → HM
Fintech / trading firm Heavier on SQL, correctness, edge cases, concurrency; lighter on frontend
Service/consulting Breadth over depth. Many small questions across Python/SQL/React/Git
Big tech 2 DSA, 1 design, 1 behavioural, sometimes a domain round

Implication for you: the DSA screen is the gate. Everything else is the decision. Most candidates fail at the gate, so 08-dsa.md gets the most hours — but the offer is decided by rounds 4–8, so don't neglect them.

2. What the interviewer is actually scoring

Almost every rubric collapses to five axes:

Axis What "weak" looks like What "strong" looks like
Problem solving Jumps to code, gets stuck, restarts States brute force, identifies the bottleneck, improves deliberately
Coding Syntax errors, no naming discipline, doesn't compile mentally Clean names, handles edges, code that reads like prose
Communication Silence, or narrating keystrokes ("now I write a for loop") Narrating decisions ("I'm using a dict here so lookup is O(1) instead of scanning")
Technical depth Correct answer, no reasoning behind it Correct answer + the trade-off + when it would be wrong
Signal of experience Ignores errors, no tests, no scale awareness Mentions failure modes, validates input, thinks about what breaks at 100×

Callout — the single biggest differentiator Weak candidates answer the question. Strong candidates answer the question and volunteer the constraint under which the answer changes. That's it. That's the whole trick, and it works in every round.

3. The communication framework (memorise this)

For coding rounds — R-E-B-O-C-T

Step Say out loud Time
Restate "So I'm given an array of ints and a target, and I return the two indices that sum to it — is that right?" 20s
Edge cases + clarify "Can the array be empty? Are there duplicates? Is exactly one answer guaranteed? Negative numbers?" 40s
Brute force "The obvious approach is a nested loop, O(n²). Let me start there so we have something correct." 30s
Optimise "The waste is that I re-scan for the complement each time. If I store what I've seen in a hash map, lookup becomes O(1) — that gets me to O(n) time, O(n) space." 1–2 min
Code Write it while narrating decisions only, not syntax 8–12 min
Test Walk a small input through by hand, out loud. Then an edge case. 2–3 min

Total ≈ 20 min for a medium. If you're over time at the "O" step, say: "I have an O(n) idea but let me code the O(n²) first so we have a working baseline" — this reads as maturity, not weakness.

For conceptual questions — D-M-T

Definition (one sentence) → Mechanism (how it works) → Trade-off (when it's wrong).

Example — "What is an index?"

"An index is a separate data structure, usually a B-tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the table. It maps column values to row locations, so a lookup goes from O(n) to roughly O(log n). The trade-off is that every insert, update and delete has to maintain the index too, and it costs disk space — so indexing a high-write, low-read column usually makes things worse."

Three sentences. Definition, mechanism, trade-off. Do this for every concept and you will sound senior.

For system design — R-C-B-D-T (expanded in 09-system-design.md)

Requirement → Constraint → Bottleneck → Design decision → Trade-off.

4. What to say when you don't know

Never say "I don't know" and stop. Never bluff. Use one of these four:

A. Adjacent knowledge

"I haven't used Celery in production, but I understand the problem it solves — moving slow work out of the request cycle. I've done the same thing with a background task in FastAPI. What I'd want to learn is how it handles retries and dead letters."

B. Reason from first principles

"I don't know the exact answer, but let me reason about it. If the write has to be durable before we respond, then we can't ack until the disk flush returns, which means..."

C. Bound the uncertainty

"I'm fairly confident the answer is X, maybe 70%. The part I'm unsure about is whether Y also applies. Should I proceed on the assumption that X holds?"

D. Ask to move on honestly

"That's a gap for me — I haven't worked with WebSockets at scale. I'd rather be straight about it than guess. Can I show you how I'd approach the same problem with polling and then you can tell me what changes?"

Callout: Interviewers write "honest about gaps" as a positive in their notes. They write "confidently wrong" as a hard no. Bluffing is the single most expensive mistake in an interview.

5. How to think aloud without being annoying

Bad narration is describing your typing:

❌ "Okay so now I'm making a variable called result, and it's going to be an empty list, and now a for loop..."

Good narration is describing your choices and doubts:

✅ "I'm keeping a running max instead of sorting, because I only need one pass. — Hmm, that breaks if the array is empty, so I'll guard that. — I'm using a set rather than a list here because I only need membership, not order."

Rule of thumb: if the code already says it, don't say it. If the code doesn't say it, say it.

When you go quiet to think (which is fine), announce it:

"Give me twenty seconds, I want to think about whether the sliding window is valid when values can be negative."

6. How to ask clarifying questions

Ask 2–4, not 10. The good ones fall into five buckets:

Bucket Example
Input shape "Is the array sorted? Can it be empty? What's the max size?"
Value domain "Can values be negative? Can they be zero? Unicode or ASCII?"
Output contract "Do I return the index or the value? What do I return if there's no answer — None or -1?"
Duplicates/uniqueness "Can the same element appear twice? Is the answer guaranteed unique?"
Constraints "Is n up to 10³ or 10⁹?" ← this one tells you the required complexity

That last one is a cheat code. n ≤ 10⁵ means you need O(n log n) or better. n ≤ 10³ means O(n²) is acceptable. Ask it and the interviewer has effectively told you the answer's shape.

Never ask: "What language should I use?" (pick Python, say so), or questions the problem statement already answers (signals you didn't read it).

7. How to recover from a mistake

Mistakes are not disqualifying. Handling them badly is. The recovery script:

  1. Notice it out loud. "Wait — this fails when the window shrinks past the start. Let me trace it."
  2. Don't panic-delete. Keep the code, fix the specific line.
  3. Say what class of bug it was. "Classic off-by-one on the right boundary — I should have used a half-open interval from the start."
  4. Move on. No apologising twice.

If the interviewer catches it before you do:

✅ "Good catch — you're right, let me trace what happens with [1]. ... Yes, right goes out of bounds. I'll change the loop condition to right < len(nums)."

Not:

❌ "Oh sorry, sorry, I'm so bad at this, let me start over."

Self-flagellation costs you points. Composure earns them.

8. How follow-up questions work (and why they're a good sign)

Follow-ups are not an attack. They mean the interviewer has already banked your first answer and is probing the ceiling of your knowledge. Getting follow-ups is good. Running out of answers three levels deep is normal and fine.

Interviewers drill along predictable axes:

                 |-- SCALE:       what happens at 10x?
                 |-- FAILURE:     what if it goes down?
Your answer -----|-- ALTERNATIVE: why not X instead?
                 |-- INTERNAL:    how does it actually work?
                 \-- COST:        what does it cost you?

Example follow-up tree — "Why did you use Redis?"

Level Question Strong answer core
1 Why Redis? Read-heavy, rarely-changing data; caching cuts DB load and p99 latency
2 What if Redis goes down? Cache-aside means we fall through to the DB — degraded, not broken. But we must guard against a thundering herd; I'd use a short lock or request coalescing on cache miss
3 What if the cached data goes stale? Depends on tolerance. TTL for "eventually right is fine"; explicit invalidation on write for "must be right"
4 How would you invalidate it? Delete the key on write (not update — updating risks a race with a concurrent read repopulating an old value)
5 Traffic 10×? Redis is single-threaded per core; first check whether it's CPU, memory, or network bound. Then: read replicas for read scaling, or Redis Cluster to shard by key
6 What breaks when you shard? Multi-key operations and transactions stop working across slots. You'd use hash tags to co-locate related keys

You are not expected to reach level 6. Reaching level 3–4 confidently is a strong hire signal.

Follow-up trees for every major topic are in 13-question-bank.md.

9. Round-by-round survival notes

DSA round. Talk before you type. Get a solution before the perfect one. Test by hand.

Python/programming round. Expect: mutable default arguments, shallow vs deep copy, generators, decorators, GIL, is vs ==. These six come up constantly. All covered in 02-python.md.

JS/React round. Expect: closures, event loop output ordering, useEffect dependency bugs, why a component re-renders, useMemo vs useCallback. They will often show you buggy code and ask what's wrong.

Backend/API round. Expect: design a REST API for X, then "how do you authenticate it", "what if the client retries", "how do you paginate". Idempotency is the question people fluff most.

SQL round. Expect: a join, then a GROUP BY … HAVING, then a window function (top-N-per-group or running total). Then "how would you make this fast" → indexes.

System design. Requirements first. Always. Candidates who draw boxes before asking questions lose immediately.

Project round. They will find the weakest technical decision in your project and push on it. Prepare for that specific push — see 10-project-interview.md.

10. Logistics that quietly cost people offers

  • Test your screen share, camera, and internet the day before, not five minutes before.
  • Have a plain text editor open. Some interviews use a shared pad with no autocomplete — practise writing Python without an IDE at least five times.
  • Keep water and paper next to you. Drawing on paper and holding it to camera is fine and often helps.
  • If you use an online judge to practise, turn off autocomplete for the last week.
  • Have 2–3 questions ready for them that aren't about salary: "What does the on-call rotation look like?", "What's the last thing that broke in production and what changed after?"

Summary card

Situation Do this
Given a problem Restate → clarify → brute force → optimise → code → test
Asked a concept Definition → mechanism → trade-off
Don't know Adjacent knowledge / first principles / bound uncertainty / honest gap
Made a mistake Notice aloud → fix the line → name the bug class → move on
Getting follow-ups Good sign. Answer 3 levels, then say where your knowledge ends
Stuck and silent "Let me think for twenty seconds about X"
Design question Requirements before boxes. Always.

Part 2

Python: Complete Interview Preparation

From the name-binding mental model through OOP, decorators, generators and the GIL — plus the traps that catch candidates.

Suggested time · 20 h

The largest section, deliberately. Python is your primary language for coding rounds and a dedicated interview topic on its own.

How to use this file: read 2.1–2.4 once properly. Then treat 2.5 (Advanced) as your revision target — that's where interviews live. Section 2.7 is code you must be able to write with no help.

2.0 The mental model that makes Python make sense

Almost every Python "gotcha" comes from one fact:

A variable is not a box. It is a name tag tied to an object.

x = [1, 2, 3] does not put a list into x. It creates a list object somewhere in memory and ties the name x to it. y = x ties a second name to the same object.

   name: x ----\
                 ---->  [ list object: 1, 2, 3 ]
   name: y ----/

Once you internalise this, the following stop being surprising: - Mutating through one name is visible through the other. - == compares contents; is compares whether two names point at the same object. - Default arguments are evaluated once, so a mutable default is shared forever. - "Passing by reference or value?" — neither. Python passes the name binding.

Say this out loud in an interview and you immediately sound like someone who's actually thought about the language.

2.1 Fundamentals MUST KNOW

2.1.1 Dynamic typing

WHAT — Types belong to objects, not to names. A name can be rebound to a different type at any time.

WHY — Faster to write, less ceremony. The cost is that type errors surface at runtime.

HOW — CPython stores a type pointer on every object. type(x) reads it.

x = 5          # x -> int object
x = "hello"    # x now -> str object; the int is unreferenced

WHEN NOT — On a large codebase or a public API, dynamic typing becomes a liability. Use type hints (§2.5.12).

INTERVIEW — "Is Python strongly or weakly typed?"

Strongly typed, and dynamically typed. Dynamic means the type is checked at runtime, not compile time. Strong means Python won't silently coerce across incompatible types — "5" + 5 raises a TypeError rather than guessing. JavaScript is weakly typed; it would give "55".

That distinction trips up a lot of candidates. Learn it.

2.1.2 Mutable vs immutable MUST KNOW (the single most-tested Python concept)

Immutable Mutable
int, float, bool, str, tuple, frozenset, bytes, None list, dict, set, bytearray, most custom classes

WHY does immutability exist? Three concrete reasons, and interviewers like all three: 1. Hashability — a dict key must not change after insertion, or you'd never find it again. Immutable objects can safely be hashed. 2. Safety — you can pass an immutable object anywhere without worrying that the callee mutates it. 3. Optimisation — CPython can cache and reuse small ints and short strings because nobody can change them.

HOW it shows up

def add_item(items):
    items.append(4)        # mutates the caller's list

nums = [1, 2, 3]
add_item(nums)
print(nums)                # [1, 2, 3, 4]  <- caller was changed

def add_number(n):
    n += 1                 # rebinds the local name only

x = 5
add_number(x)
print(x)                   # 5  <- unchanged

Both functions "do the same thing". The difference is entirely whether the object supports mutation.

COMMON MISTAKE — mutable default argument MUST KNOW asked constantly

def add(item, bucket=[]):      # BUG
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

add(1)   # [1]
add(2)   # [1, 2]  <-- surprising

The default list is created once, when the def statement executes, and reused on every call.

def add(item, bucket=None):    # CORRECT
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

FOLLOW-UP: "When would the buggy version actually be useful?" — As a crude memoisation cache. But use functools.lru_cache instead; it's explicit.

INTERVIEW — "Why can a tuple be a dict key but a list can't?"

Dict keys must be hashable, and hash must stay stable for the object's lifetime. Lists are mutable, so their contents — and therefore any content-based hash — could change while they sit in the dict, and you'd never retrieve the entry again. Python makes lists unhashable to prevent that. Careful though: a tuple is only hashable if everything inside it is. (1, [2]) raises TypeError.

2.1.3 is vs == MUST KNOW

== asks "do these have the same value?" (calls __eq__). is asks "are these the same object?" (compares identity/address).

a = [1, 2]; b = [1, 2]
a == b   # True
a is b   # False

x = 256; y = 256
x is y   # True   <- CPython caches small ints (-5..256)
x = 257; y = 257
x is y   # False in a script; may be True in a REPL line

Rule: use is only for None, True, False, and sentinel objects. Use == for everything else.

INTERVIEW gotcha — "Why does x is y behave differently for 256 and 257?"

CPython pre-allocates integer objects from −5 to 256 as a memory optimisation, so all references to 256 point at the same object. 257 gets a fresh object each time. It's an implementation detail of CPython, not part of the language spec — which is exactly why you shouldn't rely on is for value comparison.

2.1.4 Truthiness

Falsy: False, None, 0, 0.0, "", [], {}, (), set(), and any object whose __bool__ or __len__ returns false.

COMMON MISTAKE:

def f(items=None):
    if not items:      # BUG: an empty list and None take the same branch
        ...
    if items is None:  # correct when you mean "not provided"
        ...

INTERVIEW — "What's wrong with if len(x) > 0:?" Nothing wrong, but if x: is idiomatic and works for any container. Prefer it unless you specifically need to distinguish empty from None.

2.1.5 Strings MUST KNOW

Immutable. Every "modification" builds a new string.

PERFORMANCE TRAP — asked often:

# O(n^2): each += copies the whole string
s = ""
for word in words:
    s += word

# O(n): join allocates once
s = "".join(words)

Interview line: "Because strings are immutable, += in a loop is quadratic — each concatenation allocates a new string and copies everything so far. str.join computes the total length once and copies each piece once, so it's linear."

Methods worth having in muscle memory:

Method Use
.split() / .split(",") tokenise; no-arg splits on any whitespace and drops empties
.strip() .lstrip() .rstrip() trim
.join(iterable) build strings
.replace(a, b) substitute
.startswith() .endswith() prefix/suffix; accepts a tuple
.lower() .upper() .casefold() normalise (casefold for aggressive Unicode folding)
.find() vs .index() find returns −1, index raises
.isdigit() .isalpha() .isalnum() validation
f-strings f"{name} scored {score:.2f}"

Slicing: s[start:stop:step], stop exclusive. s[::-1] reverses. Negative indices count from the end. Out-of-range slices don't raise (unlike indexing).

2.1.6 Lists, tuples, sets, dicts — what they are for

list tuple set dict
Ordered ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ (insertion order, 3.7+)
Mutable ✅ ❌ ✅ ✅
Duplicates ✅ ✅ ❌ keys unique
Indexable ✅ ✅ ❌ by key
Hashable (usable as dict key) ❌ ✅* ❌ (frozenset ✅) ❌

* only if its contents are hashable.

Why choose a set over a list?

Membership testing. x in list is O(n) — it scans. x in set is O(1) average — it hashes and jumps. If you're doing membership checks inside a loop, using a list turns an O(n) algorithm into O(n²). That single swap is the most common optimisation in coding interviews.

Why choose a dict over a list?

When you need lookup by an arbitrary key rather than by position, and when you need to associate data. A list of (id, record) pairs requires a scan; a dict keyed by id is O(1).

Why choose a tuple over a list?

Three reasons: it signals "this shouldn't change" to readers, it can be used as a dict key or set element, and it's slightly smaller and faster to construct. Use tuples for fixed-shape records (a coordinate, a DB row) and lists for homogeneous collections you'll grow.

2.1.7 Loops and the iteration toolkit MUST KNOW

for i in range(n)                  # 0..n-1
for i in range(1, n)               # 1..n-1
for i in range(n-1, -1, -1)        # reverse

for item in items                  # values
for i, item in enumerate(items)    # index + value
for i, item in enumerate(items, start=1)

for a, b in zip(list_a, list_b)    # parallel; stops at the shorter one
for a, b in zip(list_a, list_b, strict=True)  # 3.10+: raises on length mismatch

for k in d                         # keys
for v in d.values()
for k, v in d.items()

COMMON MISTAKE — mutating a list while iterating it:

for item in items:
    if bad(item):
        items.remove(item)   # BUG: skips elements

items = [i for i in items if not bad(i)]   # correct

for ... else NICE TO KNOW — the else runs only if the loop finished without break. Rare, occasionally asked as trivia.

2.1.8 Comprehensions MUST KNOW

squares   = [x*x for x in nums]
evens     = [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]
labelled  = ["even" if x % 2 == 0 else "odd" for x in nums]   # ternary goes before the for
flat      = [x for row in matrix for x in row]                # left-to-right = nesting order
by_id     = {u["id"]: u for u in users}
unique    = {x % 3 for x in nums}
lazy      = (x*x for x in nums)                               # generator, not a tuple

WHEN NOT to use one: if it needs more than one if, a nested for and a transformation, or wraps past ~80 characters — write a loop. Interviewers mark unreadable comprehensions down, not up.

Interview line: "I'd use a comprehension here because it's a pure map/filter with no side effects. If I needed to log or handle exceptions per item, I'd write an explicit loop instead — comprehensions can't express that cleanly."

2.1.9 Unpacking

a, b = b, a                        # swap, no temp
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]        # first=1, rest=[2,3,4]
*init, last = [1, 2, 3, 4]         # init=[1,2,3], last=4
(x, y), z = (1, 2), 3              # nested

def f(*args, **kwargs): ...
f(*my_list, **my_dict)             # splat at call site

merged = {**d1, **d2}              # d2 wins on conflicts
merged = d1 | d2                   # 3.9+, same thing

2.2 Functions MUST KNOW

2.2.1 Arguments

def create_user(name, email, *, role="user", active=True):
    ...
  • name, email — positional-or-keyword.
  • Everything after * is keyword-only. Use this for boolean/config flags so call sites read as create_user("A", "a@x.com", active=False) rather than create_user("A", "a@x.com", False).
  • / marks the end of positional-only params (3.8+): def f(a, b, /, c). NICE TO KNOW

Order in a signature: positional-only /, positional-or-keyword, *args, keyword-only, **kwargs.

2.2.2 *args and **kwargs

WHAT — collect extra positional args into a tuple and extra keyword args into a dict.

WHY they exist — writing wrappers and decorators that must forward arbitrary arguments they don't know about.

def log_call(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):        # accept anything
        print(f"calling {func.__name__}")
        return func(*args, **kwargs)     # forward it unchanged
    return wrapper

WHEN NOT — in your own domain functions. def create_order(**kwargs) destroys discoverability and type checking. Be explicit.

2.2.3 Scope and LEGB MUST KNOW

Name resolution order: Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in.

count = 0

def increment():
    count += 1          # UnboundLocalError

Assigning to count anywhere in the function makes it local for the whole function, so the read on the right-hand side finds an unassigned local.

def increment():
    global count        # module-level
    count += 1

def outer():
    count = 0
    def inner():
        nonlocal count  # nearest enclosing function scope
        count += 1
    inner()
    return count

INTERVIEW: "Difference between global and nonlocal?" → global binds to module scope; nonlocal binds to the nearest enclosing function scope and errors if there isn't one. Engineer's perspective: both are code smells in application code — if you need them, a class or a returned value is usually the better design.

2.2.4 Closures MUST KNOW

WHAT — a nested function that keeps access to variables from the enclosing scope after the outer function has returned.

WHY — it lets you build functions with pre-baked configuration without a class.

def make_multiplier(factor):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * factor      # 'factor' is captured
    return multiply

double = make_multiplier(2)
double(5)      # 10
double.__closure__[0].cell_contents   # 2  <- the captured cell

CLASSIC TRAP MUST KNOW — closures capture the variable, not its value at creation time:

funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
[f() for f in funcs]           # [2, 2, 2]  — all see the final i

funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]   # bind at definition time
[f() for f in funcs]           # [0, 1, 2]

This is the same bug people hit in JavaScript with var in a loop — good thing to point out, it shows cross-language understanding.

2.2.5 Decorators MUST KNOW (guaranteed to appear)

WHAT — a function that takes a function and returns a replacement function.

PROBLEM IT SOLVES — you want to add behaviour (timing, auth, retries, caching, logging) to many functions without editing each one and without copy-pasting the same wrapper code. It is the "cross-cutting concern" problem.

HOW — @decorator above def f is exactly f = decorator(f).

Level 1 — the basic shape:

import functools, time

def timer(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)                 # preserve __name__, __doc__, signature
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"{func.__name__} took {time.perf_counter() - start:.4f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper

@timer
def slow_query():
    time.sleep(0.1)
    return "done"

Why functools.wraps matters — without it, slow_query.__name__ becomes "wrapper". That breaks logging, debuggers, API framework introspection (FastAPI reads signatures!), and docs. Interviewers specifically look for this line.

Level 2 — decorator with arguments (one more layer of nesting):

def retry(times=3, delay=0.5):
    def decorator(func):
        @functools.wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            last = None
            for attempt in range(times):
                try:
                    return func(*args, **kwargs)
                except Exception as e:
                    last = e
                    time.sleep(delay * (2 ** attempt))   # exponential backoff
            raise last
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@retry(times=5, delay=0.2)
def fetch_price(symbol): ...

Read it outside-in: retry(times=5) returns decorator; decorator(fetch_price) returns wrapper; fetch_price now names wrapper.

Level 3 — stacking:

@log_call        # outermost — runs first
@timer           # innermost — wraps the real function
def handler(): ...

Applied bottom-up, executed top-down. Equivalent to handler = log_call(timer(handler)).

Built-in decorators you should know: @property, @staticmethod, @classmethod, @functools.lru_cache, @functools.cached_property, @dataclass, @abstractmethod.

COMMON MISTAKES 1. Forgetting functools.wraps. 2. Forgetting to return func(...) inside the wrapper — the decorated function silently returns None. 3. Forgetting to return wrapper from the decorator. 4. Using a decorator for something that should just be a function call.

FOLLOW-UP TREE

Q Strong answer
"Where have you used one?" Auth checks and request timing on FastAPI routes; lru_cache on a pure computation
"How do you decorate a method?" Same way — the wrapper's first positional arg is self and *args forwards it transparently
"How would you write a caching decorator?" Dict keyed by (args, frozenset(kwargs.items())); note that args must be hashable, which is why lru_cache rejects list arguments
"What's the runtime cost?" One extra function call per invocation — negligible unless it's in a tight numeric loop
"How do you turn one off in tests?" Keep a reference: func.__wrapped__ (set by functools.wraps) gives you the original

2.2.6 Lambda

One expression, no statements, no annotations. Use for tiny key functions:

sorted(users, key=lambda u: (-u["score"], u["name"]))

WHEN NOT: never assign a lambda to a name (f = lambda x: x+1) — just use def; it gives a real name in tracebacks. Interviewers notice.

The (-score, name) tuple trick is worth memorising: sort by score descending, then name ascending, in one pass. Works because tuples compare element-wise.

2.3 Data structures & complexity MUST KNOW

The table to memorise

Structure Access Search Insert Delete Typical use
list O(1) by index O(n) O(1) amortised at end, O(n) at front/middle O(n) (O(1) at end) ordered sequence, stack
tuple O(1) O(n) — — fixed record, dict key
set — O(1) avg O(1) avg O(1) avg dedupe, membership
dict O(1) avg by key O(1) avg O(1) avg O(1) avg key→value lookup, counting
collections.deque O(1) ends, O(n) middle O(n) O(1) both ends O(1) both ends queue, sliding window, BFS
heapq (list) O(1) peek min O(n) O(log n) push O(log n) pop min top-K, priority queue, merge
str O(1) O(n) — — text

Worst case for dict/set is O(n) under adversarial hash collisions. Say "average O(1), worst O(n)" and you'll sound precise.

Amortised O(1) — explain it like this

A Python list over-allocates. When it fills up it allocates a bigger block (roughly 1.125× plus a constant) and copies everything — that single append is O(n). But because the growth is geometric, that expensive copy happens rarely enough that the average cost per append across many appends is constant. That's what amortised means.

deque — why it exists

from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.append(4); q.appendleft(0)
q.pop(); q.popleft()
window = deque(maxlen=3)          # auto-evicts from the left

WHY: list.pop(0) is O(n) because every remaining element shifts left. A deque is a doubly-linked list of blocks, so both ends are O(1). If you write BFS with list.pop(0) your solution is O(V²); with a deque it's O(V+E). Interviewers watch for this.

WHEN NOT: random access in the middle is O(n). If you index a lot, use a list.

heapq — why it exists

import heapq
h = []
heapq.heappush(h, 5)
smallest = heapq.heappop(h)
heapq.heapify(lst)                        # O(n), in place
heapq.nlargest(3, items, key=...)         # top-K

WHY: you need repeated access to the minimum of a changing collection. Sorting costs O(n log n) each time the data changes; a heap gives you O(1) peek and O(log n) push/pop.

Python's heap is a min-heap only. For a max-heap, push negated values (heappush(h, -x)) or tuples (-priority, item).

Top-K pattern (memorise): to find the K largest, keep a min-heap of size K. Push each element; if the heap exceeds K, pop the smallest. O(n log k) time, O(k) space — better than sorting when k ≪ n.

collections you should actually know MUST KNOW

from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque, OrderedDict, namedtuple

Counter("mississippi").most_common(2)     # [('i',4), ('s',4)]
Counter(a) == Counter(b)                  # anagram check in one line

d = defaultdict(list)
d["k"].append(1)                          # no KeyError, no setdefault dance

d = defaultdict(int)
for c in text: d[c] += 1                  # manual counter

Counter and defaultdict will shorten half your DSA solutions. Counter supports +, -, &, |.

Dict methods worth knowing: .get(k, default), .setdefault(k, default), .pop(k, default), .items()/.keys()/.values() (views, not copies — they reflect later changes), {**a, **b}, dict.fromkeys(seq).

2.4 OOP in Python MUST KNOW

2.4.1 The basics with a realistic example

class Account:
    """A bank account. Demonstrates the whole OOP surface area."""

    interest_rate = 0.04                      # CLASS variable: shared by all instances

    def __init__(self, owner: str, balance: float = 0.0):
        self.owner = owner                    # INSTANCE variables: per object
        self._balance = balance               # single underscore = "internal, don't touch"

    # instance method — operates on one object
    def deposit(self, amount: float) -> None:
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("deposit must be positive")
        self._balance += amount

    # class method — alternative constructor; receives the class
    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, data: dict) -> "Account":
        return cls(data["owner"], data.get("balance", 0.0))

    # static method — related utility, needs neither self nor cls
    @staticmethod
    def is_valid_ifsc(code: str) -> bool:
        return len(code) == 11 and code[4] == "0"

    # property — computed attribute with attribute syntax
    @property
    def balance(self) -> float:
        return self._balance

    def __repr__(self) -> str:                # for developers/debugging
        return f"Account(owner={self.owner!r}, balance={self._balance})"

    def __str__(self) -> str:                 # for users
        return f"{self.owner}: ₹{self._balance:,.2f}"

    def __eq__(self, other) -> bool:
        if not isinstance(other, Account):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.owner == other.owner

self is not a keyword — it's just the conventional name for the first parameter, which Python passes automatically. a.deposit(100) is really Account.deposit(a, 100).

2.4.2 instance vs class vs static method MUST KNOW

Receives Use when Called on
instance method self needs object state instance
@classmethod cls alternative constructors, factory methods, anything touching class-level state; works correctly with subclasses class or instance
@staticmethod nothing logically grouped helper that needs no state class or instance

Interview line: "I use classmethod for alternative constructors because cls means a subclass gets an instance of itself back, not of the parent. staticmethod is really just namespacing — if it never grows to need state, a module-level function would do the same job."

Class variable gotcha MUST KNOW

class Team:
    members = []                 # BUG: shared by every Team
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

a, b = Team("A"), Team("B")
a.members.append("x")
b.members                        # ['x']  <- leaked

Fix: assign mutable state inside __init__ (self.members = []). Same bug family as the mutable default argument.

Also: self.count += 1 where count is a class variable creates a new instance variable shadowing the class one. To change the class-level value you need Team.count += 1.

2.4.3 The four pillars, stated for interviews

Pillar One-line definition Python mechanism
Encapsulation Bundle data with the methods that operate on it; control access _private convention, __name_mangled, @property
Abstraction Expose what something does, hide how ABCs, interfaces, well-named methods
Inheritance A subclass reuses and specialises a base class class Child(Parent), super()
Polymorphism Different types respond to the same call in their own way duck typing, method overriding

Python's twist — duck typing: Python doesn't need a shared base class for polymorphism. If it has .read(), it's readable. "If it walks like a duck…" This is why Python has no interface keyword; ABCs (abc.ABC + @abstractmethod) exist for when you want the contract enforced.

Encapsulation in Python is by convention, not enforcement: - _x — "internal, don't rely on it." Nothing stops you. - __x — name-mangled to _ClassName__x. Purpose is avoiding accidental collisions in subclasses, not security. Say this precisely; candidates often claim it makes things "private", which is wrong.

2.4.4 @property — WHY it exists

PROBLEM IT SOLVES: you shipped account.balance as a plain attribute. Later you need validation or a computed value. Without properties you'd have to change every call site to get_balance(). Properties let you swap the implementation while keeping the attribute syntax.

class Order:
    def __init__(self, price, qty):
        self.price = price
        self.qty = qty

    @property
    def total(self):                 # computed, always consistent
        return self.price * self.qty

    @property
    def qty(self):
        return self._qty

    @qty.setter
    def qty(self, value):
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("qty cannot be negative")
        self._qty = value

WHEN NOT: if the getter is expensive, a property hides a costly call behind cheap-looking syntax. Either use functools.cached_property or make it an explicit method so callers know it costs something.

2.4.5 Inheritance, super(), and MRO

class BaseRepository:
    def __init__(self, session):
        self.session = session

    def get(self, id):
        raise NotImplementedError

class UserRepository(BaseRepository):
    def __init__(self, session, cache):
        super().__init__(session)       # always call super first
        self.cache = cache

    def get(self, id):                  # override
        if id in self.cache:
            return self.cache[id]
        return self.session.query(User).get(id)

MRO (Method Resolution Order) — with multiple inheritance, Python linearises the class graph using C3 linearisation; super() follows that chain, not simply "the parent". Check with Cls.__mro__.

The diamond problem: D(B, C) where both inherit A. Python's MRO is D → B → C → A → object, and A.__init__ runs once, provided every class cooperates by calling super().__init__(). That's the reason super() is preferred over Parent.__init__(self).

2.4.6 Composition over inheritance MUST KNOW — the answer interviewers want

# Inheritance — fragile: is a UserService really a kind of Database?
class UserService(Database):
    ...

# Composition — flexible: a UserService HAS a database
class UserService:
    def __init__(self, db: Database, cache: Cache, mailer: Mailer):
        self.db = db
        self.cache = cache
        self.mailer = mailer

Interview line: "Inheritance is an 'is-a' relationship and it permanently couples you to the parent's implementation — a change in the base class can break subclasses you've never looked at. Composition is 'has-a': you depend on a small interface, you can swap the implementation, and you can inject a fake in tests. I reach for inheritance only when there's a genuine substitutable type hierarchy, and for shared behaviour I prefer composition."

Aggregation vs composition (occasionally asked): composition = the part can't outlive the whole (an Order and its OrderLines). Aggregation = the part exists independently (a Team and its Employees).

2.4.7 Dunder methods worth knowing

Dunder Enables
__init__ construction
__repr__ / __str__ debugging output / user output
__eq__ + __hash__ value equality; use in sets/dict keys
__len__ len(obj), truthiness
__getitem__ / __setitem__ obj[k]
__iter__ / __next__ for x in obj
__contains__ x in obj
__enter__ / __exit__ with obj:
__call__ obj()
__lt__ sorting, heap ordering

Rule: if you define __eq__, Python sets __hash__ to None and your object becomes unhashable. Define both, or use @dataclass(frozen=True).

2.5 Advanced concepts MUST KNOW — this is where Python rounds are won

2.5.1 Iterable vs iterator MUST KNOW

  • Iterable — anything with __iter__; can be looped over repeatedly. (list, dict, str)
  • Iterator — has __iter__ and __next__; holds position; consumed once.
nums = [1, 2, 3]        # iterable
it = iter(nums)         # iterator
next(it)                # 1
list(it)                # [2, 3]
list(it)                # []  <- exhausted

Interview: "Why can I loop over a list twice but a generator only once?" → for calls iter() on the list each time, getting a fresh iterator. A generator is the iterator; iter(gen) is gen, so there's nothing to reset.

2.5.2 Generators and yield MUST KNOW

PROBLEM IT SOLVES: producing a sequence without materialising it in memory, and expressing lazy/infinite streams.

def read_large_file(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            yield line.strip()       # one line in memory at a time

def fibonacci():
    a, b = 0, 1
    while True:                      # infinite is fine — it's lazy
        yield a
        a, b = b, a + b

HOW it works: calling a generator function runs no code — it returns a generator object. Each next() runs until the next yield, then freezes the entire local state (variables, instruction pointer) and hands the value back. StopIteration is raised when the function returns.

WHEN — large or unbounded data, pipelines, when the consumer may stop early. WHEN NOT — you need len(), indexing, or multiple passes; or the dataset is small and you'd rather have a list.

# generator pipeline: constant memory over a huge file
lines   = read_large_file("trades.csv")
parsed  = (line.split(",") for line in lines)
big     = (p for p in parsed if float(p[3]) > 1_000_000)
total   = sum(float(p[3]) for p in big)

yield from delegates to a sub-iterable:

def flatten(nested):
    for item in nested:
        if isinstance(item, list):
            yield from flatten(item)
        else:
            yield item

FOLLOW-UPS

Q Answer
Memory difference vs a list? List holds all n items; generator holds one item plus frame state — O(n) vs O(1) space
Can you restart one? No. Call the generator function again for a fresh one
Generator vs yield returning a list? A function that builds and returns a list is eager; if the caller only needs the first item you've done all the work for nothing
Real use? Streaming a CSV/DB cursor, paginated API results, range() itself is lazy

2.5.3 Context managers and with MUST KNOW

PROBLEM IT SOLVES: guaranteed cleanup. Without it, an exception between "acquire" and "release" leaks the resource.

with open("f.txt") as f:      # file closed even if an exception is raised
    data = f.read()

Class form:

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self                       # bound to the 'as' name

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, tb):
        self.elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start
        return False                      # False = don't suppress exceptions

Decorator form (preferred for simple cases):

from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def transaction(session):
    try:
        yield session          # everything before yield = __enter__
        session.commit()
    except Exception:
        session.rollback()     # everything after = __exit__
        raise
    finally:
        session.close()

Gotcha worth knowing: returning a truthy value from __exit__ swallows the exception. Almost always a bug. Say this and you look like you've read the docs.

2.5.4 Exceptions MUST KNOW

try:
    risky()
except ValueError as e:            # most specific first
    log.warning("bad value: %s", e)
    raise                          # re-raise, preserving the traceback
except (KeyError, IndexError) as e:
    handle(e)
else:
    # runs only if no exception — keep the try block minimal
    commit()
finally:
    cleanup()                      # always runs

Custom exceptions — why bother:

class AppError(Exception): ...
class InsufficientFunds(AppError):
    def __init__(self, required, available):
        self.required, self.available = required, available
        super().__init__(f"need {required}, have {available}")

Callers can catch your domain error specifically instead of a bare Exception, and carry structured data. A single app-wide base class lets an API layer map all domain errors to HTTP responses in one place.

COMMON MISTAKES - except: or except Exception: swallowing everything — hides bugs and catches KeyboardInterrupt with a bare except. - raise e instead of bare raise — resets the traceback. Use raise NewError(...) from e to chain. - Using exceptions for ordinary control flow. - Putting the whole function inside try so you can't tell which line failed.

EAFP vs LBYL — Python prefers Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission:

try:                       # EAFP — idiomatic, no TOCTOU race
    value = d[key]
except KeyError:
    value = default

if key in d:               # LBYL — two lookups, race-prone in concurrent code
    value = d[key]

2.5.5 Shallow vs deep copy MUST KNOW

import copy
original = {"user": "sri", "tags": ["a", "b"]}

shallow = copy.copy(original)         # or dict(original), original.copy(), [:]
deep    = copy.deepcopy(original)

shallow["tags"].append("c")           # original["tags"] also changes
deep["tags"].append("d")              # original untouched

Shallow copy makes a new outer container but the elements are the same objects. Deep copy recursively clones everything. Deep copy is slow and can break on objects holding sockets, DB connections, or cycles — deepcopy handles cycles via a memo dict, but not unclonable resources. In production I usually prefer constructing a fresh object explicitly over deepcopy.

2.5.6 Memory: reference counting and GC SHOULD KNOW

Every object has a refcount. It reaches 0 → freed immediately.
Reference cycles (a → b → a) never reach 0 → a generational
cycle collector sweeps them periodically (3 generations, gen0 most often).

Interview: "Why does Python need a GC if it has refcounting?" → refcounting alone can't free cycles. Follow-up: "How do you avoid cycles?" → weakref for back-pointers (parent links, caches, observers).

2.5.7 The GIL MUST KNOW (asked in almost every Python round)

WHAT — the Global Interpreter Lock: a mutex in CPython that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time.

WHY it exists — CPython's memory management (refcounting) isn't thread-safe. The GIL makes it safe with one coarse lock rather than fine-grained locking on every object, which would be slower for single-threaded code and much more complex.

CONSEQUENCE

Workload Threads help? Use
CPU-bound (math, parsing, image processing) ❌ no speedup, sometimes slower multiprocessing, or a C/NumPy library that releases the GIL
I/O-bound (HTTP calls, DB queries, file reads) ✅ yes threading or asyncio

The GIL is released during blocking I/O and inside many C extensions (NumPy, hashlib), which is why threads do help for I/O and NumPy work.

FOLLOW-UP TREE

Q Answer
Why not remove it? Attempts have; fine-grained locking historically slowed single-threaded code ~2×. Python 3.13 ships an experimental free-threaded build (PEP 703) making it optional — still maturing
So Python can't do parallelism? It can — separate processes have separate GILs. Cost is IPC and memory
asyncio vs threading? Both for I/O. asyncio is cooperative, single-threaded, cheaper per task (thousands of coroutines vs hundreds of threads), but one blocking call stalls everything
Is it a language feature? No — a CPython implementation detail. Jython and IronPython have no GIL

2.5.8 Threading, multiprocessing, asyncio SHOULD KNOW

# I/O-bound: threads
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as ex:
    results = list(ex.map(fetch_url, urls))

# CPU-bound: processes
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex:
    results = list(ex.map(heavy_computation, chunks))

# I/O-bound, high concurrency: asyncio
import asyncio, aiohttp

async def fetch(session, url):
    async with session.get(url) as r:
        return await r.json()

async def main(urls):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as s:
        return await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(s, u) for u in urls))

The one asyncio rule that matters: never call a blocking function inside a coroutine. time.sleep(1) blocks the entire event loop; await asyncio.sleep(1) doesn't. If you must call blocking code, use await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...).

Interview: "What is the event loop?" → A single-threaded scheduler. When a coroutine hits await on something not ready, it yields control back to the loop, which runs another ready task. Concurrency without parallelism.

2.5.9 functools worth knowing

from functools import lru_cache, cache, wraps, partial, reduce, cached_property

@lru_cache(maxsize=128)         # memoisation; args must be hashable
def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)

fib.cache_info()                # hits/misses — nice to mention
fib.cache_clear()

add_five = partial(add, 5)      # pre-bind arguments

lru_cache is the cleanest way to demonstrate memoisation in a DP interview question — but be ready to write the explicit dict version too, because some interviewers want to see the mechanism.

2.5.10 Modules, packages, virtual environments SHOULD KNOW

  • A module is a .py file; a package is a directory (historically with __init__.py).
  • if __name__ == "__main__": — the module's name is "__main__" only when run directly, so this guards code that shouldn't execute on import. Always asked.
  • Virtual environment — python -m venv .venv gives an isolated site-packages so project A's pandas==1.5 doesn't conflict with project B's 2.2. Pin with requirements.txt or pyproject.toml; lock for reproducibility.
  • Circular imports — usually a design smell; fix by extracting shared code, or import inside the function as a last resort.

2.5.11 dataclasses SHOULD KNOW

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Trade:
    symbol: str
    qty: int
    price: float
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # NOT tags: list = []

    @property
    def notional(self) -> float:
        return self.qty * self.price

Generates __init__, __repr__, __eq__ for you. frozen=True makes it immutable and hashable. field(default_factory=list) is the dataclass-level answer to the mutable-default problem — a nice callback to make in an interview.

2.5.12 Type hints SHOULD KNOW

def get_users(ids: list[int], active: bool = True) -> list[User]: ...
def find(id: int) -> User | None: ...          # 3.10+ union syntax

Hints are not enforced at runtime — they're for mypy, IDEs, and readers. FastAPI and Pydantic do use them at runtime for validation, which is the practical reason to care.

2.5.13 Logging and testing SHOULD KNOW

import logging
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
log.info("order created: %s", order_id)    # lazy %s formatting, not f-string

Why not f-strings in log calls? The f-string is evaluated even when the level is disabled. %s args are only formatted if the record is actually emitted.

Never use print in application code — no levels, no timestamps, no handlers, no way to route to a file or aggregator.

import pytest

def test_deposit_rejects_negative():
    acct = Account("sri")
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        acct.deposit(-10)

@pytest.mark.parametrize("amount,expected", [(100, 100), (50, 50)])
def test_deposit(amount, expected):
    acct = Account("sri")
    acct.deposit(amount)
    assert acct.balance == expected

Know: AAA (Arrange–Act–Assert), fixtures, parametrize, mocking external calls, and the unit/integration distinction. That's enough for a full stack interview.

2.6 Python traps quick-reference MUST KNOW

Read this page the morning of the interview.

Trap What happens Fix
def f(x, lst=[]) default shared across calls lst=None then lst = lst or []
class C: items = [] shared across instances assign in __init__
s += x in a loop O(n²) "".join(parts)
for x in lst: lst.remove(x) skips elements build a new list
[lambda: i for i in range(3)] all return 2 lambda i=i: i
copy.copy on nested data inner objects shared copy.deepcopy
a is b for values works for small ints, fails for 257 use ==
d[k] on a missing key KeyError d.get(k, default) / defaultdict
except: bare swallows KeyboardInterrupt, hides bugs catch specific types
list.pop(0) in BFS O(n) each, O(n²) total deque.popleft()
sort() vs sorted() sort() returns None, mutates sorted() returns a new list
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 False — binary float math.isclose, or Decimal for money
range in Python 3 lazy, not a list list(range(n)) if you need one
Integer division 7/2 == 3.5, 7//2 == 3, -7//2 == -4 (floors) use int() to truncate toward zero
x = y = [] both names, one list separate assignments
Dict ordering insertion-ordered since 3.7 (guaranteed) fine to rely on now

2.7 Python logic you must be able to write without help MUST KNOW

If you can write all of these from memory in under five minutes each, you will not freeze in a coding round. Practise them without autocomplete.

Strings

def reverse_words(s: str) -> str:
    return " ".join(s.split()[::-1])

def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    cleaned = [c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum()]
    return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]

def is_anagram(a: str, b: str) -> bool:
    return Counter(a) == Counter(b)

def char_frequency(s: str) -> dict[str, int]:
    freq = {}
    for c in s:
        freq[c] = freq.get(c, 0) + 1
    return freq

def first_non_repeating(s: str) -> str | None:
    counts = Counter(s)
    for c in s:                      # dict keeps insertion order
        if counts[c] == 1:
            return c
    return None

Lists

def remove_duplicates_keep_order(items: list) -> list:
    seen, out = set(), []
    for item in items:
        if item not in seen:
            seen.add(item)
            out.append(item)
    return out

def second_largest(nums: list[int]) -> int | None:
    first = second = float("-inf")
    for n in nums:
        if n > first:
            first, second = n, first
        elif first > n > second:
            second = n
    return second if second != float("-inf") else None

def chunk(items: list, size: int) -> list[list]:
    return [items[i:i+size] for i in range(0, len(items), size)]

def flatten(nested: list) -> list:
    out = []
    for item in nested:
        if isinstance(item, list):
            out.extend(flatten(item))
        else:
            out.append(item)
    return out

def rotate(nums: list, k: int) -> list:
    k %= len(nums)                   # guard against k > n
    return nums[-k:] + nums[:-k] if k else nums[:]

Dicts / grouping

def group_by(items: list[dict], key: str) -> dict:
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for item in items:
        groups[item[key]].append(item)
    return dict(groups)

def invert(d: dict) -> dict:
    return {v: k for k, v in d.items()}          # assumes unique values

def merge_sum(a: dict, b: dict) -> dict:
    return dict(Counter(a) + Counter(b))

def top_n_by_value(d: dict, n: int) -> list:
    return sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)[:n]

Sorting

sorted(people, key=lambda p: p["age"])
sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p["score"], p["name"]))   # multi-key, mixed direction
sorted(words, key=len)
sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])

Python's sort is Timsort: stable, O(n log n) worst case, and near-O(n) on partially sorted input. "Stable" means equal elements keep their relative order — that's what lets you sort by one key, then another, to get a compound ordering.

Recursion

def factorial(n: int) -> int:
    return 1 if n <= 1 else n * factorial(n - 1)

def fib_memo(n: int, memo: dict | None = None) -> int:
    if memo is None:
        memo = {}
    if n in memo:
        return memo[n]
    if n < 2:
        return n
    memo[n] = fib_memo(n-1, memo) + fib_memo(n-2, memo)
    return memo[n]

def binary_search(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1

Recursion limit is ~1000 by default. If an interviewer asks about deep recursion: convert to iteration with an explicit stack, or (rarely) raise the limit — mention that Python has no tail-call optimisation.

Parsing

def parse_csv_line(line: str) -> dict:
    name, age, city = line.strip().split(",")
    return {"name": name, "age": int(age), "city": city}

def word_count(text: str) -> Counter:
    return Counter(text.lower().split())

2.8 Python question bank — short answer → deep → follow-up

Question 15-second answer Deep version / follow-up
List vs tuple Mutable vs immutable; tuple is hashable and slightly cheaper Follow-up: "Why is that useful?" → dict keys, safe to share, signals intent
is vs == Identity vs value Follow-up: small-int caching, why is None is the exception
Shallow vs deep copy New container vs recursive clone Follow-up: "When would deepcopy fail?" → sockets, DB handles, huge graphs
Decorator Function that wraps a function to add behaviour Follow-up: functools.wraps, decorators with args, stacking order
Generator Lazy iterator produced by yield; O(1) memory Follow-up: can't restart, no len, yield from
GIL One thread executes bytecode at a time in CPython Follow-up: threads for I/O, processes for CPU, released in C extensions
*args / **kwargs Collect extra positional / keyword args Follow-up: why decorators need them
Mutable default arg Evaluated once at def time; shared Follow-up: how dataclass solves it with default_factory
@staticmethod vs @classmethod No implicit arg vs receives cls Follow-up: why factories use classmethod (subclass-correct)
Dict internals Hash table; O(1) average lookup Follow-up: collisions → open addressing/probing → worst case O(n)
How is memory managed Refcounting + generational cycle collector Follow-up: weakref to break cycles
__str__ vs __repr__ User-facing vs unambiguous developer-facing Follow-up: "repr should ideally be eval-able"
Iterator vs iterable __next__ and stateful vs just __iter__ Follow-up: why a list can be looped twice
Context manager Guarantees cleanup via __enter__/__exit__ Follow-up: contextlib.contextmanager, suppressing exceptions
Python 2 vs 3 NICE TO KNOW Skip. Nobody serious asks this in 2026 —

2.9 What to study first if you only have three days for Python

  1. Mutable vs immutable + the two default-argument traps (§2.1.2, §2.4.2)
  2. Complexity table + deque/heapq/Counter/defaultdict (§2.3)
  3. Decorators (§2.2.5) and generators (§2.5.2)
  4. GIL, threads vs processes vs asyncio (§2.5.7)
  5. Everything in §2.6 and §2.7 — write §2.7 out by hand twice
