2A
Part 2A

Object-Oriented Python, Properly

Not the four pillars again — the questions you are actually asked. Why a class at all, when not to write one, what inheritance really costs, and seven trade-off drills.

Suggested time · 8 h

Most OOP material teaches you the four pillars, shows an Animal → Dog example, and stops. That's why so many people can define encapsulation but can't answer "why did you make that a class?"

This part is built around the questions you'll actually be asked: why does this exist, when do I reach for it, when is it the wrong tool, and what does it cost me?

Read it slowly once. Then use section 2A.12 (the trade-off drills) to test whether it stuck.

2A.1 First: what problem do classes actually solve? MUST KNOW

Forget "blueprint for objects" — that's a description, not a reason.

Here's the reason. Some data has rules that must always be true. A bank account balance must never go negative. An order's total must always equal the sum of its lines. A date range must always have start <= end.

If that data lives in a loose dict, the rules live nowhere. Every piece of code that touches it has to remember them, and one careless line breaks the invariant silently:

account = {"owner": "Sri", "balance": 500}

# somewhere else, six months later, in a file nobody has read
account["balance"] -= 900        # nothing stops this. Balance is now -400.

A class lets you put the data and the rules that protect it in the same place, and make the outside world go through a door you control:

class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner: str, balance: float = 0.0):
        self.owner = owner
        self._balance = balance

    def withdraw(self, amount: float) -> None:
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("amount must be positive")
        if amount > self._balance:
            raise InsufficientFunds(amount, self._balance)   # the rule lives here
        self._balance -= amount

Now there is exactly one place where a balance can decrease, and it is impossible to get to a negative balance without going through it.

The one-sentence version to say in an interview: "A class is for state that has invariants. It bundles data with the operations allowed on that data, so the rules live next to the thing they protect instead of being scattered across every caller."

Everything else about OOP follows from that idea. Encapsulation is how you protect the invariant. Abstraction is hiding how you enforce it. Inheritance and polymorphism are ways to let different implementations satisfy the same contract.

2A.2 When you should NOT write a class MUST KNOW

This is the more valuable half, and almost nobody asks it in tutorials.

Signal 1 — the class has one method and no meaningful state

class EmailValidator:              # ❌ this is a function wearing a costume
    def __init__(self, email):
        self.email = email
    def validate(self):
        return "@" in self.email

def is_valid_email(email: str) -> bool:    # ✅
    return "@" in email

If you construct it and immediately call the one method, there was never any state worth keeping. Use a function.

Signal 2 — the class is just a bag of data with no rules

class Point:                        # ❌ lots of ceremony, no invariant
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)             # ✅ same thing, four lines shorter, immutable, hashable
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float

If there really are no rules at all and the shape is short-lived, even a tuple or a dict may be right. Section 2A.9 has the full decision table.

Signal 3 — you're using inheritance to share code, not to model a type

class Utils:                        # ❌ "inheritance as a mixin of convenience"
    def format_currency(self, x): ...

class OrderService(Utils): ...      # is an OrderService a kind of Utils? No.

That's a module of functions, not a base class.

Signal 4 — the class has no methods that use self meaningfully

If every method is a @staticmethod, you have written a namespace. Python already has one: it's called a module.

How to phrase this in an interview: "I ask myself whether the object has state that outlives a single call, and whether there are rules about that state. If the answer to both is no, a function or a dataclass is the simpler tool and I'd rather have the simpler tool."

That answer signals judgment, which is what the OOP question is really probing.

2A.3 Instance vs class attributes — and the trap MUST KNOW

class Trade:
    exchange = "NSE"          # CLASS attribute: one copy, shared by every instance
    count = 0

    def __init__(self, symbol):
        self.symbol = symbol  # INSTANCE attribute: one per object

How lookup works — and this explains every surprise in this area:

When you read obj.x, Python looks in the instance dictionary first. If it's not there, it walks the class (and its bases). When you write obj.x = ..., Python always writes to the instance.

Two consequences:

Trap 1 — the shared mutable class attribute

class Team:
    members = []                    # ❌ ONE list, shared by every Team ever created
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

a, b = Team("A"), Team("B")
a.members.append("Sri")
b.members                           # ['Sri']  — leaked into a completely different team

Why: a.members.append(...) is a read of members (finds the class one) followed by a mutation of that object. No write to the instance ever happens.

Fix: create the mutable state in __init__, so each instance gets its own.

def __init__(self, name):
    self.name = name
    self.members = []               # ✅

Trap 2 — the counter that doesn't count

class Trade:
    count = 0
    def __init__(self):
        self.count += 1             # ❌ reads the class value (0), writes an INSTANCE value (1)

Trade(); Trade(); Trade.count       # still 0

Fix: Trade.count += 1, or type(self).count += 1 if you want subclasses to have their own counters.

When a class attribute is genuinely right: constants shared by all instances (exchange = "NSE"), default values that are immutable, and configuration that subclasses are meant to override:

class BaseStrategy:
    timeframe = "5min"              # a subclass can just set its own

class ScalpStrategy(BaseStrategy):
    timeframe = "1min"              # clean, declarative override

That last pattern is a legitimately good use and worth mentioning — it shows you know class attributes aren't just a hazard.

2A.4 The three method types, explained by what they receive MUST KNOW

The whole distinction is: what does Python hand to this function automatically?

class Order:
    tax_rate = 0.18

    def total(self):                      # instance method — gets the OBJECT
        return self.subtotal * (1 + self.tax_rate)

    @classmethod
    def from_json(cls, payload: dict):    # class method — gets the CLASS
        return cls(payload["items"], payload["customer"])

    @staticmethod
    def is_business_day(d: date) -> bool: # static — gets NOTHING
        return d.weekday() < 5
Receives Reach for it when Real example
instance method self The behaviour depends on this object's data order.total()
@classmethod cls Alternative constructors, factories, anything touching class-level state Order.from_json(...), datetime.fromtimestamp(...)
@staticmethod nothing A helper that belongs conceptually here but needs no state validation, pure conversions

Why alternative constructors use classmethod and not staticmethod MUST KNOW

This is the question behind the question, and the answer is inheritance:

class Order:
    @classmethod
    def from_json(cls, payload):
        return cls(...)              # cls is whatever class it was called on

class PriorityOrder(Order):
    pass

PriorityOrder.from_json({...})       # returns a PriorityOrder ✅

If you had hard-coded return Order(...) in a staticmethod, the subclass would silently get the wrong type back. cls makes the factory subclass-correct, and that's the reason the decorator exists.

Trade-off worth stating: "staticmethod is really just namespacing — it gives you nothing that a module-level function doesn't. I use it when the helper is meaningless outside the class's context and I want it discoverable there. If it's generally useful, I'd rather it be a plain function so it's importable and testable on its own."

2A.5 Encapsulation in Python — tell the truth about it MUST KNOW

Python has no private. What it has is a convention and a name-mangling mechanism, and candidates routinely describe the second one wrongly.

Form What Python does What it means socially
self.balance nothing special public API, I promise not to break it
self._balance nothing at all "internal — don't touch, and I may change it without warning"
self.__balance renames it to self._Account__balance "don't let a subclass accidentally collide with this name"

The correction to have ready: double underscore is not a privacy feature. It exists to stop accidental name collisions in subclasses. You can still reach it:

acct = Account("Sri", 100)
acct._Account__balance = -999999      # nothing stops you

Python's stance is "we're all consenting adults here." The _ prefix is a contract between developers, not a guarantee enforced by the runtime. In practice that works fine, because the cost of violating it is that your code breaks on the next upgrade — and everyone knows it.

@property — the reason you don't need Java-style getters

In Java you write getBalance() from day one, because if you ever expose the field directly you can never add logic later without breaking every caller.

Python doesn't have that problem. Start with a plain attribute. If you later need validation or computation, convert it to a property and every existing call site keeps working unchanged:

class Order:
    def __init__(self, price, qty):
        self.price = price
        self.qty = qty                  # goes through the setter below

    @property
    def total(self):                    # computed — always consistent, can't drift
        return self.price * self.qty

    @property
    def qty(self):
        return self._qty

    @qty.setter
    def qty(self, value):
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("qty cannot be negative")
        self._qty = value

When a property is the wrong choice: when it's expensive. order.total looks free, so callers will put it in a loop. If it hits the database or does real work, either make it an explicit method (order.compute_total()) so the cost is visible, or use functools.cached_property if it's safe to compute once.

Interview line: "Properties let me start simple and add rules later without a migration. The risk is that they hide cost behind attribute syntax, so I keep them cheap — anything expensive gets to be a method, because the parentheses are a signal to the reader."

2A.6 Inheritance: what you're really signing up for MUST KNOW

Inheritance gives you two things at once, and people usually want only one of them:

  1. Subtyping — "a PriorityOrder can be used anywhere an Order is expected."
  2. Implementation reuse — "I get the parent's methods for free."

The trouble is that #2 is seductive and #1 is the actual contract. When you inherit for reuse, you inherit the parent's entire implementation, including decisions you didn't read.

The fragile base class problem

class Playlist:
    def __init__(self):
        self.songs = []

    def add(self, song):
        self.songs.append(song)

    def add_many(self, songs):
        for s in songs:
            self.add(s)                 # ← implementation detail: calls add()

class CountingPlaylist(Playlist):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.added = 0

    def add(self, song):
        self.added += 1
        super().add(song)

p = CountingPlaylist()
p.add_many(["a", "b"])
p.added                                 # 2 — correct, today

Now the parent's author "optimises" add_many to self.songs.extend(songs). Nothing about the public API changed. The subclass silently stops counting.

This is the argument against inheritance, and it's worth being able to tell as a story. The subclass depended on how the parent was written, not on what it promised. That coupling isn't visible in either file.

The Liskov test, in plain language

If code works with the parent, it must still work when handed a child — without knowing.

The classic violation:

class Rectangle:
    def set_width(self, w): self.w = w
    def set_height(self, h): self.h = h

class Square(Rectangle):        # a square IS-A rectangle in mathematics…
    def set_width(self, w): self.w = self.h = w
    def set_height(self, h): self.w = self.h = h

def stretch(rect):              # …but this reasonable function now breaks
    rect.set_width(5)
    rect.set_height(4)
    assert rect.w * rect.h == 20    # fails for a Square

The lesson isn't about squares. It's that "is-a" in English is not the same as "is substitutable for" in code. Ask the substitutability question, not the English one.

Other Liskov smells to name: a subclass that raises NotImplementedError for a method the parent supports, that tightens the accepted inputs, or that weakens what it guarantees to return.

2A.7 Composition over inheritance — with the "when to still inherit" part MUST KNOW

# Inheritance — is a UserService really a kind of Database?
class UserService(Database):
    def get_user(self, uid):
        return self.query("SELECT ...")      # depends on Database's internals

# Composition — a UserService HAS a database
class UserService:
    def __init__(self, db: Database, cache: Cache, mailer: Mailer):
        self.db = db
        self.cache = cache
        self.mailer = mailer

What composition buys you, concretely:

  • Testability. Pass a fake db in tests. With inheritance you'd have to construct a real Database or monkeypatch it.
  • A smaller surface. You depend on the three or four methods you actually call, not on everything the parent exposes.
  • Runtime flexibility. You can swap the cache for a no-op in development. Inheritance is fixed at class-definition time.
  • No accidental API leakage. With inheritance, every public method of Database becomes a public method of UserService, whether you want it or not. That's rarely intended, and it's a good point to raise unprompted.

So when is inheritance the right call?

Don't over-swing. Inheritance is correct when:

  • There's a genuine substitutable type hierarchy and callers will treat children uniformly — Exception subclasses, Enum, Django models, BaseHTTPRequestHandler.
  • A framework requires it. Inheriting unittest.TestCase or a DRF APIView is not a design failure; it's how the framework does registration.
  • You're defining an interface — an abstract base with abstract methods and no implementation to speak of. There's very little to couple to when the parent is nearly empty, which is exactly why this case is safe.

The complete answer: "Inheritance is 'is-a' and it couples me to the parent's implementation, so a change in the base can break subclasses nobody looked at. Composition is 'has-a' — I depend on a small interface, I can swap it, and I can inject a fake in tests. I use inheritance when there's a real substitutable hierarchy or a framework demands it, especially where the base is an abstract interface with little implementation to depend on. For sharing behaviour, I compose."

Aggregation vs composition (occasionally asked): composition means the part can't outlive the whole — an Order and its OrderLines. Aggregation means it can — a Team and its Employees; delete the team, the people still exist.

2A.8 Polymorphism, duck typing, ABCs and Protocols SHOULD KNOW→MUST KNOW

Python doesn't need a shared base class for polymorphism. If the object has the method, it works:

def render(items):
    for item in items:
        print(item.to_html())      # anything with .to_html() is welcome

That's duck typing: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck." It's why Python has no interface keyword.

But sometimes you want the contract enforced, or at least documented. Two tools, and knowing the difference is a strong signal:

ABCs — nominal typing ("you must declare that you're one of us")

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class PaymentProvider(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def charge(self, amount: Decimal, token: str) -> str: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def refund(self, charge_id: str) -> None: ...

class StripeProvider(PaymentProvider):     # must implement both, or instantiation fails
    def charge(self, amount, token): ...
    def refund(self, charge_id): ...

You get a loud failure at object-creation time if a method is missing. Good for a plugin boundary you own, where a half-implemented provider would be a disaster in production.

Protocols — structural typing ("if you have the shape, you qualify")

from typing import Protocol

class SupportsCharge(Protocol):
    def charge(self, amount: Decimal, token: str) -> str: ...

def checkout(provider: SupportsCharge, amount, token):
    return provider.charge(amount, token)

No inheritance required. A third-party class you can't modify still satisfies it. Type checkers verify it; at runtime it's ordinary duck typing.

ABC Protocol
Requires inheriting yes no
Enforced at runtime (instantiation) static analysis (mypy)
Works with third-party classes only if you wrap them yes
Good for plugin contracts you own, shared base behaviour describing what you need from an argument

How to use this in an interview: "For a contract I own and want enforced loudly, I use an ABC. For describing what a function needs from its argument — especially when the caller might pass something from a library I don't control — I use a Protocol, because it doesn't force an inheritance relationship that doesn't otherwise exist."

Very few candidates mention Protocols. It's a cheap way to sound current.

2A.9 Choosing the right shape for your data MUST KNOW

This decision comes up constantly in real code and almost as often in interviews.

Shape Use when Cost
dict Truly dynamic keys; JSON you're passing through No validation, no autocomplete, typos are silent (d["nmae"])
TypedDict You must keep the dict shape (JSON boundary) but want type checking Static only; nothing enforced at runtime
tuple Tiny, positional, obvious — a coordinate, a DB row Meaningless at the call site: what was t[2] again?
NamedTuple Immutable record, wants tuple behaviour (unpacking, comparison) Still a tuple, so it compares equal to plain tuples — occasionally surprising
@dataclass The default for a record with a few rules Slight overhead; mutable unless you say frozen=True
Full class Real invariants, non-trivial behaviour, controlled mutation Most code to write and maintain
pydantic.BaseModel Data crossing a trust boundary (API input, config) A dependency; validation cost on every construction 
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Trade:
    symbol: str
    qty: int
    price: Decimal
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # NOT tags: list = []

    @property
    def notional(self) -> Decimal:
        return self.qty * self.price

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.qty <= 0:
            raise ValueError("qty must be positive")   # a rule, in a dataclass

Three details worth knowing because they get asked: - field(default_factory=list) is the dataclass-level answer to the mutable-default trap. A plain = [] is a ValueError at class-definition time — the language stops you, which is a nice callback to make. - frozen=True makes it immutable and hashable, so it can go in a set or be a dict key. - slots=True drops the per-instance __dict__: less memory, faster attribute access, but you can't add attributes dynamically. Worth mentioning if you're creating millions of these.

The default I'd recommend saying out loud: "I start with a frozen dataclass. It gives me a real type, a readable repr, value equality and immutability for almost no code. I promote it to a full class when it grows invariants that need controlled mutation, and I drop to a dict only at genuine JSON boundaries."

2A.10 Dunder methods: making your object behave like a built-in SHOULD KNOW

Dunders are how Python asks your object to participate in the language. len(x) calls x.__len__(). a + b calls a.__add__(b). There's no magic — just an agreed set of names.

@dataclass
class Money:
    amount: Decimal
    currency: str = "INR"

    def __add__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Money) or other.currency != self.currency:
            return NotImplemented          # let Python try the reflected op / raise TypeError
        return Money(self.amount + other.amount, self.currency)

    def __lt__(self, other):               # unlocks sorting, min(), max(), heapq
        return self.amount < other.amount

    def __str__(self):                     # for users
        return f"₹{self.amount:,.2f}"

    def __repr__(self):                    # for developers — ideally eval-able
        return f"Money({self.amount!r}, {self.currency!r})"

    def __bool__(self):
        return self.amount != 0

The ones worth knowing, grouped by what they unlock:

You want Implement
len(obj), truthiness __len__
obj[k] __getitem__ / __setitem__
for x in obj __iter__ (and __next__ on the iterator)
x in obj __contains__ (falls back to __iter__)
with obj: __enter__ / __exit__
obj() __call__
sorting, min, max, heaps __lt__
set/dict membership __eq__ and __hash__
debugging that doesn't hurt __repr__

The __eq__ / __hash__ contract MUST KNOW

Two rules, and violating them causes bugs that look like the universe is broken:

  1. If a == b, then hash(a) == hash(b). Otherwise a dict lookup will miss an equal key.
  2. A hashable object's hash must never change. Which is why mutable objects generally shouldn't be hashable.

Python protects you: if you define __eq__, it sets __hash__ = None, making your object unhashable. That's deliberate — you defined a new notion of equality, so the old identity hash is now wrong. Define both, or use @dataclass(frozen=True) which does it for you.

__repr__ discipline: always write one. The default <Order object at 0x7f...> tells you nothing at 2am, and repr is what you see in logs, tracebacks, debuggers and list printing. The convention is that repr should ideally be valid code to recreate the object.

2A.11 MRO and cooperative multiple inheritance SHOULD KNOW

With single inheritance, super() means "my parent". With multiple inheritance it means something more precise: "the next class in the MRO" — which may not be my parent at all.

class A:
    def __init__(self): print("A"); 

class B(A):
    def __init__(self): print("B"); super().__init__()

class C(A):
    def __init__(self): print("C"); super().__init__()

class D(B, C):
    def __init__(self): print("D"); super().__init__()

D()                  # D, B, C, A   — A runs ONCE, not twice
D.__mro__            # D → B → C → A → object

Notice that B.__init__'s super() resolved to C, not to A. super() doesn't walk the class's own parents — it walks the MRO of the object being constructed. That's what makes multiple inheritance work without duplicate initialisation, and it's the reason to write super().__init__() rather than A.__init__(self).

Python computes the MRO with C3 linearisation, which guarantees: a class comes before its parents, and the order you listed the bases is respected. If no consistent order exists, Python refuses to create the class at all.

Mixins done right

A mixin is a small class that adds one capability and is never instantiated alone:

class TimestampMixin:
    created_at: datetime
    def age_seconds(self) -> float:
        return (datetime.now() - self.created_at).total_seconds()

class SerializableMixin:
    def to_json(self) -> str:
        return json.dumps(asdict(self))

class Order(TimestampMixin, SerializableMixin, Base):
    ...

Rules that keep mixins from becoming a mess: keep them tiny and single-purpose, don't give them state if you can avoid it, name them ...Mixin, and never build deep hierarchies out of them.

Honest interview position: "I use multiple inheritance sparingly and almost only for small stateless mixins. Once behaviour is spread across several bases, working out where a method comes from means reading the MRO, and that's a real cost for the next reader. If I need to combine substantial behaviours, composition is easier to follow."

2A.12 Trade-off drills — reason these out loud MUST KNOW

These are the OOP questions that have no single right answer. What's being scored is your reasoning. For each: cover the answer, argue it yourself, then compare.

Q1. "This dataclass has grown three methods and a validation rule. Keep it a dataclass or promote it to a full class?"

Think first, then open

Keep it. A dataclass is a normal class — the decorator only generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__. Methods, properties and __post_init__ validation are all fine.

The real trigger for hand-writing __init__ is when construction itself is non-trivial: you need to accept several different argument shapes, do work before assigning, or the generated signature is wrong for your API. Until then, deleting the generated boilerplate would be losing something for nothing.

Q2. "You have Bird.fly(). Now you need a penguin. What do you do?"

Think first, then open

The trap is class Penguin(Bird) with def fly(self): raise NotImplementedError — a Liskov violation, because every function that takes a Bird and calls fly() now breaks at runtime.

The fix is to notice that the hierarchy was modelled on biology rather than on behaviour. Flying is a capability, not a defining trait of birds. So: Bird has what all birds have, and FlyingBird (or a CanFly protocol) has fly(). Functions that need flight ask for the thing that flies.

The general lesson to state: model your hierarchy on the behaviour callers depend on, not on real-world taxonomy.

Q3. "Why not just make everything public? _ doesn't stop anyone anyway."

Think first, then open

Because the point isn't enforcement, it's the contract about what may change. Anything public is something I've implicitly promised to keep working. If every attribute is public, I can't refactor internals without risking someone's code.

The _ prefix is how I say "this is mine, I may change it in the next release." That freedom is the entire value, and it works fine in practice because the cost of ignoring it is your code breaking on upgrade.

Corollary worth adding: this is also the argument for keeping public surfaces small. Every public method is a promise.

Q4. "Should this be a @property or a method?"

Think first, then open

Ask two questions.

Is it cheap? Attribute syntax implies free. If it does I/O or heavy work, make it a method so the parentheses warn the reader — or cached_property if computing once is safe.

Is it conceptually an attribute of the thing? order.total reads like a fact about the order → property. order.recalculate_from_source() is an action → method.

The failure mode to name: a property that silently hits the database, called inside a loop, producing an N+1 problem nobody can see at the call site.

Q5. "Two classes need the same 40 lines of logic. Inheritance, mixin, or a helper function?"

Think first, then open

Default to the function, and pass it what it needs. It has no coupling, it's independently testable, and it can't be broken by a base-class change.

Use a mixin if the logic genuinely needs self and belongs to the objects' identity, and if it's small and stateless.

Use inheritance only if the two classes are genuinely the same kind of thing and callers will treat them uniformly — that is, if you'd want the base type in a signature.

The reasoning to state: shared code is not by itself a reason to create a type relationship. Reuse is not a taxonomy.

Q6. "Why does your service take a db argument instead of creating its own connection?"

Think first, then open

Because a dependency I construct is a dependency I can't replace. Taking it as a parameter means: tests pass a fake with no database at all; the connection strategy (pool size, replica routing, transaction scope) is decided by the caller who has the context; and the service's real dependencies are visible in one place — the signature — rather than buried in the body.

The cost, stated honestly: someone has to wire it all up, and construction becomes more verbose. That's what a small factory function or a DI container is for. It's a real cost and worth naming rather than pretending composition is free.

Q7. "When would you actually write __slots__?"

Think first, then open

When you're creating a very large number of small objects and memory or attribute-access speed shows up in a profile — market data ticks, graph nodes, parsed records in the millions.

The costs: no dynamic attribute assignment, no __dict__, and multiple inheritance gets fiddly. So it's an optimisation with real ergonomic cost, which means it needs a measurement behind it. "I'd add it if a profile told me to" is a better answer than either "always" or "never".

2A.13 The OOP question bank

Question Short answer The follow-up they'll ask
Why use a class here? The state has invariants worth protecting in one place "When wouldn't you?" → no state, or no rules → function or dataclass
Encapsulation in Python? Convention (_) plus name mangling (__); not enforced "What does __ actually do?" → prevents subclass collisions, not access
classmethod vs staticmethod? Gets cls vs gets nothing "Why do factories use classmethod?" → subclass-correct
Composition over inheritance? Depend on a small interface, swappable, testable "When do you still inherit?" → substitutable types, frameworks, ABCs
Explain Liskov A child must be usable wherever the parent is "Give an example" → Square/Rectangle, or fly() on a penguin
ABC vs Protocol? Nominal + runtime vs structural + static "Which for a third-party class?" → Protocol
__eq__ and __hash__? Equal objects must hash equally; hash must be stable "Why does defining __eq__ break set()?" → __hash__ set to None
What is the MRO? C3 linearisation; the order super() follows "Why super() over Parent.__init__?" → diamond runs the base once
dataclass vs NamedTuple vs dict? Rules + mutability + boundary "Which at an API boundary?" → pydantic/TypedDict, validate at the edge
Multiple inheritance — good idea? Small stateless mixins only "Why the caution?" → readers must simulate the MRO to find a method

2B
Part 2B

Functions, Decorators and the Functional Toolkit

map, filter, reduce and the honest verdict on each. Closures, decorators built from first principles, functools, itertools — and when every one of them is the wrong tool.

Suggested time · 8 h

The one idea underneath this entire part:

In Python, a function is just an object. You can put it in a list, pass it as an argument, return it from another function, attach attributes to it, and store it in a dict.

Everything here — map, filter, reduce, sorted(key=...), closures, decorators, partial, callbacks, strategy patterns — is a consequence of that one fact. If it clicks, none of the rest is magic.

def shout(s): return s.upper()

f = shout                      # a name pointing at a function object
f("hi")                        # 'HI'
funcs = [str.upper, str.strip] # functions in a container
dispatch = {"upper": str.upper, "lower": str.lower}   # a dict of behaviours
dispatch["upper"]("hi")        # 'HI'  — this is a switch statement, done properly

2B.1 map, filter, reduce — what they are, and the honest verdict MUST KNOW

Three operations that cover a surprising amount of data work:

Operation Question it answers Shape
map "Transform every item" n items → n items
filter "Keep the items that pass a test" n items → ≤ n items
reduce "Collapse everything into one value" n items → 1 value 
from functools import reduce

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

list(map(lambda x: x * x, nums))        # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, nums))# [2, 4]
reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, nums)        # 15
reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, nums, 100)   # 115  ← the initial value

In Python 3, map and filter are lazy. They return iterators, not lists. Nothing is computed until you iterate. That matters: map(expensive, million_items) costs nothing until consumed, and if you only take the first ten, only ten are computed.

How reduce actually works

It's a fold from the left. Nothing more:

reduce(f, [a, b, c, d])
  →  f(f(f(a, b), c), d)

Step by step for reduce(add, [1,2,3,4]): add(1,2)=3 → add(3,3)=6 → add(6,4)=10.

Always pass the initial value when the list might be empty. reduce(add, []) raises TypeError; reduce(add, [], 0) returns 0. The initial value also lets the accumulator be a different type from the elements — which is when reduce is genuinely useful:

# accumulator is a dict, elements are objects — this is a real fold
reduce(lambda acc, o: {**acc, o.id: o}, orders, {})

The honest verdict on when to use them MUST KNOW

Here is the thing most tutorials won't say plainly: in Python, a comprehension is usually the better choice than map or filter with a lambda.

list(map(lambda x: x * 2, nums))        # ok
[x * 2 for x in nums]                   # better — more readable, and faster

list(filter(lambda x: x > 2, nums))     # ok
[x for x in nums if x > 2]              # better

list(map(lambda x: x * 2, filter(lambda x: x > 2, nums)))   # hard to read
[x * 2 for x in nums if x > 2]                              # obviously better

Two reasons, and both are defensible in an interview:

  1. Readability. The comprehension reads left to right in the order things happen. Chained map(filter(...)) reads inside-out.
  2. Speed. map with a lambda is usually slower than a comprehension, because every element pays the cost of a Python-level function call. The comprehension inlines the expression.

So when does map genuinely win?

When you already have a named function — especially a C-level built-in. Then there's no lambda, no extra Python call frame, and map is both faster and cleaner:

list(map(int, ["1", "2", "3"]))         # ✅ clean and fast
[int(x) for x in ["1", "2", "3"]]       # fine, marginally slower

list(map(str.strip, lines))             # ✅ reads beautifully
sum(map(len, words))                    # ✅ no intermediate list at all

When you want laziness over a huge stream. map over a 10 GB file is O(1) memory; a list comprehension materialises everything. (Though a generator expression gives you the same laziness with comprehension syntax.)

When mapping over several iterables at once:

list(map(operator.add, [1, 2, 3], [10, 20, 30]))    # [11, 22, 33]

And when does reduce win?

Rarely — and knowing why rarely is the mark of someone who's thought about it. Guido removed reduce from builtins in Python 3 (it lives in functools now) with the argument that almost every real use is either a loop that reads better, or a specialised builtin that reads much better:

reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, nums)          # ❌ don't
sum(nums)                                 # ✅

reduce(lambda a, b: a * b, nums)          # ❌
math.prod(nums)                           # ✅ (3.8+)

reduce(lambda a, b: a if a > b else b, nums)   # ❌
max(nums)                                      # ✅

reduce(lambda a, b: a | b, sets)          # ❌
set().union(*sets)                        # ✅

reduce is defensible when the fold is genuinely custom and the accumulator differs in type from the elements — merging nested config dictionaries, composing a chain of functions, building a state machine's final state from a list of events:

def deep_merge(a: dict, b: dict) -> dict: ...
final_config = reduce(deep_merge, config_layers, {})     # ✅ reads as "fold these together"

apply_all = reduce(lambda f, g: lambda x: g(f(x)), transforms)   # function composition

The full trade-off answer: "map and filter are lazy and fine, but with a lambda a comprehension is usually both more readable and faster, because the lambda adds a Python function call per element. I reach for map when I already have a named function — especially a built-in like int or str.strip — where there's no lambda overhead and it reads better. I mostly avoid reduce: for sums, products and maxima there are dedicated builtins that say what they mean. I'd use it for a genuine custom fold where the accumulator is a different type, like merging config layers."

That answer demonstrates you know the tools and the community's reasoning about them, which is exactly what the question is fishing for.

2B.2 Comprehensions vs generator expressions MUST KNOW

Same syntax, one character apart, very different behaviour:

squares_list = [x * x for x in range(10_000_000)]      # builds all 10M — ~400 MB
squares_lazy = (x * x for x in range(10_000_000))      # builds nothing — a few hundred bytes

Use a generator expression when: - You're only iterating once, which is most of the time. - You're feeding an aggregate: sum(x*x for x in nums) — note you can drop the extra brackets. - The data is large or unbounded. - The consumer might stop early: any(is_valid(x) for x in huge) short-circuits at the first True and never touches the rest.

Use a list comprehension when: - You need len(), indexing, or to iterate more than once. - The result is small and you want a concrete value you can inspect in a debugger.

sum(len(line) for line in open("huge.log"))       # ✅ constant memory
sum([len(line) for line in open("huge.log")])     # ❌ builds the whole list first

Also available: set {...} and dict {k: v for ...} comprehensions. There is no "tuple comprehension" — (...) is a generator; use tuple(...) around one if you need a tuple.

Where comprehensions stop being the right tool: more than one if, a nested for and a transformation, needing a try/except per item, or any side effect. At that point write the loop. A comprehension that needs a comment is worse than the loop it replaced.

2B.3 Closures — the mechanism behind everything else MUST KNOW

A closure is a function plus the variables it captured from the scope where it was defined — which stay alive even after that scope has returned.

def make_multiplier(factor):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * factor        # 'factor' is captured
    return multiply

double = make_multiplier(2)
triple = make_multiplier(3)
double(5), triple(5)             # (10, 15) — two independent captures

double.__closure__[0].cell_contents      # 2 — you can see the captured cell

Why this matters practically: it's how you build a function with configuration baked in, without writing a class. It's the mechanism behind useState in React, behind debounce, behind memoisation, and behind every decorator.

The late-binding trap MUST KNOW

Closures capture the variable, not its value at creation time:

funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
[f() for f in funcs]                      # [2, 2, 2]  ← all see the final i

By the time any lambda runs, the loop has finished and i is 2. Fixes:

funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]              # bind at definition time
funcs = [functools.partial(lambda i: i, i) for i in range(3)]   # same idea, explicit

This is exactly the JavaScript var-in-a-loop bug. Mentioning the parallel in an interview shows you understand the mechanism rather than having memorised one language's quirk.

nonlocal — writing to a captured variable

def counter():
    count = 0
    def increment():
        nonlocal count           # without this, count += 1 is an UnboundLocalError
        count += 1
        return count
    return increment

Without nonlocal, assigning to count would create a new local in increment, and the read on the right-hand side would find it unassigned.

Interview line: "A closure lets me pre-bake configuration into a function without a class. When the state is one value and there's one operation, that's lighter than a class. When there are several pieces of state or several methods, a class is clearer — a closure with three nonlocal variables is a class with extra steps."

2B.4 Decorators, built from first principles MUST KNOW

Every decorator confusion disappears once you accept one line:

@d above def f is exactly f = d(f). That's the whole feature.

The problem they solve

You have twenty API handlers. You want each one timed, logged and permission-checked. Without decorators you either paste the same six lines into twenty functions, or you wrap each call site. Both mean that changing the logging format is a twenty-file edit.

Decorators let the behaviour live in one place and be applied in twenty places, with one line each. That's the "cross-cutting concern" problem, and it's the right framing to give.

Level 0 — the idea, with no syntax

def shout(text):
    return text.upper()

def add_excitement(func):        # takes a function
    def wrapper(text):           # builds a replacement
        return func(text) + "!!!"
    return wrapper               # returns the replacement

shout = add_excitement(shout)    # rebind the name
shout("hello")                   # 'HELLO!!!'

@add_excitement above def shout does exactly that last rebinding. Nothing else.

Level 1 — the real shape

import functools, time

def timer(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)                      # ← the line interviewers look for
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):               # accept ANY signature
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)          # forward everything, unchanged
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
        print(f"{func.__name__} took {elapsed:.4f}s")
        return result                           # ← don't forget this
    return wrapper

@timer
def fetch_prices(symbol, limit=100): ...

Four things to get right, and each is a common bug:

Line Why it's there What breaks without it
*args, **kwargs The wrapper doesn't know the signature it's replacing Only works for one specific signature
return func(...) Forward the real return value The function silently returns None
return wrapper The decorator must return the replacement Your function becomes None
@functools.wraps Copies __name__, __doc__, signature, __wrapped__ Broken logs, broken docs, and frameworks like FastAPI that read signatures stop working

That last one is worth expanding, because it's the difference between knowing the syntax and having used it: FastAPI builds its request parsing and OpenAPI schema by introspecting your handler's signature. A decorator without wraps presents (*args, **kwargs) and the framework has nothing to work with.

Level 2 — a decorator that takes arguments

One more layer of nesting. Read it outside-in:

def retry(times=3, delay=0.5, exceptions=(Exception,)):
    def decorator(func):                              # ← the actual decorator
        @functools.wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            last = None
            for attempt in range(times):
                try:
                    return func(*args, **kwargs)
                except exceptions as e:
                    last = e
                    if attempt < times - 1:
                        time.sleep(delay * (2 ** attempt))   # exponential backoff
            raise last
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@retry(times=5, delay=0.2, exceptions=(ConnectionError, TimeoutError))
def fetch_quote(symbol): ...

Why three levels? Because @retry(times=5) is a function call that happens first; whatever it returns is then used as the decorator. So: retry(times=5) → returns decorator; decorator(fetch_quote) → returns wrapper; fetch_quote now names wrapper.

The trick for writing one under pressure: count the parentheses at the call site. @retry → two levels. @retry(...) → three levels.

Level 3 — stacking, and the order question MUST KNOW

@log_calls        # outermost
@timer
@retry(times=3)   # innermost — closest to the real function
def place_order(): ...

Equivalent to place_order = log_calls(timer(retry(times=3)(place_order))).

  • Applied bottom-up (the one nearest the def wraps first).
  • Executed top-down (the outermost wrapper's code runs first at call time).

So log_calls sees the total time including all retries; timer measures the retry loop; retry wraps only the real function. Order changes meaning — if you put timer innermost, you'd time a single attempt instead of the whole operation. Being able to say that is a genuinely strong answer.

Level 4 — decorating methods

The same code works, because self just arrives as the first positional argument and *args forwards it:

class OrderService:
    @timer
    def place(self, order): ...          # 'self' is args[0] inside wrapper

But watch the order with @property, @classmethod and @staticmethod — those must be outermost, because they return descriptors rather than plain functions:

class C:
    @property
    @timer                  # ✅ property wraps the timed function
    def value(self): ...

Class-based decorators

When the decorator needs its own state, a class with __call__ can be clearer than nested closures:

class CountCalls:
    def __init__(self, func):
        functools.update_wrapper(self, func)
        self.func = func
        self.count = 0

    def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        self.count += 1
        return self.func(*args, **kwargs)

@CountCalls
def ping(): ...

ping(); ping()
ping.count           # 2 — state is inspectable, which a closure makes awkward

Real decorators you'd actually write

Decorator What it does Where
@timer / @log_calls Observability Anywhere you need timings
@retry(...) Transient failure handling Broker APIs, HTTP calls, flaky I/O
@lru_cache / @cache Memoisation Pure, expensive, repeated computations
@requires_role("admin") Authorisation Web handlers
@validate_schema(Model) Input validation API boundaries
@rate_limit(10, per=60) Throttling Public endpoints
@transactional Wrap in a DB transaction Service methods
@deprecated Emit a warning Public library APIs
@app.get("/users") Registration Frameworks — note this one doesn't wrap at all, it just records the function in a routing table

That last row is worth calling out. Not every decorator modifies behaviour; some exist purely for their side effect at import time. Recognising that is a sign you've read framework source.

When NOT to use a decorator MUST KNOW

Decorators hide control flow. That is exactly their value and exactly their cost.

  • Don't use one for logic specific to a single function — just write it inline.
  • Don't hide something surprising. A decorator that silently swallows exceptions or mutates arguments will cost someone hours.
  • Don't stack more than two or three. By the fourth, nobody can tell what actually runs.
  • Careful in hot loops — each layer adds a Python function call. Usually irrelevant; occasionally not.
  • Debugging cost: a traceback goes through wrapper frames. functools.wraps sets __wrapped__, so func.__wrapped__ gets you the original — useful in tests when you want to bypass the decorator entirely.

The balanced answer: "Decorators are the right tool when the same concern applies to many functions and is orthogonal to what those functions do — timing, retries, auth, caching. They cost you explicitness: the reader has to know what the decorator does to understand the function. So I keep them small, obvious, well-named, and I don't stack many."

2B.5 functools — the parts worth knowing MUST KNOW

from functools import (lru_cache, cache, wraps, partial, reduce,
                       cached_property, singledispatch, total_ordering)

lru_cache / cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def option_price(spot, strike, iv, days):
    ...

option_price.cache_info()      # CacheInfo(hits=42, misses=8, maxsize=128, currsize=8)
option_price.cache_clear()
  • @cache (3.9+) is lru_cache(maxsize=None) — unbounded.
  • Arguments must be hashable, so no lists or dicts. Convert to tuples first. This is the single most common failure and a good detail to volunteer.
  • Only safe on pure functions. Caching something that depends on the database or the clock gives you stale results with no error.
  • It's a memory leak waiting to happen if unbounded and called with many distinct arguments. Set a maxsize.
  • On a method, the cache is keyed on self too, which keeps the instance alive forever. That's a real production leak. Prefer cached_property, or cache a module-level function.

partial — pre-bind arguments

from functools import partial

def send(channel, message, retries=3): ...

send_to_ops = partial(send, "ops-alerts")     # channel is now fixed
send_to_ops("Deploy finished")

Useful for callbacks, and it's the clean fix for the late-binding trap in loops. partial vs a lambda: partial is slightly faster, has a useful repr, and is picklable (so it works with multiprocessing, which lambdas don't).

cached_property

class Report:
    @cached_property
    def rows(self):
        return expensive_query()      # runs once per instance, then it's a plain attribute

Caveat: it never invalidates. If the underlying data changes, you get a stale answer. del obj.rows clears it.

singledispatch — polymorphism without a class hierarchy

@singledispatch
def serialize(obj):
    raise TypeError(f"cannot serialize {type(obj)}")

@serialize.register
def _(obj: datetime) -> str:
    return obj.isoformat()

@serialize.register
def _(obj: Decimal) -> str:
    return str(obj)

Dispatches on the first argument's type. The nice property: you can add support for a new type without touching the original function — open/closed, without inheritance. Good when you can't modify the classes you're serialising.

total_ordering

Define __eq__ and __lt__, and get <=, >, >= generated for you. A small, cheap win.

2B.6 itertools — the tools worth having in reach SHOULD KNOW

All of these are lazy and memory-efficient. You don't need to memorise the module, but these eight come up:

from itertools import (chain, islice, groupby, accumulate, product,
                       combinations, permutations, zip_longest, cycle, tee, starmap)

chain([1,2], [3,4])                      # 1 2 3 4 — concatenate without building a list
chain.from_iterable(list_of_lists)       # flatten one level, lazily

islice(huge_iterator, 10)                # take the first 10 — works on generators, where [:10] doesn't
islice(it, 5, 15)                        # a slice of a stream

accumulate([1,2,3,4])                    # 1 3 6 10 — running totals
accumulate(prices, max)                  # running maximum

product("AB", repeat=2)                  # AA AB BA BB — nested loops, flattened
combinations([1,2,3], 2)                 # (1,2) (1,3) (2,3) — order doesn't matter
permutations([1,2,3], 2)                 # (1,2) (1,3) (2,1) ... — order matters

zip_longest([1,2,3], "ab", fillvalue=None)   # zip() would stop at the shorter one
starmap(pow, [(2,3), (3,2)])                 # unpacks each tuple as arguments

groupby — and its trap MUST KNOW

from itertools import groupby

data = [("a", 1), ("a", 2), ("b", 3), ("a", 4)]
for key, group in groupby(data, key=lambda x: x[0]):
    print(key, list(group))
# a [('a',1),('a',2)]
# b [('b',3)]
# a [('a',4)]        ← 'a' appears TWICE

itertools.groupby groups consecutive items, like Unix uniq. It does not gather all items with the same key. You must sort by the same key first, or use collections.defaultdict(list) if you don't want the sort cost.

Second gotcha: each group is a lazy iterator that's invalidated as soon as you advance to the next group. list(group) it before moving on, or you'll get empty groups.

This one is a great answer to give unprompted, because almost everyone who has used groupby has been bitten by it once.

tee — with a warning

a, b = tee(iterator) gives you two independent iterators over the same stream. But it has to buffer everything one consumes before the other does — so if you exhaust a fully before touching b, you've stored the entire stream in memory. Fine for small look-aheads; not a free lunch.

2B.7 Sorting: key, and why it beats cmp MUST KNOW

sorted(users, key=lambda u: u["age"])
sorted(users, key=lambda u: (-u["score"], u["name"]))   # score DESC, then name ASC
sorted(words, key=len)
sorted(files, key=os.path.getmtime)
sorted(items, key=operator.itemgetter("price"))         # faster than a lambda
sorted(objs, key=operator.attrgetter("created_at"))

The tuple trick is worth memorising: key=lambda u: (-u["score"], u["name"]) sorts by two fields in opposite directions in one pass, because tuples compare element by element.

Why key and not a comparison function? key is called once per element (n calls). A comparator would be called on every comparison (n log n calls). For anything non-trivial that's a large difference — this is exactly why Python 3 dropped cmp. If you truly need comparison semantics, functools.cmp_to_key exists, but it costs you that advantage.

Stability: Python's sort is Timsort — stable, O(n log n) worst case, near-linear on partly-sorted input. Stable means equal elements keep their original relative order, which is what lets you sort by one key and then another to build a compound ordering incrementally.

2B.8 Generators as pipelines MUST KNOW

Generators are how you write a data pipeline that uses constant memory no matter how big the input.

def read_lines(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            yield line.rstrip("\n")

def parse(lines):
    for line in lines:
        yield line.split(",")

def large_trades(rows, threshold):
    for row in rows:
        if float(row[3]) > threshold:
            yield row

# nothing has been read yet — this is just wiring
rows   = parse(read_lines("trades.csv"))
big    = large_trades(rows, 1_000_000)
total  = sum(float(r[3]) for r in big)     # NOW it streams, one row at a time

Each stage pulls one item from the stage before it. Memory is O(1) regardless of file size, and each stage is independently testable.

yield from delegates to a sub-iterable and is the clean way to write recursive generators:

def flatten(nested):
    for item in nested:
        if isinstance(item, (list, tuple)):
            yield from flatten(item)
        else:
            yield item

The costs, stated honestly: no len(), no indexing, single use, and debugging is harder because there's no intermediate list to inspect. Also, an exception in the middle of a pipeline gives you a traceback through several generator frames.

When I'd use a list instead: small data, needing more than one pass, or when I want to look at the intermediate result in a debugger. Laziness is a tool for size and for early exit, not a default virtue.

2B.9 Trade-off drills — reason these out loud MUST KNOW

Q1. "Rewrite [f(x) for x in items if p(x)] using map and filter. Which do you prefer and why?"

Think first, then open

list(map(f, filter(p, items))).

I prefer the comprehension. It reads in execution order — source, filter, transform — whereas the map(filter(...)) version reads inside-out. It's also usually faster if f and p are lambdas, because each element pays a Python function call.

I'd switch to map if f were an existing named function, especially a builtin: map(int, items) beats [int(x) for x in items] on both counts. The general principle: prefer whichever form has fewer lambdas.

Q2. "Your colleague wrote reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, prices). Review it."

Think first, then open

Three points, in order of importance:

  1. sum(prices) says the same thing, is faster (C-level loop), and doesn't require the reader to mentally simulate a fold.
  2. It crashes on an empty list. sum returns 0. If reduce is kept, it needs an initial value.
  3. If these are money values, neither is right without care — floats accumulate error, so Decimal or integer paise.

Point 3 is the one that separates a code reviewer from a syntax checker. Volunteer it.

Q3. "When would you cache with a plain dict instead of lru_cache?"

Think first, then open

When I need control that the decorator doesn't give me:

  • Unhashable arguments — I can build my own key (serialise the list to a tuple).
  • Invalidation — lru_cache only offers "clear everything". A dict lets me evict one entry when the underlying data changes.
  • TTL — the decorator has no notion of time; I'd store (value, timestamp).
  • Visibility/sharing — I might want the cache in Redis so it's shared across processes.
  • On methods, because lru_cache keys on self and keeps instances alive.

lru_cache is the right default for a pure function with hashable arguments and no invalidation requirement. Beyond that it's the wrong shape.

Q4. "You need to run the same validation before ten API handlers. Decorator, base class, or middleware?"

Think first, then open

It depends on scope and on where the concern belongs.

  • Middleware if it applies to every request — request IDs, logging, CORS, generic auth. One place, no per-handler noise.
  • Decorator if it applies to these ten specific handlers, and which ones is a per-handler decision — @requires_role("admin") reads well right above the function and is self-documenting.
  • Base class / dependency if the framework has a first-class mechanism — FastAPI's Depends is the idiomatic version of this and gives testability and override for free.
  • Base class inheritance is the one I'd avoid: it couples the handlers into a hierarchy for a reason that isn't about their type.

The reasoning to state: match the mechanism's blast radius to the concern's blast radius.

Q5. "Why does this decorator break FastAPI?" — given a decorator with no functools.wraps.

Think first, then open

Because FastAPI reads the handler's signature to work out what to parse from the request and to build the OpenAPI schema. Without wraps, the object it sees is wrapper(*args, **kwargs) — no parameter names, no type annotations, so no request parsing and an empty schema.

functools.wraps copies __name__, __doc__, __module__, __qualname__, __dict__ and sets __wrapped__, and inspect.signature follows __wrapped__. That's the mechanism, not just the incantation.

Q6. "Generator or list here?" — code that reads a 5 GB log and returns matching lines.

Think first, then open

Generator, for two reasons. Memory: the list would hold every match at once and could be gigabytes on its own. And early exit: if the caller only wants the first match, a generator stops reading after it, whereas the list version reads all 5 GB first.

I'd return a list only if the caller needs len(), indexing, or more than one pass — and in that case I'd make it explicit at the call site with list(...) so the memory decision is visible to whoever reads it, rather than buried in the function.

Q7. "You've written a closure with three nonlocal variables. Is that fine?"

Think first, then open

It works, but it's a class in disguise. Three pieces of mutable state and the operations on them is exactly what a class expresses, and the class version gives you a name for the concept, a repr for debugging, the ability to inspect state, and somewhere to hang a second method when you inevitably need one.

The rule I'd give: one captured value and one operation → closure. Several values, or more than one operation → class.

2B.10 Question bank

Question Short answer Follow-up they'll ask
map vs comprehension? Comprehension usually wins on readability and speed; map wins with a named function "Why is map(lambda…) slower?" → a Python call per element
Why is reduce not a builtin? Most real uses read better as a loop or a dedicated builtin "When would you use it?" → custom fold, accumulator of a different type
List vs generator comprehension? Eager and reusable vs lazy and single-use "Which for sum()?" → generator, no intermediate list
What is a closure? Function plus its captured defining scope "Show me the late-binding bug" → [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
What does @d do? f = d(f) "How would you write one with arguments?" → one more nesting level
Why functools.wraps? Preserves name, doc, signature, sets __wrapped__ "What actually breaks?" → logs, docs, FastAPI signature introspection
Decorator execution order? Applied bottom-up, executed top-down "Does the order change behaviour?" → yes; timer inside vs outside retry
lru_cache constraints? Hashable args, pure function, bounded size "On a method?" → keys on self, keeps instances alive
partial vs lambda? Faster, better repr, picklable "Why does picklable matter?" → multiprocessing
groupby gotcha? Groups consecutive items only "So what do you do?" → sort by the same key, or defaultdict(list)
sorted(key=) vs a comparator? key runs n times, a comparator runs n log n times "Is the sort stable?" → yes, Timsort
singledispatch? Type-based dispatch on the first argument "Why not a method?" → works on classes you don't own
