2C
Part 2C

Java: The Core Language

Python trusts you at runtime; Java checks you at compile time. Memory model, strings, equals/hashCode, collections, generics, exceptions — with the Python contrast throughout.

Suggested time · 10 h

If you're coming from Python, the fastest way to hold Java in your head is this:

Python trusts you at runtime. Java checks you at compile time.

Almost every difference falls out of that. Static types, checked exceptions, access modifiers, generics, final — they all exist so the compiler can catch a class of mistake before the code ever runs. That's the trade Java makes: more ceremony up front, fewer surprises in production, and far better tooling because the compiler knows what everything is.

Where this part gives a Python comparison, use it. Interviewers like candidates who can explain why two languages made different choices.

2C.1 The memory model: stack, heap, and what a variable holds MUST KNOW

This one model explains passing semantics, == vs .equals(), null, and most garbage-collection questions. Learn it first.

  • Primitives (int, long, double, boolean, char, byte, short, float) hold the value itself. A local primitive lives on the stack.
  • Everything else is a reference. The variable holds an address; the object lives on the heap.
int a = 5;
int b = a;          // b is a COPY of the value
b = 10;             // a is still 5

int[] x = {1, 2, 3};
int[] y = x;        // y copies the REFERENCE — same array
y[0] = 99;          // x[0] is now 99 too

If you read Part 2A, that second case is exactly the Python "two names, one object" picture. Java just makes the distinction explicit by having primitives that genuinely copy.

"Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?" MUST KNOW

The correct answer, and the one that trips people up:

Java is always pass-by-value. For objects, the value being copied is the reference. So the method can mutate the object the reference points at, but it can never make the caller's variable point somewhere else.

void mutate(StringBuilder sb) { sb.append("!"); }      // caller sees the change
void reassign(StringBuilder sb) { sb = new StringBuilder("new"); }  // caller sees nothing

reassign swapped its own local copy of the reference. The caller's variable is untouched. Say it that way and you've answered it properly — "pass-by-reference" is the common wrong answer.

Where things live

Region Holds Cleaned by
Stack (per thread) Local variables, primitives, references, call frames Popped when the method returns
Heap (shared) All objects and arrays Garbage collector
Metaspace Class metadata, static fields GC, on class unload

Two consequences worth stating: StackOverflowError comes from too-deep recursion (the stack is small, typically under a megabyte), and OutOfMemoryError comes from the heap filling up. Different problems, different fixes.

Garbage collection, at the level you'll be asked SHOULD KNOW

An object is collectible when nothing reachable from a GC root (stack frames, static fields, active threads) can reach it. That's it — reference counting isn't used, so unlike CPython, cycles are collected automatically.

The generational idea: most objects die young, so the heap is split into a small young generation collected often and cheaply, and an old generation collected rarely. Objects surviving several young collections are promoted.

  • Minor GC — young gen only, fast.
  • Major/Full GC — includes old gen, slower, longer pause.
  • Modern default is G1; ZGC and Shenandoah target very low pauses on large heaps.

The useful thing to say: "Memory leaks in Java aren't dangling pointers — they're unintended reachability. A static collection that you keep adding to, listeners you never unregister, or a ThreadLocal in a pooled thread. The object is garbage conceptually, but something still references it, so the GC correctly keeps it alive."

System.gc() is a suggestion, not a command. Never call it in application code, and be ready to say so.

2C.2 Strings: immutability, the pool, and == MUST KNOW

String is immutable. Every "modification" produces a new object.

Why immutable? Four reasons, and interviewers like all of them: the hash can be cached (which is why String is the ideal HashMap key), instances can be shared safely across threads with no synchronisation, security-sensitive values like file paths can't be changed after a permission check, and identical literals can be pooled.

The string pool and the == trap

String a = "hello";
String b = "hello";
a == b;                          // true  — both point at the SAME pooled literal

String c = new String("hello");
a == c;                          // false — 'new' forces a distinct heap object
a.equals(c);                     // true  — same characters

String d = c.intern();
a == d;                          // true  — intern() returns the pooled instance

The rule: == compares references; .equals() compares content. Always use .equals() for strings. The pool makes == appear to work for literals, which is exactly what makes the bug so nasty when it eventually fails.

Compile-time constants get folded: "hel" + "lo" == "hello" is true, because the compiler resolves it into a single literal. Anything computed at runtime does not.

Concatenation performance MUST KNOW

// O(n²) — each += allocates a new String and copies everything so far
String s = "";
for (String w : words) s += w;

// O(n) — one growable buffer
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (String w : words) sb.append(w);
String s = sb.toString();

This is the same trap as Python's s += x in a loop, with the same fix in spirit ("".join(...) there, StringBuilder here). Being able to point out the parallel is a nice touch.

Note the compiler already turns a single a + b + c expression into a StringBuilder — the problem is only the loop, where you get a fresh builder every iteration.

StringBuilder vs StringBuffer: identical API; StringBuffer is synchronised and therefore slower. Use StringBuilder unless you genuinely share the builder across threads, which you almost never should.

2C.3 equals and hashCode — the contract MUST KNOW

This is the single most-asked Java object question, because getting it wrong produces bugs that look supernatural.

The contract: 1. If a.equals(b), then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). Mandatory. 2. Equal hash codes do not imply equality — collisions are allowed and normal. 3. Both must be consistent: same object, same answer, as long as the fields used haven't changed.

Why it matters mechanically: HashMap finds an entry by first computing hashCode() to pick a bucket, then using equals() inside that bucket. If you override equals but not hashCode, two equal objects land in different buckets and the map never finds the second one:

class Point {
    int x, y;
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { /* compares x and y */ }
    // hashCode NOT overridden -> inherits identity hash
}

Set<Point> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add(new Point(1, 1));
set.contains(new Point(1, 1));    // false! Different bucket.
set.add(new Point(1, 1));         // now the set has two "equal" points

The correct implementation:

@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;                        // cheap identity shortcut
    if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;
    Point p = (Point) o;
    return x == p.x && y == p.y;
}

@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(x, y);                         // use the same fields
}

Three rules that follow: - Use the same fields in both. Different fields is the contract violation in disguise. - Prefer immutable fields. If a field changes after the object is in a HashSet, its bucket is now wrong and it becomes unreachable — the object is in the set but contains says no. - A record generates both correctly from all components. That's the modern answer and the one to reach for.

Follow-up you should expect: "What if two objects always return the same hashCode?" → Legal but terrible: every entry lands in one bucket and lookup degrades from O(1) to O(n). Since Java 8 a heavily-collided bucket converts from a linked list to a balanced tree, so it's O(log n) rather than O(n) — but you've still lost the point of hashing.

2C.4 The Collections Framework MUST KNOW

Know the interfaces first, then the implementations.

Collection ──┬── List   (ordered, duplicates allowed, indexed)
             ├── Set    (no duplicates)
             └── Queue  (ordering for processing)
Map (separate hierarchy — key → value)

The complexity table to memorise

Implementation get/contains add remove Ordering Use when
ArrayList O(1) index, O(n) search O(1) amortised at end O(n) insertion The default list. Random access, iteration
LinkedList O(n) O(1) at ends O(1) given the node insertion Rarely. Use ArrayDeque for a queue
HashMap O(1) avg O(1) avg O(1) avg none The default map
LinkedHashMap O(1) avg O(1) avg O(1) avg insertion (or access) Predictable iteration; LRU caches
TreeMap O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) sorted by key Range queries, sorted iteration
HashSet O(1) avg O(1) avg O(1) avg none The default set
LinkedHashSet O(1) avg O(1) avg O(1) avg insertion Dedupe while keeping order
TreeSet O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) sorted Sorted unique values, first/ceiling
ArrayDeque — O(1) both ends O(1) both ends insertion Stack and queue. Faster than Stack/LinkedList
PriorityQueue O(1) peek O(log n) O(log n) heap order Top-K, scheduling, Dijkstra

The judgement calls interviewers probe

"ArrayList or LinkedList?" — ArrayList, almost always. The textbook answer says LinkedList wins for insertions, but that assumes you already hold the node. In practice you have to walk to the position, which is O(n), and ArrayList's contiguous memory is far more cache-friendly, so even its O(n) System.arraycopy shift usually beats pointer-chasing. Say: "I'd use ArrayList by default and only consider LinkedList if I'm inserting and removing at both ends — and then I'd reach for ArrayDeque instead, which does that better."

"HashMap or TreeMap?" — HashMap unless you need ordering. TreeMap buys you sorted iteration and navigation (floorKey, ceilingKey, subMap) at O(log n) per operation. If you only need order occasionally, a HashMap plus a sort at the end is often cheaper overall.

"How does HashMap work internally?" MUST KNOW An array of buckets. hash(key) picks the index. Collisions chain in a linked list, which converts to a red-black tree at 8 entries in one bucket (and back at 6), so pathological cases are O(log n) instead of O(n). When size exceeds capacity × loadFactor (default 0.75) the table doubles and everything is rehashed. If you know the target size, pre-size it: new HashMap<>(expected / 0.75f + 1).

"Why is Arrays.asList() fixed-size?" — It's a view over the array, so add/remove throw UnsupportedOperationException. Use new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(...)) or List.of(...) (immutable, Java 9+).

Iteration and ConcurrentModificationException MUST KNOW

for (String s : list) {
    if (s.isEmpty()) list.remove(s);      // ConcurrentModificationException
}

list.removeIf(String::isEmpty);           // ✅ the clean fix

Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();    // ✅ when you need more control
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next().isEmpty()) it.remove();
}

The collection tracks a modification count; the iterator checks it and fails fast rather than silently skipping elements. This is Java being loud where Python quietly gives you wrong results — a nice contrast to draw.

Concurrency-safe collections SHOULD KNOW

ConcurrentHashMap (segment/bucket-level locking, no global lock — always prefer it to Hashtable or Collections.synchronizedMap), CopyOnWriteArrayList (great for read-heavy listener lists, terrible for frequent writes), BlockingQueue (producer–consumer).

2C.5 Generics MUST KNOW

The problem they solve: before generics, collections held Object, so every read needed a cast and a wrong cast blew up at runtime. Generics move that failure to compile time.

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Sri");
String s = names.get(0);        // no cast, and the compiler guarantees it

Type erasure MUST KNOW — the concept behind most generics questions

Generics exist only at compile time. The compiler checks types, then erases them and inserts casts. At runtime, List<String> and List<Integer> are both just List.

Consequences you should be able to list: - new T[] is illegal — the runtime doesn't know what T is. - You can't overload on List<String> vs List<Integer> — same erased signature. - instanceof List<String> doesn't compile; only instanceof List<?> does. - The reason it was done this way is backward compatibility: pre-generic code had to keep working. (Contrast: C# reified generics and broke that compatibility deliberately.)

Wildcards and PECS SHOULD KNOW

void copy(List<? extends Number> src, List<? super Integer> dst)

The mnemonic is PECS — Producer extends, Consumer super: - If you only read from it (it produces values), use ? extends T. - If you only write to it (it consumes values), use ? super T.

Why: with List<? extends Number> the compiler knows every element is a Number, so reading is safe — but it doesn't know the exact subtype, so adding is forbidden. With List<? super Integer> it knows the list accepts Integer, so writing is safe, but reads only give you Object.

2C.6 Exceptions MUST KNOW

Throwable
 ├── Error              — JVM-level, don't catch (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError)
 └── Exception
      ├── RuntimeException  — UNCHECKED (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException)
      └── everything else   — CHECKED (IOException, SQLException)

Checked exceptions must be caught or declared with throws. Unchecked ones need not be.

The design question MUST KNOW

Use a checked exception when the caller can reasonably recover — a file might not exist, so the caller can prompt for another. Use unchecked for programming errors — a null argument or an invalid index is a bug, and there's nothing sensible to do but fail.

Be ready for the honest counterpoint, because it's a real debate: checked exceptions were arguably a design mistake. They don't compose with lambdas and streams, they encourage catch (Exception e) {}, and every modern JVM language (Kotlin, Scala) dropped them. Most Java teams today lean heavily on unchecked exceptions with a well-designed hierarchy. Having a position with reasons is what's being scored.

public class AppException extends RuntimeException {
    private final String code;
    public AppException(String code, String message, Throwable cause) {
        super(message, cause);           // ALWAYS pass the cause — don't lose the stack trace
        this.code = code;
    }
}

try-with-resources

try (var conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     var stmt = conn.prepareStatement(SQL)) {
    return stmt.executeQuery();
}                                        // closed automatically, even on exception

Anything implementing AutoCloseable works. This is Java's version of Python's with, and it exists for the same reason: cleanup must survive exceptions.

Common mistakes

  • catch (Exception e) {} — swallowing. Now the bug is invisible.
  • throw new RuntimeException(e.getMessage()) — loses the cause and the original stack. Pass e itself.
  • Catching Throwable — you just caught OutOfMemoryError.
  • A return inside finally silently discards a pending exception.
  • Using exceptions for normal control flow — they're expensive (stack capture) and they hide the happy path.

2C.7 static, final, and initialisation order SHOULD KNOW

static belongs to the class, not an instance: one copy, shared. Static methods can't touch instance state and can't be overridden (they're hidden if redeclared — a favourite trick question, since dispatch is by the reference's compile-time type, not the object's runtime type).

final means three different things depending on where it sits:

On a Means
variable the reference can't be reassigned — the object can still be mutated
method cannot be overridden
class cannot be extended (String, Integer) 
final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("ok");                 // fine — mutating the object
list = new ArrayList<>();       // compile error — reassigning the reference

This is exactly Python's const-style confusion in JavaScript, and the same explanation works: the binding is fixed, the object is not.

Initialisation order, when asked: static fields and static blocks (once, in declaration order, at class load) → instance fields and instance blocks → constructor. Parent's initialisation completes before the child's.

2C.8 Autoboxing, Integer caching, and other traps MUST KNOW

Integer a = 127, b = 127;
a == b;                      // true  — Integer cache covers -128..127

Integer c = 128, d = 128;
c == d;                      // false — separate objects
c.equals(d);                 // true

The JVM caches small Integer objects, exactly as CPython caches small ints. Same lesson: never use == on boxed types. Use .equals(), or unbox to primitives.

Other traps worth having ready:

Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
int n = counts.get("missing");        // NullPointerException — unboxing a null

double x = 0.1 + 0.2;                 // 0.30000000000000004 — use BigDecimal for money
new BigDecimal(0.1);                  // wrong: takes the broken double
new BigDecimal("0.1");                // right: use the String constructor

int[] arr = new int[3];               // [0, 0, 0] — primitives default
Integer[] boxed = new Integer[3];     // [null, null, null] — references default to null

long ms = 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 30;   // int overflow before the assignment!
long ms = 1000L * 60 * 60 * 24 * 30;  // fixed

Autoboxing in a hot loop is a real cost: Long sum = 0L; for (long i...) sum += i; allocates an object per iteration. Use the primitive.

2C.9 Modern Java worth knowing SHOULD KNOW

Mentioning these signals that you've written Java recently rather than in 2014.

var users = new ArrayList<User>();          // 10: local type inference, still static typing

record Point(int x, int y) { }              // 16: final class + ctor + equals/hashCode/toString

String msg = """
    Multi-line text
    with real newlines""";                  // 15: text blocks

// 21: pattern matching + sealed types make exhaustive switches possible
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square { }

double area = switch (shape) {
    case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius();
    case Square s -> s.side() * s.side();
};                                          // compiler verifies all cases are covered

if (obj instanceof String s && s.length() > 3) { ... }   // 16: no separate cast

record deserves special mention as the direct counterpart to Python's @dataclass(frozen=True): immutable, generated equals/hashCode/toString, and the right default for DTOs and value objects.

2C.10 Java vs Python — the comparisons that come up MUST KNOW

Topic Python Java
Typing Dynamic, strong; hints are advisory Static, strong; the compiler enforces
Equality == value, is identity .equals() value, == identity
Immutable defaults str, tuple, frozenset String, boxed primitives, record
Memory Reference counting + cycle GC Tracing generational GC
Concurrency GIL — threads for I/O, processes for CPU Real threads, true parallelism, and therefore real locking problems
Interfaces Duck typing / Protocols interface, checked at compile time
Data classes @dataclass record
Lambdas Full expressions, any signature Only for functional interfaces
Package management pip + venv Maven / Gradle
Startup vs throughput Fast start, slower execution Slower start, JIT-optimised throughput

The comparison question to be ready for: "When would you pick Java over Python for a service?" "CPU-bound work that needs real parallelism, because Java has no GIL and can use all cores in one process. Large codebases with many contributors, where static types and compile-time checking pay for themselves in refactoring safety. Long-running, high-throughput services where JIT warm-up is amortised. I'd pick Python for data work, ML, scripting, and for getting something in front of users quickly — the ecosystem and the iteration speed are hard to beat."

2C.11 Question bank

Question Short answer The follow-up
Pass by value or reference? Always by value; for objects the reference is copied "So can a method change my object?" → yes, mutate; no, reassign
== vs .equals()? Reference identity vs content "Why does == work for "a"?" → string pool
Why is String immutable? Hash caching, thread safety, security, pooling "What do I use to build one in a loop?" → StringBuilder
equals/hashCode contract? Equal objects must have equal hash codes "What breaks if I skip hashCode?" → HashSet.contains returns false
How does HashMap work? Bucket array, hash → index, chain then tree at 8 "What happens on resize?" → double and rehash at 0.75 load
ArrayList vs LinkedList? ArrayList almost always; cache locality wins "When LinkedList?" → basically never; use ArrayDeque
Checked vs unchecked? Recoverable vs programming error "Are checked exceptions a good idea?" → have a position
What is type erasure? Generics are compile-time only "Why?" → backward compatibility with pre-generic code
What does final do? Depends on variable / method / class "Does it make the object immutable?" → no
Integer a = 128; a == b? false — outside the cache range "Why is 127 true?" → Integer cache −128..127
How does GC decide? Reachability from GC roots, generational "What causes a leak then?" → unintended reachability
String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer? Immutable / mutable / mutable + synchronised "Which in a loop?" → StringBuilder

2D
Part 2D

Object-Oriented Java, Properly

The same questions as Part 2A, but Java gives you real access modifiers, compile-time interfaces and sealed hierarchies — so some answers change.

Suggested time · 8 h

Java is where most people first meet OOP, which is unfortunate, because it means they learn the syntax of the four pillars without ever being asked why any of it exists.

This part mirrors Part 2A. Same questions — why a class, when not to, what does inheritance cost — but Java gives you tools Python doesn't (real access modifiers, compile-time interfaces, sealed hierarchies), so the answers change in interesting places.

2D.1 The same starting question: why a class? MUST KNOW

Unchanged from Part 2A: a class is for state that has invariants.

public class Account {
    private final String owner;
    private BigDecimal balance;          // private: nobody can reach past the rules

    public Account(String owner, BigDecimal balance) {
        if (balance.signum() < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative opening balance");
        this.owner = owner;
        this.balance = balance;
    }

    public void withdraw(BigDecimal amount) {
        if (amount.signum() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        if (amount.compareTo(balance) > 0) throw new InsufficientFundsException(amount, balance);
        balance = balance.subtract(amount);      // the ONLY path to a smaller balance
    }

    public BigDecimal balance() { return balance; }   // read-only to the outside
}

What Java adds over Python here is enforcement. In Python, _balance is a request. In Java, private is checked by the compiler: there is no legitimate way to reach balance from outside the class. The invariant is not a convention, it's a guarantee.

That difference is worth naming in an interview, because it explains why Java code tends to have more, smaller classes: the language actually rewards drawing boundaries.

And the same warning: when not to write one

  • A class with one method and no state is a function. In Java you can't have free functions, so it becomes a static method on a utility class — that's fine, and it's honest. Don't dress it up with a constructor and instance fields it doesn't need.
  • A bag of data with no rules should be a record, not a class with five getters.
  • A class where every method is static is a namespace. Mark it final with a private constructor so nobody instantiates it, and move on.
public final class Money {
    private Money() { }                                  // not instantiable
    public static BigDecimal round(BigDecimal v) { ... }
}

2D.2 Access modifiers: the thing Python doesn't have MUST KNOW

Modifier Same class Same package Subclass (other package) Anywhere
private ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌
(package-private, no keyword) ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌
protected ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌
public ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

Two things candidates usually get wrong:

  • The default is package-private, not public. It's genuinely useful — it lets a package expose a small public surface while its classes talk freely among themselves. Most people never use it deliberately, and mentioning it is a small differentiator.
  • protected also grants package access, which surprises people. It's wider than "subclasses only".

The principle: every public member is a promise you now have to keep. Start private, widen only when a real caller needs it. The reason Java teams end up with cleaner module boundaries than Python teams isn't discipline — it's that the compiler makes the boundary real.

Getters and setters — the nuance

The reflex "make fields private and generate getters and setters for all of them" produces a class with no encapsulation at all, just more typing. A setter for every field is exactly as exposed as a public field.

The real question is: which mutations does this object actually allow? withdraw(amount) is encapsulation; setBalance(x) is not. Expose operations, not fields.

2D.3 Interfaces vs abstract classes MUST KNOW

The most-asked Java design question, and modern Java changed the answer, so a stale answer stands out.

interface abstract class
Multiple inheritance ✅ implement many ❌ extend one
Instance state ❌ (only static final constants) ✅ fields
Constructors ❌ ✅
Method bodies ✅ since Java 8 (default, static, private) ✅ always
Access modifiers on members public by default any
Relationship expressed "can do" — a capability "is a" — a kind of thing

Since Java 8, interfaces can have default methods, so "interfaces can't have implementations" is no longer true and saying it dates you. What interfaces still can't have is instance state and constructors — and that is now the real distinction to lead with.

public interface Auditable {
    String auditId();                                  // the contract

    default String auditLine() {                       // shared behaviour, no state
        return "%s @ %s".formatted(auditId(), Instant.now());
    }
}

Why default methods were added

To let interfaces evolve without breaking every implementer. When Java 8 added stream() to Collection, every existing implementation in the world would have failed to compile — unless the new method came with a default body. Knowing that reason is much better than knowing the syntax.

The decision, stated cleanly

"I default to an interface, because it describes a capability without constraining the implementer's hierarchy — and a class can implement several. I use an abstract class when I need shared state or a constructor that enforces an invariant across subclasses, since interfaces still can't hold instance fields. In practice the strongest combination is a small interface for the contract plus, if it earns its place, an abstract base providing common implementation for those who want it — that's exactly the List / AbstractList pattern in the JDK."

The diamond problem with default methods: if two interfaces provide the same default method, the class must override it and can disambiguate with InterfaceName.super.method(). Java sidesteps the classic diamond by refusing to guess.

2D.4 Polymorphism and how dispatch actually works MUST KNOW

class Animal { void speak() { System.out.println("..."); } }
class Dog extends Animal { @Override void speak() { System.out.println("Woof"); } }

Animal a = new Dog();
a.speak();        // "Woof" — chosen by the RUNTIME type

Overriding is dynamic. The JVM looks at the object's actual class, not the reference's declared type. That's runtime polymorphism, and it's the mechanism behind every strategy/plugin design.

Overloading is static. Which overload runs is decided by the compiler from the declared types:

void print(Object o) { System.out.println("Object"); }
void print(String s) { System.out.println("String"); }

Object o = "hello";
print(o);         // "Object" — the compiler saw an Object reference

That surprises people, and it's a common trick question. Overriding = runtime, overloading = compile time.

Two more that follow the same rule: static methods are hidden, not overridden (dispatch is by declared type), and fields are never polymorphic — Animal a = new Dog(); a.name reads Animal's field.

@Override — always write it

It's not decoration. If your signature doesn't actually match anything in the parent, the compiler tells you. Without it, a typo silently creates a brand-new method that never gets called, and you spend an afternoon on it.

2D.5 Inheritance: the same costs, plus a Java-specific one MUST KNOW

Everything in Part 2A applies — the fragile base class problem, Liskov, "is-a in English isn't is-substitutable-for in code". Java adds one more consideration: you only get one superclass. Spending it on code reuse means you can't spend it on a genuine type relationship later.

// ❌ inheritance for reuse — and now UserService can never extend anything else
public class UserService extends JdbcTemplate { }

// ✅ composition
public class UserService {
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final CacheClient cache;
    public UserService(JdbcTemplate jdbc, CacheClient cache) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.cache = cache;
    }
}

The composition version also gets you constructor injection for free, which is exactly what Spring wants (Part 6B) and what makes the class unit-testable with mocks.

The Java-specific inheritance traps

Calling an overridable method from a constructor. The subclass's override runs before the subclass's fields are initialised:

class Base {
    Base() { init(); }                     // ❌ calls the override
    void init() { }
}
class Child extends Base {
    private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();
    @Override void init() { items.add("x"); }   // NullPointerException — items is still null
}

The rule: never call an overridable method from a constructor. Make it private, static or final.

Design for inheritance, or forbid it. If a class wasn't designed to be extended — no documented protected hooks, no thought about which methods are safe to override — mark it final. String and Integer are final for exactly this reason. "Leave it open just in case" is how fragile base classes are born.

2D.6 record, sealed, and modelling data properly SHOULD KNOW→MUST KNOW

public record Trade(String symbol, int qty, BigDecimal price) {

    public Trade {                                     // compact constructor: validation
        if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive");
        Objects.requireNonNull(symbol);
    }

    public BigDecimal notional() {                     // derived value
        return price.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(qty));
    }
}

A record gives you a final class, final fields, a canonical constructor, accessors, and correct equals/hashCode/toString — in one line. It is the direct counterpart to Python's @dataclass(frozen=True), and it should be your default for DTOs, value objects, and anything you'd otherwise write with five getters.

When a record is wrong: when the thing needs controlled mutation, when it needs to be extended, or when a framework requires a no-arg constructor and setters (older JPA entities, some serialisation libraries).

Sealed hierarchies — exhaustiveness the compiler checks

public sealed interface PaymentResult
        permits Approved, Declined, Pending { }

public record Approved(String chargeId) implements PaymentResult { }
public record Declined(String reason)   implements PaymentResult { }
public record Pending(Instant retryAt)  implements PaymentResult { }

String describe(PaymentResult r) {
    return switch (r) {
        case Approved a -> "charged " + a.chargeId();
        case Declined d -> "declined: " + d.reason();
        case Pending p  -> "retry at " + p.retryAt();
    };                                    // no default needed — the compiler knows the set is closed
}

Why this is worth mentioning: if someone later adds a fourth result type, every switch over PaymentResult stops compiling until it's handled. That converts a whole class of "we forgot to handle that case" production bugs into build failures. It's the closest Java gets to algebraic data types, and it's a genuinely strong thing to bring up.

2D.7 Immutability as a design default MUST KNOW

public final class Money {                              // final: no subclass can break it
    private final BigDecimal amount;                    // final fields
    private final Currency currency;

    public Money add(Money other) {
        requireSameCurrency(other);
        return new Money(amount.add(other.amount), currency);   // returns a NEW object
    }
}

Why immutability is the default worth arguing for: - Thread safety for free. An object that never changes needs no synchronisation. In a language with real threads, that is a much bigger deal than in Python. - Safe as a map key, because the hash can't drift. - No defensive copying when you pass it around; nobody can change it behind your back. - Easier reasoning. The value you read is the value that was there.

The cost is allocation: every change makes an object. Usually irrelevant — the JVM allocates young objects extremely cheaply and collects them almost for free — but in a genuinely hot loop, a mutable builder is the right escape hatch. That's the same trade as String vs StringBuilder.

Defensive copying, when you must hold mutable state:

private final List<String> tags;

public Order(List<String> tags) {
    this.tags = List.copyOf(tags);           // copy in — caller can't mutate ours afterwards
}
public List<String> tags() {
    return Collections.unmodifiableList(tags);   // don't hand out the live list
}

Returning the internal collection directly is one of the most common real encapsulation leaks in Java code. final on the field stops reassignment; it does nothing about the contents.

2D.8 Static nested vs inner classes SHOULD KNOW

public class Outer {
    private int value;

    static class Nested { }        // independent — no reference to Outer
    class Inner { }                // holds an implicit reference to the Outer instance
}

The practical point: an inner (non-static) class keeps its outer instance alive. Put one in a long-lived collection and you've pinned the entire outer object, which is a classic memory leak.

Rule: make nested classes static unless they genuinely need the outer instance. Effective Java says so, and interviewers who know the book will notice.

2D.9 Trade-off drills MUST KNOW

Q1. "Interface or abstract class for a PaymentProvider?"

Think first, then open

Interface. It's a capability — "this thing can charge and refund" — and it doesn't need state. It also leaves implementers free to extend something else, which matters when you're wrapping a vendor SDK class.

I'd add an abstract base only if several providers genuinely shared state or setup — a common HTTP client, retry configuration, shared logging. Even then I'd keep the interface as the type in every signature and treat the abstract class as an optional convenience, so a provider that doesn't fit the base can still participate.

The JDK pattern to cite: List (interface) plus AbstractList (optional convenience base).

Q2. "You need to add a method to an interface with 40 implementers. Options?"

Think first, then open

A default method — that's precisely why they were added in Java 8. All 40 keep compiling; those that need different behaviour override it.

The caveat to raise: a default method has no access to instance state, so it can only be written in terms of other interface methods. If the sensible implementation needs fields, a default won't work and you've got a real migration.

The alternative, if the new method genuinely doesn't belong to every implementer, is a second interface. Adding a method that half the implementers must throw UnsupportedOperationException from is an interface-segregation violation, and a default that lies is worse than a compile error.

Q3. "Why is String final? What breaks if it weren't?"

Think first, then open

Because a subclass could override equals, hashCode, or length and lie. That breaks everything downstream: the string pool could hand out an instance that isn't really equal to itself, HashMap keys become unreliable, and — the security case — a path or URL could be validated by a permission check and then report different contents afterwards.

Immutability plus final is what makes String safe to share freely across threads and cache aggressively. The general principle: if a class's guarantees matter to code that didn't write it, don't let anyone subclass it.

Q4. "You have equals overridden but HashSet.contains returns false. Diagnose."

Think first, then open

Almost certainly hashCode wasn't overridden, so equal objects hash to different buckets and the set never even reaches the equals comparison.

Two other candidates worth naming: hashCode uses different fields than equals, or a field used in hashCode was mutated after the object was added — the object is now sitting in the wrong bucket and is unreachable, which is why hash-key fields should be immutable.

The fix I'd reach for: make it a record if the shape allows, since it generates both from all components and can't drift.

Q5. "Should this class be final?"

Think first, then open

Default to yes, unless I've deliberately designed it for extension.

Designing for extension is real work: deciding which methods are safe to override, documenting the self-use (which internal methods call which), providing protected hooks, and never calling an overridable method from the constructor. If I haven't done that work, leaving the class open is offering a guarantee I can't keep, and any change I make later may break a subclass I've never seen.

The counter-consideration is testability with mocking frameworks that need to subclass — though modern mocks handle finals, and depending on an interface avoids the question entirely.

Q6. "Record or class for an API response object?"

Think first, then open

Record, in almost every case. It's immutable, gets correct equals/hashCode/toString, and states clearly that it's a value rather than an entity with behaviour. Jackson supports records natively.

I'd fall back to a class when a framework demands a no-arg constructor and setters — some older JPA and serialisation setups — or when the object needs to change after construction, which usually means it's an entity rather than a DTO and shouldn't be crossing the API boundary anyway.

The broader point: keeping API DTOs separate from persistence entities means an internal column can't silently leak into the public contract. That applies in any language — it's the same argument as separate input and output schemas in Part 6.

Q7. "Two classes share 40 lines of logic. Inheritance, interface default method, or a helper?"

Think first, then open

Same answer as Part 2A, with Java's extra constraint.

Default to a helper — a static method on a utility class, or better, its own small collaborator class that both compose. No coupling, independently testable, no inheritance slot spent.

A default method only if the logic can be expressed purely in terms of the interface's own methods, since it can't touch fields.

Inheritance only if the two really are the same kind of thing and callers would want the base type in a signature. Remember you only get one superclass — spending it on code reuse forecloses a genuine type relationship later.

2D.10 Question bank

Question Short answer Follow-up
Interface vs abstract class? Capability vs kind-of; interfaces have no instance state "Can interfaces have code?" → yes since 8, default
Why were default methods added? So interfaces could evolve without breaking implementers "Example?" → Collection.stream() in Java 8
Overloading vs overriding? Compile-time vs runtime dispatch "Object o = "hi"; print(o)?" → the Object overload
Can you override a static method? No — it's hidden; dispatch is by declared type "What about fields?" → also not polymorphic
Why final on String? Guarantees can't be subverted; pooling and security "What else is final?" → boxed primitives, records
What does a record give you? Final class, final fields, accessors, equals/hashCode/toString "When not?" → mutation needed, or a framework wants setters
What are sealed types for? A closed set the compiler can check exhaustively "What's the payoff?" → adding a case breaks the build, not production
Static nested vs inner class? Inner holds a reference to the outer instance "Why care?" → leaks, keeps the outer alive
Default access modifier? Package-private, not public "Is that useful?" → yes, real package boundaries
Why not call overridable methods in a constructor? The override runs before subclass fields are initialised "Fix?" → make it private, static or final
How do you make a class immutable? final class, final private fields, no setters, defensive copies "Why bother?" → thread safety with no locks

2E
Part 2E

Java Lambdas, Streams and Concurrency

A lambda is an instance of a functional interface, not a function object. Streams, Optional, and real threads — where Java differs most from Python.

Suggested time · 10 h

Part 2B made the case that in Python, a function is just an object and everything functional follows from that. Java gets to a similar place by a different route, and the route matters:

A Java lambda is not a function object. It is an instance of a functional interface.

There are no free-floating functions in Java. When you write x -> x * 2, the compiler works out which single-abstract-method interface you meant and builds an implementation of it. That's why Java lambdas need a target type, why they can only appear where an interface is expected, and why the standard library ships a fixed catalogue of them.

2E.1 Functional interfaces and lambdas MUST KNOW

A functional interface is any interface with exactly one abstract method. That's the whole definition.

@FunctionalInterface                     // optional, but it makes the compiler enforce it
interface Validator {
    boolean test(String input);
}

Validator notEmpty = s -> !s.isBlank();  // the lambda IS a Validator

The built-in ones you must know MUST KNOW

Interface Signature Reads as Used by
Function<T,R> R apply(T) transform map
Predicate<T> boolean test(T) test filter
Consumer<T> void accept(T) do something, return nothing forEach
Supplier<T> T get() produce, take nothing lazy defaults, orElseGet
BiFunction<T,U,R> R apply(T,U) combine two merge
UnaryOperator<T> T apply(T) transform, same type replaceAll
BinaryOperator<T> T apply(T,T) fold two into one reduce

There are primitive specialisations (IntPredicate, ToIntFunction, IntUnaryOperator…) whose entire purpose is avoiding autoboxing. IntStream.sum() over a million ints allocates nothing; Stream<Integer> allocates a million boxed objects. That's a real, measurable difference and a good detail to volunteer.

Method references — four flavours

users.forEach(System.out::println);        // instance method of a particular object
names.stream().map(String::toUpperCase);   // instance method of an arbitrary receiver
strings.stream().map(Integer::parseInt);   // static method
list.stream().map(User::new);              // constructor

Prefer a method reference when the lambda would just call one method — String::toUpperCase reads better than s -> s.toUpperCase(). Prefer a lambda the moment anything else is happening.

Effectively final MUST KNOW

int count = 0;
list.forEach(x -> count++);      // compile error: must be final or effectively final

A lambda captures the value, not the variable — so Java simply forbids capturing something that changes. This is the deliberate opposite of Python's late-binding closure trap in Part 2B: Python lets you capture a mutating variable and surprises you at run time; Java refuses to compile.

The workaround is to not need mutable capture: use stream().count(), an AtomicInteger if you genuinely need a shared counter, or a reduce. If you find yourself reaching for a one-element array to smuggle state out of a lambda, that's the language telling you to write a loop.

2E.2 Streams MUST KNOW

A stream is not a collection. It holds no data. It's a description of a computation over a source, and nothing happens until a terminal operation asks for a result.

List<String> topSymbols = trades.stream()          // source
    .filter(t -> t.qty() > 100)                    // intermediate — lazy
    .map(Trade::symbol)                            // intermediate — lazy
    .distinct()                                    // intermediate — lazy
    .sorted()                                      // intermediate — STATEFUL
    .limit(10)                                     // intermediate — short-circuiting
    .toList();                                     // TERMINAL — now it runs

The three properties that explain everything about streams

1. Lazy. Intermediate operations build a pipeline; nothing executes until the terminal operation. A stream with no terminal operation does literally nothing — a classic "why doesn't my code run?" bug:

list.stream().map(this::save);      // ❌ never executes anything

2. One element at a time, all the way through. Elements are pulled through the whole pipeline individually, not stage by stage. So filter runs on element 1, then map runs on element 1, then element 2 enters. That's what allows short-circuiting:

huge.stream().filter(expensive).findFirst();     // stops at the first match

This is the same pull model as the Python generator pipeline in Part 2B, and the same benefit.

3. Single use. Once consumed, a stream is dead. Reusing one throws IllegalStateException. If you need two passes, you need two streams (or a collection).

Stateful vs stateless operations SHOULD KNOW

map, filter, peek are stateless — each element is handled independently. sorted, distinct, limit, skip are stateful — they need to see other elements. sorted in particular must buffer the entire stream before it can emit anything, which quietly destroys laziness and makes sorted on an infinite stream hang forever.

Practical consequence: put filter before map and before sorted. Filtering first means less work for every later stage, and it's the most common easy win in stream code.

collect and the Collectors worth knowing MUST KNOW

import static java.util.stream.Collectors.*;

List<String> list   = s.collect(toList());        // or .toList() in 16+ (immutable)
Set<String> set     = s.collect(toSet());
String joined       = s.collect(joining(", ", "[", "]"));

Map<String, List<Trade>> bySymbol =
    trades.stream().collect(groupingBy(Trade::symbol));

Map<String, Long> countBySymbol =
    trades.stream().collect(groupingBy(Trade::symbol, counting()));

Map<String, BigDecimal> notionalBySymbol =
    trades.stream().collect(groupingBy(Trade::symbol,
        reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO, Trade::notional, BigDecimal::add)));

Map<Boolean, List<Trade>> partitioned =
    trades.stream().collect(partitioningBy(t -> t.qty() > 100));

Map<String, Trade> byId =
    trades.stream().collect(toMap(Trade::id, t -> t));   // throws on duplicate keys!

groupingBy with a downstream collector is the workhorse — it's GROUP BY with an aggregate, and it's worth being fluent in.

Two traps: - toMap throws IllegalStateException on a duplicate key. Pass a merge function: toMap(Trade::id, t -> t, (a, b) -> b). - Collectors.toList() gives no mutability guarantee; .toList() (Java 16+) returns an immutable list. If you then call .add(), you get UnsupportedOperationException — worth knowing which one you used.

reduce

Optional<BigDecimal> total = amounts.stream().reduce(BigDecimal::add);       // may be empty
BigDecimal total = amounts.stream().reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add); // with identity

The identity form is safer and is what you almost always want. Same reasoning as Python's reduce(f, xs, initial): it handles the empty case and lets the accumulator differ in type.

And the same verdict as Part 2B: for sums and counts there are better-named tools. mapToInt(Trade::qty).sum() says what it means and avoids boxing.

2E.3 When NOT to use a stream MUST KNOW

This is the part that separates people who've used streams from people who've read about them.

Don't use a stream when a loop is clearer.

// stream, for no benefit
IntStream.range(0, list.size()).forEach(i -> process(list.get(i)));

// loop, obviously better
for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) process(list.get(i));

Don't use a stream when you need to break out early with side effects, or return from the middle. A lambda can't return from the enclosing method, can't break, and can't continue. Contorting a stream around that produces worse code than the loop.

Don't use a stream when checked exceptions are involved. Lambdas can't throw checked exceptions, so you end up wrapping everything in try/catch inside the lambda — noisy and worse than a plain loop. This is one of the strongest practical arguments against checked exceptions generally.

Don't mutate external state from a stream.

List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
list.stream().forEach(out::add);          // ❌ works, but it's a loop in disguise
List<String> out = list.stream().toList(); // ✅

With a parallel stream the mutating version is an outright data race.

Debugging cost is real. Stepping through a stream in a debugger is unpleasant, and a stack trace goes through lambda frames with synthetic names. peek helps for logging, but a loop you can breakpoint is sometimes the honest choice.

The balanced answer: "Streams are excellent for declarative transformations — filter, map, group, collect — where the intent is clearer than the mechanics. I use a loop when I need early exit with side effects, when checked exceptions are involved, when I'm mutating something, or when the stream version needs more mental effort than the loop. Clarity decides it, not fashion."

2E.4 Parallel streams — and why they're usually the wrong answer MUST KNOW

list.parallelStream().map(this::transform).toList();

One word, and now you're multi-threaded. That's the danger.

What actually happens: the work is split and run on the common ForkJoinPool, which by default has cores − 1 threads and is shared by the entire JVM. A blocking task in a parallel stream starves every other parallel stream in your application.

Parallel helps only when all of these hold: - The data set is genuinely large (rule of thumb: tens of thousands of elements or more). - The per-element work is CPU-bound, not I/O. - The source splits cheaply — ArrayList and arrays do; LinkedList and Stream.iterate do not. - The operations are stateless and side-effect free. - The merge step is cheap. groupingBy into a HashMap in parallel can cost more in merging than parallelism saves.

Never use a parallel stream for I/O. Blocking calls hold ForkJoinPool threads hostage. Use a dedicated ExecutorService, or CompletableFuture with your own pool.

The answer that shows judgement: "I'd measure before and after, because parallel streams are frequently slower — the split and merge overhead plus the boxing usually beats the gains unless the data set is large and the work is CPU-bound. I'd also never put blocking I/O in one, because it runs on the shared common pool and can starve the rest of the application."

Since Java 21, virtual threads are the better tool for I/O concurrency: cheap to create by the thousand, and they release the carrier thread while blocked. Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Mentioning it signals you're current.

2E.5 Optional MUST KNOW

Optional exists to make "there might be no value" visible in the type, so the compiler can remind you instead of a NullPointerException doing it in production.

Optional<User> findById(String id);                     // the signature tells you it may be empty

String name = findById(id)
    .map(User::name)
    .filter(n -> !n.isBlank())
    .orElse("unknown");

findById(id).ifPresentOrElse(this::send, () -> log.warn("no user {}", id));

User user = findById(id)
    .orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id));      // the idiomatic "must exist"

orElse vs orElseGet — the trap. orElse(expensive()) evaluates its argument every time, even when the Optional has a value. orElseGet(() -> expensive()) only evaluates on the empty path. If the fallback does work, always use orElseGet.

Where Optional should and should not appear

Place Use it? Why
Return type of a method that may find nothing ✅ This is what it's for
Field of a class ❌ Not Serializable, adds an object per field
Method parameter ❌ The caller now has to wrap; use an overload instead
Collection element ❌ An empty collection already means "nothing"

Never call .get() without checking. optional.get() on an empty Optional throws NoSuchElementException — you've reintroduced the null pointer with extra steps and a worse message. Use orElseThrow with a meaningful exception.

Interview line: "Optional is a return type, not a general null replacement. It makes absence part of the API contract, which is the whole benefit. Putting it in fields or parameters adds allocation and ceremony without giving you that benefit — a nullable field with @Nullable and an overloaded method are better tools for those jobs."

2E.6 Concurrency — where Java differs most from Python MUST KNOW

Python has the GIL, so threads are for I/O and processes are for CPU. Java has real threads with true parallelism, which means genuine speedups on multiple cores — and genuine race conditions, visibility bugs and deadlocks.

The two problems concurrency creates

1. Race conditions (atomicity). count++ is three operations: read, add, write. Two threads can interleave and lose an update.

2. Visibility. Each thread may cache values; without synchronisation, one thread's write may never become visible to another. A thread can loop forever on a boolean running flag another thread already set to false. volatile fixes visibility (and forbids reordering) but does not make compound operations like ++ atomic.

The toolkit, cheapest first

// 1. Don't share mutable state at all — immutability, or confinement to one thread
// 2. Atomics — lock-free, for single variables
AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
counter.incrementAndGet();

// 3. Concurrent collections
Map<String, Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum);              // atomic read-modify-write

// 4. synchronized — mutual exclusion, gives both atomicity AND visibility
synchronized (lock) { shared.add(x); }

// 5. Explicit locks — when you need tryLock, timeouts, or fairness
ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

// 6. Executors — never create raw threads in application code
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
Future<Result> f = pool.submit(task);

The ordering matters and is worth stating: "The cheapest fix is not to share mutable state — immutable objects need no synchronisation at all. Then atomics for a single variable, then concurrent collections, and synchronized only when I need to make several operations atomic together. Every lock I add is a chance for contention and deadlock."

CompletableFuture for composition SHOULD KNOW

CompletableFuture<Quote> q = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchQuote(sym), pool);
CompletableFuture<Position> p = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchPosition(sym), pool);

q.thenCombine(p, this::buildView)
 .exceptionally(ex -> fallbackView(sym))
 .thenAccept(this::render);

The two fetches run concurrently; thenCombine joins them. Always pass your own executor — the default is the shared common pool.

Deadlock, and the one-line prevention

Two threads each holding a lock the other wants. The standard prevention: always acquire locks in a consistent global order (for example, ascending account ID in a transfer). Also: keep critical sections short, never do I/O while holding a lock, and prefer tryLock with a timeout when you can't guarantee ordering.

2E.7 Trade-off drills MUST KNOW

Q1. "Rewrite this loop as a stream. Should you?" — a loop that filters orders, calls an API for each, and collects results.

Think first, then open

Probably not, for two reasons.

The API call likely throws a checked exception, and lambdas can't. You'd end up with try/catch inside the lambda, which is noisier than the loop.

The call is I/O, so the interesting optimisation isn't stream syntax, it's concurrency — and parallelStream is the wrong tool because it blocks the shared common pool. The right shape is an ExecutorService (or virtual threads on 21+) with CompletableFuture, or a batch endpoint if the API has one.

I'd stream the pure filtering and mapping and keep the I/O in an explicit structure where failure handling is visible.

Q2. "Why is parallelStream() slower here?" — a parallel stream over a 200-element LinkedList.

Think first, then open

Three reasons stack up.

Too little data. 200 elements can't repay thread coordination; the fork/join overhead dominates.

LinkedList splits badly. The framework has to traverse to split, so the partitions are uneven and computing them costs O(n). ArrayList and arrays split by index in constant time.

Boxing, if the elements are boxed numbers — millions of small allocations, and cache behaviour to match.

And the shape of the answer matters more than the list: I'd say I measured it, because "parallel is slower" is only credible with a number.

Q3. "orElse or orElseGet here?" — fallback is userRepository.findDefault().

Think first, then open

orElseGet. orElse evaluates its argument eagerly — so orElse(userRepository.findDefault()) hits the database on every call, including the ones where the Optional was present and the value is thrown away.

orElse is fine for a cheap constant like orElse("unknown"). The rule: if the fallback does any work, it must be orElseGet.

The same distinction applies to orElseThrow(() -> new NotFound(id)) — the supplier form avoids constructing an exception (and capturing a stack trace) on the happy path.

Q4. "Your HashMap is shared across threads. synchronized, Collections.synchronizedMap, or ConcurrentHashMap?"

Think first, then open

ConcurrentHashMap, and it isn't close.

Collections.synchronizedMap puts one lock around the whole map, so every reader blocks every other reader — and it still isn't safe for compound operations, because if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) is two calls with a gap. ConcurrentHashMap locks per bucket, so unrelated keys don't contend, and it gives atomic compound operations: putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, merge.

My own synchronized block is the right answer only when I need several operations across different structures to be atomic together — and then I'd think hard about whether that shared state should exist.

Q5. "Where should Optional appear in your API?"

Think first, then open

Return types, where absence is a legitimate outcome — a lookup that may find nothing. That puts "might be empty" into the signature so the caller can't ignore it.

Not fields: it's an extra object per field, it isn't Serializable, and a nullable field with @Nullable documents the same thing for free.

Not parameters: it forces every caller to wrap, including the ones that definitely have a value. Two overloads are clearer.

Not inside collections: an empty list already expresses "no elements", and List<Optional<T>> makes every consumer do double work.

Q6. "You need a counter incremented from a lambda. It won't compile. Now what?"

Think first, then open

The compile error is the language doing its job — captured variables must be effectively final, because the lambda captures a value and mutation would be a race waiting to happen.

The question to ask is what I actually want. If I want a count, stream().filter(p).count() is the answer and I never needed the variable. If I want a sum, mapToInt(...).sum(). If I genuinely need a shared counter across threads, AtomicInteger or LongAdder (better under high contention).

Wrapping the value in a one-element array to smuggle it out compiles, but it's fighting the design — at that point the loop is the honest choice.

2E.8 Question bank

Question Short answer Follow-up
What is a functional interface? An interface with exactly one abstract method "Name four built-in ones" → Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier
Is a stream a collection? No — it holds no data, it describes a computation "So when does it run?" → at the terminal operation
Intermediate vs terminal? Lazy pipeline steps vs the one that triggers execution "Name a stateful intermediate" → sorted, distinct
Can you reuse a stream? No — IllegalStateException "How do you do two passes?" → collect first
map vs flatMap? 1→1 vs 1→many, flattened one level "Example?" → list of orders → all their line items
Collectors.toList() vs .toList()? No mutability guarantee vs immutable "What breaks?" → .add() throws
When is parallelStream worth it? Large, CPU-bound, cheaply splittable, side-effect free "Why not for I/O?" → blocks the shared common pool
orElse vs orElseGet? Eager vs lazy fallback "Which for a DB lookup?" → orElseGet
Why must captured variables be final? Lambdas capture values; mutation would be a race "Workaround?" → don't need it; or AtomicInteger
volatile vs synchronized? Visibility only vs visibility + atomicity "Does volatile fix count++?" → no
ConcurrentHashMap vs synchronizedMap? Bucket-level locking + atomic compounds vs one global lock "Give an atomic compound" → merge, computeIfAbsent
Java concurrency vs Python's? Real parallelism, no GIL — and real race conditions "So what's harder?" → visibility, locking, deadlock

Part 3

JavaScript for React / Full Stack Interviews

Mostly output prediction and “what’s the bug”. Scope, this, the event loop, and async you can reason about.

Suggested time · 8 h

JavaScript rounds are mostly output prediction and "what's the bug". They test whether you understand scope, this, and the event loop — not whether you've memorised API surface.

3.1 var / let / const and hoisting MUST KNOW

Scope Hoisted? Re-declare Re-assign
var function yes, initialised to undefined yes yes
let block yes, but in the temporal dead zone no yes
const block same as let no no (binding is fixed)

Hoisting means declarations are processed before any code runs. var declarations are initialised to undefined; let/const are not initialised, so touching them before the declaration throws.

console.log(a);   // undefined
var a = 1;

console.log(b);   // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
let b = 1;

const does not mean immutable:

const user = { name: "A" };
user.name = "B";        // fine — the object is mutable
user = {};              // TypeError — the binding is not

Use Object.freeze() for shallow immutability.

The classic loop question MUST KNOW

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));   // 3 3 3
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));   // 0 1 2

Why: var has one function-scoped binding, so all three callbacks close over the same i, which is 3 by the time the timers fire. let creates a fresh binding per iteration. Pre-ES6 you'd fix this with an IIFE that captures the value.

This is the exact same bug as the Python [lambda: i for i in range(3)] trap. Mentioning the parallel is a good move.

3.2 Closures MUST KNOW

A function plus the lexical environment it was created in.

function counter() {
  let count = 0;                     // private state
  return {
    increment: () => ++count,
    get: () => count,
  };
}
const c = counter();
c.increment();  c.get();   // 1

Why it matters in interviews: closures are the mechanism behind module privacy, useState in React, debounce/throttle, memoisation, and event handlers that "remember" data. Almost every practical JS question uses one.

Memory note: closures keep their captured scope alive. A closure holding a large array prevents it being garbage collected — a real source of leaks in long-lived apps.

3.3 this MUST KNOW (the highest-frequency JS interview topic)

this is determined by how a function is called, not where it's defined. Four rules, checked in this order:

  1. new binding — new Foo() → this is the new object.
  2. Explicit binding — f.call(obj), f.apply(obj), f.bind(obj) → this is obj.
  3. Implicit binding — obj.f() → this is obj.
  4. Default — plain f() → undefined in strict mode / modules, globalThis otherwise.

Arrow functions break all four: they have no this of their own; they inherit it lexically from the enclosing scope at definition time. That's why they can't be used as constructors and why bind has no effect on them.

const obj = {
  name: "A",
  regular() { return this.name; },        // "A"
  arrow: () => this?.name,                // undefined — 'this' is the module scope
  delayed() {
    setTimeout(function () { console.log(this.name); }, 0);   // undefined
    setTimeout(() => console.log(this.name), 0);              // "A"
  },
};

The lost-this bug (extremely common):

const fn = obj.regular;
fn();                       // undefined — the call site lost the object

const bound = obj.regular.bind(obj);
bound();                    // "A"

This is why React class components needed this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this) in the constructor — and why arrow-function class fields replaced it.

call vs apply vs bind: call(thisArg, a, b) invokes immediately with individual args; apply(thisArg, [a, b]) invokes immediately with an array; bind returns a new permanently-bound function without invoking it.

3.4 The event loop MUST KNOW

The model to say out loud:

JavaScript has a single call stack. Asynchronous work is handed off to the runtime (browser or Node). When it completes, the callback is placed in a queue. The event loop moves a callback onto the stack only when the stack is empty. There are two queues: the microtask queue (promises, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) and the macrotask queue (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O). After every task, the entire microtask queue is drained before the next macrotask runs.

That last sentence is the whole answer to every output-ordering question.

Call stack  ->  runs synchronous code
                    |
                    v
   [ all microtasks drained ]  <- promises
                    |
                    v
   [ one macrotask ]           <- setTimeout, I/O
                    |
                    v  (repeat)

The canonical question:

console.log("1");
setTimeout(() => console.log("2"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3"));
console.log("4");
// 1, 4, 3, 2

Sync code runs first (1, 4). Then the microtask queue drains (3). Then the macrotask (2). setTimeout(…, 0) does not mean "now" — it means "after the current task and all pending microtasks".

Harder variant:

async function f() {
  console.log("A");
  await null;                 // everything after await is a microtask
  console.log("B");
}
f();
console.log("C");
// A, C, B

async functions run synchronously up to the first await. The rest is scheduled as a microtask.

3.5 Promises and async/await MUST KNOW

// Promise chain
fetchUser(id)
  .then(user => fetchOrders(user.id))
  .then(orders => render(orders))
  .catch(err => showError(err))       // catches errors from any earlier step
  .finally(() => setLoading(false));

// async/await — same thing, readable
async function load(id) {
  try {
    const user = await fetchUser(id);
    const orders = await fetchOrders(user.id);
    render(orders);
  } catch (err) {
    showError(err);
  } finally {
    setLoading(false);
  }
}

States: pending → fulfilled or rejected. Settled promises never change.

The combinators — know all four:

Method Resolves when Rejects when
Promise.all all fulfil (array of results) any rejects (fail fast)
Promise.allSettled all settle (array of {status, value/reason}) never
Promise.race first to settle, either way first settles as a rejection
Promise.any first to fulfil all reject (AggregateError)

The performance mistake interviewers look for MUST KNOW

// Sequential — 3 seconds if each takes 1s
const a = await fetchA();
const b = await fetchB();
const c = await fetchC();

// Parallel — 1 second
const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB(), fetchC()]);

Use await in sequence only when a later call depends on an earlier result.

Other traps: - forEach does not await: arr.forEach(async x => await f(x)) returns immediately. Use for...of for sequential, Promise.all(arr.map(...)) for parallel. - An unhandled rejection is a crash in Node and a console error in browsers. Always terminate chains with .catch or wrap in try. - await in a loop is sequential by design — sometimes correct (rate limiting), often accidental.

3.6 Prototypes and classes SHOULD KNOW

Every object has an internal link ([[Prototype]], exposed as __proto__) to another object. Property lookup walks that chain until it finds the property or hits null.

function Animal(name) { this.name = name; }
Animal.prototype.speak = function () { return `${this.name} makes a sound`; };

class Dog extends Animal {
  speak() { return `${this.name} barks`; }   // overrides via the prototype chain
}

Interview line: "JavaScript classes are syntactic sugar over prototypal inheritance. class doesn't add a new inheritance model — methods still live on Constructor.prototype and lookup still walks the chain. The differences are that class bodies are always strict mode, classes aren't hoisted in a usable way, and you must call new."

Object.create(proto) makes the prototype link explicit. instanceof walks the prototype chain.

3.7 Array methods you must be fluent in MUST KNOW

arr.map(x => x * 2)                       // transform, same length
arr.filter(x => x > 2)                    // subset
arr.reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0)        // fold to one value
arr.find(x => x.id === 3)                 // first match, or undefined
arr.findIndex(...)  arr.some(...)  arr.every(...)  arr.includes(...)
arr.flat(2)   arr.flatMap(x => [x, x])
arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)                 // MUTATES; default sort is lexicographic!
[...arr].sort(...)                        // non-mutating

The sort trap: [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9] because the default comparator converts to strings. Always pass a comparator for numbers.

reduce for grouping (the practical interview use):

const byRole = users.reduce((acc, u) => {
  (acc[u.role] ||= []).push(u);
  return acc;
}, {});

Mutating vs non-mutating matters in React: - Mutating: push, pop, splice, sort, reverse, shift, unshift - Non-mutating: map, filter, slice, concat, [...spread], toSorted (newer)

3.8 Copying and equality MUST KNOW

const shallow = { ...obj };               // nested objects still shared
const shallow2 = Object.assign({}, obj);
const deep = structuredClone(obj);        // modern, handles Dates/Maps/cycles
const crude = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj));  // loses Date, undefined, functions, NaN

Reference vs value:

{} === {}                 // false — different objects
[1] === [1]               // false
"a" === "a"               // true — primitives compare by value

== does type coercion; === doesn't. Always use ===, with one accepted exception: x == null checks for both null and undefined in one go.

Notorious coercion results (know a couple, don't memorise the list): [] == false → true, null == undefined → true, NaN === NaN → false (use Number.isNaN), 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3.

3.9 Debounce and throttle MUST KNOW (frequently asked to implement)

Debounce — run only after activity has stopped for N ms. Use for search-as-you-type, autosave, resize handlers.

Throttle — run at most once per N ms regardless of how often it's called. Use for scroll handlers, mousemove, rate-limiting API calls.

function debounce(fn, delay) {
  let timer;
  return function (...args) {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), delay);
  };
}

function throttle(fn, limit) {
  let waiting = false;
  return function (...args) {
    if (waiting) return;
    fn.apply(this, args);
    waiting = true;
    setTimeout(() => (waiting = false), limit);
  };
}

Write these from memory. Note the function (not arrow) so this forwards correctly, and ...args so arguments pass through — interviewers watch for both.

3.10 Event delegation, bubbling, capturing SHOULD KNOW

Events propagate: capture (window → target), then target, then bubble (target → window). Listeners default to the bubble phase.

Event delegation — attach one listener to a parent and inspect event.target:

list.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  const item = e.target.closest("li");
  if (item) handle(item.dataset.id);
});

Why: one listener instead of a thousand (memory + setup cost), and it automatically works for elements added to the DOM later. That second reason is the one candidates forget.

e.stopPropagation() halts propagation; e.preventDefault() cancels the default browser action. They are not the same thing.

3.11 Modules SHOULD KNOW

export const x = 1;              // named
export default function () {}    // default
import def, { x as y } from "./m.js";
const mod = await import("./m.js");   // dynamic — enables code splitting

ESM is static (imports are hoisted and analysable, which is what makes tree-shaking possible) and always strict mode. CommonJS (require/module.exports) is dynamic and synchronous — still the Node default in many projects.

3.12 Output questions — practise these

// 1
console.log(typeof null);                      // "object"  (historic bug)
console.log(typeof NaN);                       // "number"
console.log([] + {});                          // "[object Object]"
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);                // false

// 2
const o = { a: 1 };
const p = o;
p.a = 2;
console.log(o.a);                              // 2 — same reference

// 3
function f() { return this; }
const g = f.bind({x: 1});
const h = g.bind({x: 2});
console.log(h().x);                            // 1 — bind can't be re-bound

// 4
console.log("start");
setTimeout(() => console.log("timeout"));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("promise"));
(async () => { console.log("async body"); await 0; console.log("after await"); })();
console.log("end");
// start, async body, end, promise, after await, timeout

// 5
let x = 1;
{ let x = 2; console.log(x); }                 // 2
console.log(x);                                // 1

How to answer these: don't just say the output. Say why. "typeof null is 'object' because of how values were tagged in the original 1995 implementation — it's a known bug kept for backwards compatibility."

3.13 JavaScript question bank

Question 15-second answer Follow-up they'll ask
var vs let Function vs block scope; TDZ on let "Show me the loop + setTimeout difference"
What's a closure Function + its captured lexical scope "Where does React use one?" → useState
How does this work Determined by call site; four binding rules "What about arrow functions?"
Event loop Single stack; microtasks drain fully between macrotasks Output-ordering puzzle
Promise.all vs allSettled Fail-fast vs collect-everything "Which for a dashboard with 5 independent widgets?" → allSettled
== vs === Coercion vs strict "When is == acceptable?" → x == null
Shallow vs deep copy Spread copies one level; structuredClone recurses "Why does JSON round-tripping lose data?"
Debounce vs throttle After silence vs at most once per interval "Which for infinite scroll?" → throttle
Event delegation One parent listener + e.target "Why not just add listeners to each?"
Prototype chain Lookup walks [[Prototype]] links "Are ES6 classes different?" → sugar only
Hoisting Declarations processed first; let sits in TDZ "What's the TDZ for?" → catch use-before-declare
