Part 4

React Interview Preparation

Why a component re-renders, hooks without the bugs, and how a production app is actually structured.

Suggested time · 10 h

React rounds test three things: do you understand why a component re-renders, can you use hooks without creating bugs, and can you structure a real application. Everything else is detail.

4.1 The mental model MUST KNOW

React is a function of state. UI = f(state). You don't manipulate the DOM; you describe what the UI should look like for the current state, and React works out the minimal DOM changes.

The three consequences that explain almost all React behaviour:

  1. Rendering is calling your component function. It produces a description (React elements), not DOM.
  2. State changes trigger a re-render. So does a parent re-rendering, or a context value changing.
  3. Every render has its own props, state, and closures. This is why stale-closure bugs happen in useEffect and setTimeout.

4.2 Virtual DOM and reconciliation MUST KNOW

WHAT — an in-memory tree of plain objects describing the UI.

PROBLEM IT SOLVES — direct DOM manipulation is verbose and error-prone, and naive full re-renders are slow because DOM operations are expensive. The virtual DOM lets React compare the new description to the previous one and apply only the differences.

HOW — the diffing heuristics: - Different element type at the same position → tear down the subtree and rebuild it. - Same type → keep the DOM node, update only changed attributes, recurse into children. - Children in a list are matched by key.

The honest framing to use in an interview: "The virtual DOM isn't faster than perfectly hand-written DOM updates — it's a way to get good enough performance while writing declarative code. The win is developer experience with a predictable performance ceiling."

That nuance impresses interviewers, because the usual candidate answer is "virtual DOM is fast" which isn't really true.

Why keys matter MUST KNOW

{items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} ... />)}      // BUG if the list reorders/inserts
{items.map(item => <Row key={item.id} ... />)}     // correct

With index keys, inserting at the front shifts every item's key. React thinks item 0's content changed rather than that a new item appeared, so it mutates every row instead of inserting one — and any component state (an input's value, a checkbox) stays attached to the wrong item. Stable IDs let React match elements across renders correctly.

Index keys are acceptable only when the list is static, never reordered, never filtered, and items have no state.

4.3 State and props MUST KNOW

Props — read-only inputs from the parent. State — data the component owns and can change.

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Three rules of state:

  1. Never mutate it. React compares by reference (Object.is). Mutating an object leaves the reference the same, so React sees no change and skips the re-render.
items.push(newItem); setItems(items);      // BUG — no re-render
setItems([...items, newItem]);             // correct
setUser({ ...user, name: "A" });           // correct
  1. Updates are asynchronous and batched.
setCount(count + 1);
setCount(count + 1);       // only +1 total — both read the same stale 'count'

setCount(c => c + 1);
setCount(c => c + 1);      // +2 — functional updater reads the latest value

Use the functional form whenever the new state depends on the old one. This is the single most common React bug in interviews.

  1. Don't duplicate derivable state.
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);     // BAD — can drift out of sync
const count = items.length;                // GOOD — derive during render

Lifting state up — when two siblings need the same data, move it to their nearest common parent and pass it down. That's it; that's the whole pattern.

Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs:

<input value={value} onChange={e => setValue(e.target.value)} />   // controlled: React owns it
<input ref={inputRef} defaultValue="hi" />                          // uncontrolled: DOM owns it

Controlled is the default choice — you get validation, formatting and conditional disabling for free. Uncontrolled is fine for simple forms, file inputs (which must be uncontrolled), or when re-rendering on every keystroke is a measured problem.

4.4 The hooks, one by one MUST KNOW

useState

Covered above. Note: the initialiser runs on every render unless you pass a function — useState(expensiveInit()) calls it every time; useState(() => expensiveInit()) calls it once.

useEffect MUST KNOW — the most misunderstood hook

WHAT PROBLEM IT ACTUALLY SOLVES: synchronising your component with something outside React — a network request, a subscription, a timer, the document title, a non-React library.

The framing that gets you hired: "useEffect is not a lifecycle hook, it's a synchronisation primitive. If I find myself using it to transform data or respond to a user event, that's a sign the logic belongs during render or in the event handler instead."

useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  fetch(`/api/users/${id}`, { signal: controller.signal })
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(setUser)
    .catch(err => { if (err.name !== "AbortError") setError(err); });

  return () => controller.abort();   // cleanup: runs before the next effect and on unmount
}, [id]);                             // dependency array

Dependency array semantics: - [] — run once after mount (and again in StrictMode dev double-invoke). - [a, b] — run when a or b change by Object.is. - omitted — run after every render.

Why infinite loops happen MUST KNOW

useEffect(() => { setData(compute()); });                   // no deps -> render -> effect -> render...
useEffect(() => { setUser({...user, seen: true}); }, [user]); // sets the dep it depends on
useEffect(() => { fetch(url).then(setData); }, [{ id }]);     // new object literal every render

Rules: never omit deps carelessly; never set state that's in your own dependency array unconditionally; remember that objects, arrays and functions are new references on every render — memoise them or depend on primitive fields ([user.id], not [user]).

When you should NOT use an effect:

You're doing Do this instead
Transforming props into display data Compute it during render
Filtering a list based on state Compute during render (memoise only if measured slow)
Responding to a button click Put the logic in the onClick handler
Resetting state when a prop changes Give the component a key so React remounts it
Deriving state from other state Just derive it

The cleanup race condition — the reason AbortController is above: without it, if id changes quickly, a slow first response can land after a fast second one and overwrite it. An ignore flag works too:

useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;
  load(id).then(d => { if (!ignore) setData(d); });
  return () => { ignore = true; };
}, [id]);

Bringing this up unprompted is a strong signal.

useMemo and useCallback MUST KNOW

Both cache across renders. useMemo caches a value; useCallback caches a function identity. useCallback(fn, deps) is literally useMemo(() => fn, deps).

const sorted = useMemo(() => bigList.sort(cmp), [bigList]);
const handleClick = useCallback(() => onSelect(id), [onSelect, id]);

WHEN to use them — only three legitimate reasons: 1. The computation is genuinely expensive (measured, not guessed). 2. The value is passed to a React.memo child, where a new reference would defeat the memoisation. 3. The value is in another hook's dependency array, where a new reference would re-run the effect every render.

WHEN NOT: everywhere else. They aren't free — each one costs a dependency comparison and holds memory, and they clutter the code. Wrapping every function in useCallback is a common junior tell.

Interview answer: "I don't memoise by default. useMemo and useCallback are optimisations that trade memory and complexity for render time, so I want a reason: an expensive computation, a React.memo boundary I'd otherwise break, or a dependency array I'd otherwise invalidate. Otherwise the comparison cost can exceed what I'm saving."

Important gotcha: useCallback on a handler passed to a plain child does nothing useful — the child re-renders anyway because its parent did. It only helps in combination with React.memo.

useRef SHOULD KNOW→MUST KNOW

Two distinct uses: 1. DOM access — <input ref={inputRef} />, then inputRef.current.focus(). 2. Mutable value that persists across renders without causing one — timer IDs, previous values, "has mounted" flags, latest-callback refs.

const renderCount = useRef(0);
renderCount.current++;                 // changing this does NOT re-render

useRef vs useState: both persist across renders; only useState triggers a re-render. If the value is displayed, it's state. If it's bookkeeping, it's a ref.

useContext MUST KNOW

const ThemeContext = createContext(null);
<ThemeContext.Provider value={theme}>{children}</ThemeContext.Provider>
const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);

PROBLEM IT SOLVES — prop drilling: passing a value through six components that don't use it.

THE TRAP: every consumer re-renders when the context value changes by reference.

<Ctx.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>   // new object every render -> everyone re-renders
<Ctx.Provider value={useMemo(() => ({ user, setUser }), [user])}>   // better

Also: split contexts by update frequency. A rapidly-changing value and a static one in the same context means the static consumers re-render for nothing.

useReducer SHOULD KNOW

Use when state transitions are complex or several fields update together.

const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);
dispatch({ type: "submit_started" });

useState vs useReducer: useState for independent, simple values. useReducer when the next state depends on the previous in non-trivial ways, when multiple values change together, or when you want the transition logic testable in isolation outside the component.

Custom hooks MUST KNOW

A function starting with use that calls other hooks. It shares logic, not state — each caller gets its own independent state.

function useDebounced(value, delay = 300) {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const t = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(t);
  }, [value, delay]);
  return debounced;
}

function useFetch(url) {
  const [state, setState] = useState({ data: null, loading: true, error: null });
  useEffect(() => {
    let ignore = false;
    setState(s => ({ ...s, loading: true }));
    fetch(url)
      .then(r => { if (!r.ok) throw new Error(r.status); return r.json(); })
      .then(data => !ignore && setState({ data, loading: false, error: null }))
      .catch(error => !ignore && setState({ data: null, loading: false, error }));
    return () => { ignore = true; };
  }, [url]);
  return state;
}

Being able to write useFetch with loading, error and cleanup handled is a very common practical round.

The Rules of Hooks (and why they exist) MUST KNOW

Only call hooks at the top level, and only from React functions.

Why: React identifies hooks by call order, not by name — it keeps an array per component and walks it in the same order every render. A hook inside an if would shift every subsequent hook's index, so state would be handed to the wrong hook.

4.5 Why does React re-render? MUST KNOW

A component re-renders when: 1. Its own state changes. 2. Its parent re-renders (regardless of whether props changed). 3. A context it consumes gets a new value. 4. Its own key changes (remount).

It does NOT re-render because a prop object was mutated — no new reference, no signal.

Causes of unnecessary re-renders: - Parent re-renders, children re-render by default. - New object/array/function literals passed as props each render. - Context value recreated each render. - State placed too high in the tree, so a change re-renders a huge subtree.

Fixes, in order of preference: 1. Move state down. If only one leaf needs it, put it there. Free, no memoisation. 2. Lift content up / composition. Pass expensive subtrees as children — they're created in the parent's parent and don't re-render. 3. React.memo on the child + stable props via useMemo/useCallback. 4. useMemo on genuinely expensive computations.

Interview line: "I'd reach for structural fixes before memoisation — moving state closer to where it's used, or passing subtrees as children, removes the re-render entirely rather than making it cheaper. React.memo is what I use when the structure is already right and I've measured a problem in the Profiler."

React.memo does a shallow prop comparison and skips the render if props are equal. It's useless if you pass a fresh object or inline arrow every render — which is exactly why useCallback and React.memo are usually discussed together.

4.6 Data fetching, loading and error states MUST KNOW

Every real component has four states. Interviewers check whether you handle all four.

function UserList() {
  const { data, loading, error } = useFetch("/api/users");

  if (loading) return <Spinner />;
  if (error) return <ErrorMessage error={error} onRetry={...} />;
  if (!data?.length) return <EmptyState />;      // ← the one people forget
  return <ul>{data.map(u => <li key={u.id}>{u.name}</li>)}</ul>;
}

loading / error / empty / success. Mention the empty state unprompted.

In production I'd use a data library — React Query / TanStack Query or SWR — because they give caching, deduplication, background refetch, stale-while-revalidate and retry for free, and they remove most useEffect fetching code. Say this; it shows you know where the ceiling of hand-rolled fetching is.

4.7 Routing, auth, protected routes SHOULD KNOW

<BrowserRouter>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="/users/:id" element={<UserDetail />} />
    <Route element={<RequireAuth />}>
      <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
    </Route>
    <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
  </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>

function RequireAuth() {
  const { user, loading } = useAuth();
  const location = useLocation();
  if (loading) return <Spinner />;
  if (!user) return <Navigate to="/login" state={{ from: location }} replace />;
  return <Outlet />;
}

The auth question that always follows: "where do you store the token?"

"In-memory is safest against XSS but lost on refresh. localStorage survives refresh but any injected script can read it. The pattern I'd prefer is a short-lived access token in memory plus a refresh token in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie — the cookie can't be read by JavaScript, and CSRF is handled by SameSite plus a CSRF token. The trade-off is more backend complexity."

Critical point to make: client-side route guards are UX, not security. The API must authorise every request independently — anyone can bypass the frontend.

4.8 Performance toolkit SHOULD KNOW

Technique Use when
React.memo + stable props A child re-renders often with identical props
useMemo Measured expensive computation
Code splitting: React.lazy + Suspense Large route-level bundles
Virtualisation (react-window) Lists of hundreds/thousands of rows
Debounced input Search-as-you-type hitting an API
Moving state down / composition Big subtree re-rendering for a small change
Key-based remount Resetting state when an entity changes 
const Dashboard = React.lazy(() => import("./Dashboard"));
<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}><Dashboard /></Suspense>

Error boundaries catch render-time errors in the subtree below them. They're still class components (or a library like react-error-boundary), and they do not catch errors in event handlers, async code, or the boundary itself.

4.9 Context vs Redux MUST KNOW

Context Redux Toolkit
Purpose Dependency injection — pass a value down State management — store, actions, reducers, middleware
Good for Theme, locale, current user, feature flags Complex shared state with many writers, undo, time-travel debugging
Re-render control Poor — all consumers re-render on value change Good — useSelector subscribes to a slice
DevTools None Excellent time-travel debugging
Boilerplate Minimal Moderate (much reduced by RTK)

The answer to give: "Context solves prop drilling; it isn't a state manager. For a few low-frequency global values I use Context with a memoised value. When state is updated from many places, has complex derived data, or needs debugging tooling, Redux Toolkit earns its keep. But most apps I've seen reaching for Redux actually had server state — and for that, React Query is a better fit than either, because it handles caching and invalidation rather than making you write it."

Redux essentials if asked: single store, state is read-only, changes come from dispatched actions handled by pure reducers. RTK's createSlice generates action creators and reducers together and uses Immer so you can write "mutating" syntax that produces immutable updates. createAsyncThunk for async flows.

4.10 Production application structure SHOULD KNOW

src/
  app/            store, router, providers
  features/
    orders/       components/ hooks/ api.js slice.js types.ts
    users/
  components/     shared presentational components (Button, Modal)
  hooks/          shared hooks
  lib/            api client, formatters, constants
  pages/          route-level components

Feature-based, not type-based. Grouping by components/, hooks/, services/ at the top level means one feature's code is scattered across five folders. Grouping by feature means a change is local, and deleting a feature is deleting a folder.

Other things worth saying: one API client module with interceptors for auth and error normalisation; environment config via env vars, never hardcoded URLs; presentational components kept free of data fetching so they're testable and reusable.

4.11 React question bank

Question Short answer Follow-up
Why keys? Stable identity so React matches elements across renders "Why is index bad?" → insertion/reorder corrupts state
Virtual DOM In-memory tree diffed to compute minimal DOM updates "Is it faster than direct DOM?" → no, it's predictable, not optimal
useEffect purpose Synchronise with systems outside React "When shouldn't you use it?" → derived data, event handlers
Infinite loop cause Effect sets state that's in its own deps, or deps recreated each render "How do you debug it?" → log deps, check reference identity
useMemo vs useCallback Cache a value vs cache a function reference "When is useCallback pointless?" → child isn't memoised
Why did it re-render? Own state, parent render, context value, key change "How do you find out?" → React DevTools Profiler
Controlled vs uncontrolled React state owns the value vs DOM owns it "When uncontrolled?" → file inputs, perf-critical forms
Context vs Redux DI vs state management "What about server state?" → React Query
useRef vs state Persists without re-rendering "Give a real use" → timer id, previous value, focus
Rules of hooks Top level only; React functions only "Why?" → hooks are matched by call order
Error boundary Class component catching render errors below it "What doesn't it catch?" → events, async, itself
How to optimise a slow list Virtualise, memoise rows, stable keys, avoid inline props "What would you measure first?" → Profiler flame chart

5
Part 5

Web, HTTP and REST APIs

Short but high-yield. Where backend rounds start, and where candidates lose points on idempotency and CORS.

Suggested time · 5 h

This section is short but high-yield. Backend rounds almost always start here, and candidates lose points on idempotency, status codes and CORS more than anything else.

5.1 Client–server and the request lifecycle MUST KNOW

What happens when you type a URL and press enter — a classic warm-up question. The answer they want:

  1. DNS resolution — hostname → IP (browser cache → OS cache → resolver → root/TLD/authoritative).
  2. TCP handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), then TLS handshake for HTTPS (certificate validation, key exchange).
  3. HTTP request sent — method, path, headers, optional body.
  4. Possibly through a CDN → load balancer → reverse proxy → application server.
  5. Server processes: routing → middleware (auth, logging) → handler → database → response.
  6. HTTP response — status line, headers, body.
  7. Browser parses HTML, builds the DOM, fetches subresources, runs JS, paints.

Say "and the connection is likely reused via keep-alive / HTTP-2 multiplexing rather than reopened for every asset" and you've covered the follow-up in advance.

5.2 HTTP methods MUST KNOW

Method Purpose Safe Idempotent Body
GET Read ✅ ✅ no
POST Create / non-idempotent action ❌ ❌ yes
PUT Replace entire resource ❌ ✅ yes
PATCH Partial update ❌ ❌ (usually) yes
DELETE Remove ❌ ✅ optional

Safe = doesn't change server state. Idempotent = doing it N times has the same effect as doing it once.

Idempotency MUST KNOW — the concept candidates fluff

WHY IT MATTERS: networks fail. A client sends POST /payments, the server processes it, and the response is lost. The client retries. Without idempotency you've charged the customer twice.

How to implement it:

"The client generates an idempotency key — a UUID — and sends it as a header. The server stores the key with the result of the first successful request. On a retry with the same key, it returns the stored response instead of re-executing. You need a uniqueness constraint on that key in the database so two concurrent retries can't both slip through, and a TTL so the table doesn't grow forever."

That paragraph, delivered in a backend round, is worth a lot. Stripe's API is the canonical example if you want to name one.

Why DELETE is idempotent but not safe: deleting twice leaves the same end state (gone), even though the second call returns 404. Repeating it doesn't compound the effect.

5.3 Status codes MUST KNOW

Code Meaning Use it when
200 OK Success with body GET, PUT, PATCH success
201 Created Resource created POST success; include a Location header
202 Accepted Queued, not yet done Async/background processing
204 No Content Success, empty body DELETE success
301 / 302 Moved permanently / found Redirects
304 Not Modified Client's cache is still valid Conditional GET with ETag/If-None-Match
400 Bad Request Malformed / invalid input Validation failure
401 Unauthorized Not authenticated — who are you? Missing or invalid token
403 Forbidden Authenticated but not allowed Valid token, insufficient permission
404 Not Found Resource doesn't exist
409 Conflict State conflict Duplicate email, version conflict
422 Unprocessable Well-formed but semantically wrong Business-rule violation
429 Too Many Requests Rate limited Include Retry-After
500 Internal Server Error Unhandled server fault Never leak stack traces
502 / 503 / 504 Bad gateway / unavailable / timeout Upstream problems

401 vs 403 is asked constantly. 401 = "I don't know who you are." 403 = "I know who you are and you can't do this."

Design point worth volunteering: for a lookup of a resource the caller isn't allowed to see, returning 404 instead of 403 avoids leaking existence. That's a real security trade-off (discoverability vs clarity) and interviewers like hearing it.

5.4 Headers, cookies, sessions SHOULD KNOW

Headers you should know: Content-Type, Accept, Authorization, Cache-Control, ETag, If-None-Match, Set-Cookie, Location, Retry-After, X-Request-Id, Origin.

Cookie flags — all four matter: - HttpOnly — JavaScript can't read it (XSS mitigation). - Secure — HTTPS only. - SameSite=Lax|Strict|None — controls sending on cross-site requests (CSRF mitigation). - Max-Age / Expires — lifetime.

Sessions vs tokens MUST KNOW

Server session (cookie + session store) JWT
Where state lives Server (Redis/DB) In the token itself
Revocation Easy — delete the session Hard — token is valid until expiry
Scaling Needs shared session store Stateless; any server can verify
Size Small cookie Larger; sent on every request
Best for Traditional web apps, when instant logout matters APIs, microservices, mobile clients

JWT MUST KNOW

Three base64url parts: header.payload.signature. - The signature proves integrity and authenticity — that the token was issued by you and hasn't been altered. - It does not provide confidentiality. The payload is encoded, not encrypted. Never put secrets in a JWT. Candidates get this wrong constantly.

The revocation problem and the standard answer:

"A JWT can't be un-issued, so the usual pattern is short-lived access tokens — 5 to 15 minutes — plus a long-lived refresh token that is stored server-side and can be revoked. Worst case, a compromised access token is valid for a few minutes. If you need instant revocation you keep a denylist of token IDs, but at that point you've reintroduced the state you were trying to avoid, which is worth saying out loud."

Never accept alg: none, and validate exp, iss, aud, and the signature algorithm on every request.

5.5 CORS MUST KNOW (guaranteed question if you've built anything)

WHAT — a browser mechanism that restricts a page on origin A from reading responses from origin B unless B opts in.

WHY it exists — the same-origin policy stops evil.com from making authenticated requests to yourbank.com using the user's cookies and reading the response. CORS is the controlled relaxation of that.

HOW - Simple request (GET/POST with basic content types): browser sends Origin; server replies with Access-Control-Allow-Origin. If it doesn't match, the browser blocks the response from JavaScript. - Preflight — for other methods, custom headers, or application/json: the browser first sends an OPTIONS request. The server must answer with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Methods, -Headers, and -Max-Age. - With credentials (cookies), Access-Control-Allow-Origin must be an explicit origin — the wildcard * is rejected — and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is required.

Three things to state that mark you out: 1. CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server. curl and Postman ignore it entirely. 2. It's not a security control for your API. It protects the user's browser. Your API still needs authentication and authorisation. 3. "Fixing CORS" means configuring the server, not the client. Candidates who say "I disabled it in the browser" get marked down.

5.6 CSRF vs XSS SHOULD KNOW

XSS CSRF
Attack Inject and run script in your page Trick the browser into sending an authenticated request
Enabled by Rendering untrusted input as HTML/JS Cookies sent automatically on cross-site requests
Defence Escape output, CSP, HttpOnly cookies, avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, check Origin

Note the interaction: if you're vulnerable to XSS, CSRF defences don't save you — injected script runs on your origin and can read the token.

5.7 REST design MUST KNOW

Principles that actually matter in an interview: resources identified by URLs, standard HTTP methods for operations, stateless requests (each carries everything needed), consistent representations (JSON), meaningful status codes.

URL design:

GET    /api/v1/users                 list
POST   /api/v1/users                 create
GET    /api/v1/users/123             read
PUT    /api/v1/users/123             replace
PATCH  /api/v1/users/123             partial update
DELETE /api/v1/users/123             delete
GET    /api/v1/users/123/orders      sub-resource

Rules: plural nouns, no verbs in paths (/getUsers is wrong — the method is the verb), lowercase and hyphenated, nest at most one level deep.

Pagination — three options and their trade-offs:

Style Query Pros Cons
Offset/limit ?page=2&limit=20 Simple, jump to any page Slow at deep offsets; items shift if data changes between pages
Cursor/keyset ?after=eyJpZCI6MTIzfQ&limit=20 Consistent, fast at any depth No random page access
Time-based ?since=2026-01-01 Natural for feeds Ties to a timestamp column

Say: "For a large or frequently changing dataset I'd use cursor pagination — offset gets slower the deeper you go because the database still has to scan and discard those rows, and rows can be skipped or duplicated if data changes between requests."

Filtering / sorting: ?status=active&sort=-created_at&fields=id,name. Whitelist sortable and filterable fields — passing user input into a query is how you get injection and full table scans.

Versioning:

Approach Example Note
URL path /api/v1/users Most common, most visible, easiest to route
Header Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json Cleaner URLs, harder to test/debug
Query param ?version=1 Simple, easy to abuse

Say you prefer URL versioning for its explicitness, and that the real goal is to avoid breaking changes — additive changes (new optional fields) don't need a new version at all.

Consistent error shape:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
    "message": "Email is already registered",
    "details": [{"field": "email", "issue": "duplicate"}],
    "request_id": "req_9f2c1a"
  }
}

The request_id is what turns a user's bug report into a log search. Mention it.

Rate limiting — token bucket (allows bursts, refills at a steady rate) or sliding window. Return 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining. Limit per API key or user, not per IP alone (NAT and proxies share IPs).

5.8 Caching SHOULD KNOW

Layers, outermost first: browser cache → CDN → reverse proxy → application cache (Redis) → database buffer pool.

HTTP caching headers: - Cache-Control: max-age=3600, public — cacheable for an hour by anyone. - Cache-Control: no-store — never cache (auth responses, personal data). - ETag + If-None-Match — the server can reply 304 Not Modified with no body, saving bandwidth.

Cache strategies:

Strategy How Trade-off
Cache-aside (lazy) App checks cache; on miss, reads DB and populates Simple, most common; first request is slow; risk of stampede
Write-through Write to cache and DB together Cache always fresh; slower writes
Write-behind Write to cache, flush to DB async Fast writes; data loss risk on crash

Invalidation — the hard part. TTL when staleness is tolerable; explicit deletion on write when it isn't. Delete the key rather than updating it — updating races with a concurrent read that could repopulate a stale value.

Thundering herd / cache stampede: when a hot key expires, thousands of requests hit the database simultaneously. Fixes: a short lock so only one request rebuilds, request coalescing, or jittered TTLs so keys don't all expire together.

5.9 REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC NICE TO KNOW (one paragraph is enough)

REST: simple, cacheable over HTTP, ubiquitous; can over-fetch and under-fetch. GraphQL: the client asks for exactly the fields it wants, one round trip for nested data; harder to cache, and you must guard against expensive nested queries. gRPC: binary protobuf over HTTP/2, fast and strongly typed, ideal for service-to-service; awkward from browsers. Pick REST unless you have a specific reason.

5.10 API question bank

Question Short answer Follow-up
PUT vs PATCH Full replace vs partial update "Is PATCH idempotent?" → not necessarily
401 vs 403 Not authenticated vs not permitted "Which for an expired token?" → 401
What is idempotency Repeating the call has the same effect "How do you make POST idempotent?" → idempotency key
Explain CORS Browser rule; server opts in via headers "Does it secure my API?" → no, browser-only
Where to store a JWT Memory + httpOnly refresh cookie "Why not localStorage?" → readable by XSS
How to paginate Offset for simple, cursor for large/changing "Why is deep offset slow?" → scans and discards
How to version URL path; avoid breaking changes "How do you deprecate?" → sunset headers + timeline
How to rate limit Token bucket per key; 429 + Retry-After "Where — app or gateway?" → gateway if you have one
Cache invalidation TTL, or delete-on-write "Why delete rather than update?" → race with reads
Stateless — why Any server can serve any request; enables horizontal scaling "What breaks?" → sticky sessions, in-memory state

6
Part 6

Backend Development with Python

Concepts first, FastAPI as the illustration. Layering, transactions, pooling, auth and everything around them.

Suggested time · 8 h

Concepts first, FastAPI as the illustration. Interviewers care that you understand why the layers exist, not which decorator you type.

6.1 Layered architecture MUST KNOW

PROBLEM IT SOLVES: the default beginner backend puts SQL, validation, business rules and HTTP handling in one function. It can't be tested without a database, can't be reused from a background job, and every change risks breaking something unrelated.

Request
  |
  v
Router / Controller     HTTP only: parse, validate shape, map errors to status codes
  |
  v
Service                 Business rules, orchestration, transactions
  |
  v
Repository              Data access. The only layer that knows SQL/ORM
  |
  v
Model / Database

The rule: dependencies point downward only. The service must not know it's being called over HTTP. The repository must not know about business rules.

# repository.py — data access only
class OrderRepository:
    def __init__(self, session: Session):
        self.session = session

    def get(self, order_id: int) -> Order | None:
        return self.session.get(Order, order_id)

    def add(self, order: Order) -> Order:
        self.session.add(order)
        self.session.flush()          # get the PK without committing
        return order

# service.py — business rules, no HTTP, no SQL
class OrderService:
    def __init__(self, orders: OrderRepository, inventory: InventoryClient, events: EventBus):
        self.orders, self.inventory, self.events = orders, inventory, events

    def place_order(self, user_id: int, items: list[ItemSpec]) -> Order:
        if not items:
            raise ValidationError("order must contain at least one item")
        if not self.inventory.reserve(items):
            raise OutOfStockError(items)
        order = self.orders.add(Order(user_id=user_id, items=items))
        self.events.publish("order.placed", order.id)
        return order

# router.py — HTTP only
@router.post("/orders", status_code=201, response_model=OrderOut)
def create_order(payload: OrderIn, service: OrderService = Depends(get_order_service)):
    return service.place_order(payload.user_id, payload.items)

Why interviewers like this: the service is unit-testable with fake repositories, the same logic can be called from a CLI or a worker, and swapping Postgres for something else touches one layer.

When NOT to bother: a three-endpoint internal tool. Say so — recognising when architecture is over-engineering is itself a senior signal.

6.2 Validation and schemas MUST KNOW

Never trust client input. Validate at the boundary, then work with typed objects internally.

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field, field_validator

class UserCreate(BaseModel):            # input schema
    email: EmailStr
    password: str = Field(min_length=8, max_length=128)
    age: int = Field(ge=13, le=120)

    @field_validator("password")
    @classmethod
    def has_digit(cls, v: str) -> str:
        if not any(c.isdigit() for c in v):
            raise ValueError("password must contain a digit")
        return v

class UserOut(BaseModel):               # output schema
    id: int
    email: EmailStr
    created_at: datetime
    # note: no password_hash — separate output schema prevents leaking fields

Say this: "I keep separate input and output schemas. If I reuse the DB model as the response model, adding an internal column later silently exposes it in the API. Separate schemas make the public contract explicit."

That accidental-field-exposure point is a real production bug class and it lands well.

6.3 Dependency injection SHOULD KNOW

PROBLEM IT SOLVES: if a service constructs its own database connection, you can't substitute a fake in tests and you can't change the connection strategy without editing the service.

def get_session():
    session = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield session
    finally:
        session.close()

def get_order_service(session: Session = Depends(get_session)) -> OrderService:
    return OrderService(OrderRepository(session), InventoryClient(), EventBus())

In tests you override the dependency with a fake — no monkeypatching, no real database. That's the whole benefit: explicit dependencies are substitutable dependencies.

6.4 Middleware SHOULD KNOW

Code that runs around every request. Standard uses: request ID generation, logging, timing, authentication, CORS, compression, error normalisation.

@app.middleware("http")
async def add_request_id(request: Request, call_next):
    request_id = request.headers.get("X-Request-Id", str(uuid4()))
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["X-Request-Id"] = request_id
    log.info("%s %s %s %.3fs", request.method, request.url.path,
             response.status_code, time.perf_counter() - start)
    return response

Middleware vs decorator: middleware applies to every request and is the right place for cross-cutting infrastructure. A decorator (or FastAPI dependency) is the right place for per-endpoint concerns like a specific permission check.

6.5 Transactions MUST KNOW

ACID, briefly: Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (constraints hold), Isolated (concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work), Durable (committed data survives a crash).

def transfer(session, from_id, to_id, amount):
    try:
        sender = session.query(Account).with_for_update().get(from_id)   # row lock
        receiver = session.query(Account).with_for_update().get(to_id)
        if sender.balance < amount:
            raise InsufficientFunds(amount, sender.balance)
        sender.balance -= amount
        receiver.balance += amount
        session.commit()
    except Exception:
        session.rollback()
        raise

The two points to make: the debit and credit must be in one transaction or a crash between them loses money; and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE prevents two concurrent transfers both reading the same balance and both succeeding.

Deadlock note: two transfers in opposite directions can deadlock by locking rows in different orders. Fix: always lock in a deterministic order (e.g. ascending account ID). Bringing this up unprompted is a strong signal.

Keep transactions short. Never make an HTTP call inside one — you hold locks for the duration of someone else's network latency.

6.6 Connection pooling SHOULD KNOW

PROBLEM: opening a database connection costs a TCP handshake, authentication, and server-side memory — tens of milliseconds, repeated per request. And databases cap concurrent connections.

SOLUTION: keep a pool of open connections; borrow and return.

engine = create_engine(
    DATABASE_URL,
    pool_size=10,          # steady connections
    max_overflow=20,       # burst capacity
    pool_timeout=30,       # wait before giving up
    pool_pre_ping=True,    # detect connections dropped by the DB or a proxy
)

Sizing rule of thumb: more connections is not better. Past the point where the database is CPU/disk saturated, extra connections add context-switching and lock contention. Postgres in particular does better with a smaller pool plus PgBouncer than with hundreds of direct connections.

6.7 Background jobs and async processing SHOULD KNOW

RECOGNISE THE NEED: anything slow, retryable, or not needed for the response — sending email, generating a PDF, processing an upload, calling a flaky third party.

# Simple: FastAPI BackgroundTasks — runs in the same process
@router.post("/signup")
def signup(payload: UserCreate, bg: BackgroundTasks, svc = Depends(...)):
    user = svc.create(payload)
    bg.add_task(send_welcome_email, user.email)   # response returns immediately
    return user

When that isn't enough: in-process background tasks die with the process, don't retry, and don't scale independently. For anything that must not be lost I'd use a real queue — Celery with Redis/RabbitMQ, or a database-backed queue — because it gives durability, retries with backoff, dead-letter handling, and separate worker scaling.

Return 202 Accepted with a job ID for long jobs, and let the client poll or receive a webhook.

6.8 Authentication and authorisation MUST KNOW

def hash_password(pw: str) -> str:
    return bcrypt.hashpw(pw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=12)).decode()

def create_access_token(user_id: int) -> str:
    return jwt.encode(
        {"sub": str(user_id), "exp": datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(minutes=15)},
        SECRET_KEY, algorithm="HS256",
    )

def current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme)) -> User:
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=["HS256"])
    except jwt.ExpiredSignatureError:
        raise HTTPException(401, "token expired")
    except jwt.PyJWTError:
        raise HTTPException(401, "invalid token")
    ...

Password rules interviewers check for: - Use bcrypt / argon2 / scrypt — deliberately slow, with a per-password salt. Never MD5, SHA-1, or plain SHA-256 (fast = brute-forceable). - Never log or return the hash. - Use a constant-time comparison. - Generic error on login failure — "invalid credentials", not "no such user", which enumerates accounts.

Authorisation: authentication is who you are, authorisation is what you may do. Check ownership on every object access — GET /orders/123 must verify the order belongs to the caller, or you have an IDOR vulnerability. This is one of the most common real-world API bugs and a great thing to raise unprompted.

6.9 Configuration and secrets SHOULD KNOW

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str
    secret_key: str
    debug: bool = False
    class Config:
        env_file = ".env"

settings = Settings()      # fails loudly at startup if something is missing

Rules: config comes from the environment, never from committed code; .env is gitignored; production secrets live in a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault); fail fast at startup if a required setting is absent, rather than crashing on the first request that needs it.

6.10 Error handling MUST KNOW

class AppError(Exception):
    status_code = 500
    code = "INTERNAL_ERROR"

class NotFound(AppError):
    status_code, code = 404, "NOT_FOUND"

class ValidationError(AppError):
    status_code, code = 400, "VALIDATION_ERROR"

@app.exception_handler(AppError)
async def handle_app_error(request: Request, exc: AppError):
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=exc.status_code,
        content={"error": {"code": exc.code, "message": str(exc),
                           "request_id": request.state.request_id}},
    )

The design point: domain code raises domain exceptions and knows nothing about HTTP. One handler at the edge maps them to status codes. Adding a new error type means adding a class, not editing every route.

Never leak internals — log the stack trace server-side with the request ID; return a generic message and that ID to the client.

6.11 Logging and observability SHOULD KNOW

log.info("order_placed", extra={"order_id": o.id, "user_id": u.id, "amount": o.total})

Structured (JSON) logs are searchable; free-text logs are not. Include a request/correlation ID on every line so one user's journey can be traced across services.

The three pillars: logs (what happened), metrics (how much/how fast — p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, throughput), traces (where the time went across services). Knowing that p99 matters more than average — because averages hide the tail that users actually complain about — is a good line to have ready.

6.12 Testing SHOULD KNOW

        /\        E2E — few, slow, high confidence
       /  \
      /    \      Integration — some; real DB, real HTTP
     /______\     Unit — many, fast, isolated

def test_place_order_rejects_empty(order_service):
    with pytest.raises(ValidationError):
        order_service.place_order(user_id=1, items=[])

def test_create_user_endpoint(client):
    r = client.post("/users", json={"email": "a@b.com", "password": "secret123"})
    assert r.status_code == 201
    assert "password" not in r.json()          # regression guard on field leakage

Mock external systems (payment gateways, email); use a real database (a test container or transactional rollback per test) for repository tests, because mocked SQL tests pass while the real query is broken.

6.13 Backend question bank

Question Short answer Follow-up
Why layer the app? Testability, reuse, isolated change "When is it overkill?" → tiny services
Why not use the ORM model as the API schema? Leaks internal fields; couples contract to storage "How do you keep them in sync?" → explicit mapping + tests
What is a transaction Atomic unit; all or nothing "How do you avoid deadlocks?" → consistent lock ordering
Why connection pooling Connection setup is expensive; DBs cap connections "Bigger pool = faster?" → no, contention
Sync vs async backend Async wins for I/O-bound concurrency "What ruins it?" → one blocking call stalls the loop
How do you hash passwords bcrypt/argon2 with salt, high cost factor "Why not SHA-256?" → too fast to brute-force
Where do background jobs go Queue + workers for durability and retries "What if a job fails 5 times?" → dead-letter queue + alert
How do you handle errors Domain exceptions + one edge handler "What do you return to the client?" → code, message, request_id
N+1 query problem One query per row in a loop "How do you fix it?" → eager loading / join / batch
How do you secure an API AuthN, per-object authZ, validation, rate limits, TLS, secrets management "What's the most-missed one?" → object-level authorisation

6A
Part 6A

FastAPI in Depth

FastAPI is built on ASGI and your type hints — the hints are the runtime configuration. Dependencies, async correctness, auth, testing, and the Spring Boot comparison.

Suggested time · 8 h

Part 6 taught the concepts — layering, validation, transactions, error handling — and used FastAPI to illustrate them. This part is about the framework itself, at the same depth as the Spring Boot part that follows.

The mental model to start from:

FastAPI is built on two things: ASGI, and your type hints. The type hints are not documentation. They are the runtime configuration — FastAPI reads your function signature to decide what to parse from the request, how to validate it, what to put in the OpenAPI schema, and what to serialise back.

That single fact explains almost every FastAPI question, including the ones that look unrelated. It's also why functools.wraps matters so much (Part 2B): a decorator that erases your signature erases everything FastAPI knows about the endpoint.

6A.1 The request lifecycle MUST KNOW

@router.post("/orders", response_model=OrderOut, status_code=201)
async def create_order(
    payload: CreateOrderRequest,                       # body — parsed and validated
    limit: int = Query(50, le=200),                    # query param, with a constraint
    x_request_id: str | None = Header(None),           # header
    service: OrderService = Depends(get_order_service),# dependency
    user: User = Depends(current_user),                # auth dependency
):
    return service.place_order(user.id, payload.items)

FastAPI works out each parameter's source from its type and default:

Declaration Where it comes from
Pydantic model, no default request body
Simple type matching a path placeholder path
Simple type not in the path query
Header(...), Cookie(...), Form(...), File(...) as named
Depends(...) the dependency system

Then, in order: middleware → dependency resolution (including auth) → body parsing and validation → your function → response_model filtering and serialisation → middleware on the way out.

Two consequences worth knowing:

  • Validation happens before your code runs. A bad body never reaches your function; FastAPI raises RequestValidationError and returns 422.
  • response_model filters the output. If your function returns an object with extra fields, they are stripped. That's a safety net against leaking internal fields — and a source of confusion when a field you expected silently disappears because it isn't on the model.

6A.2 Pydantic: validation at the boundary MUST KNOW

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field, field_validator, ConfigDict

class CreateOrderRequest(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")     # reject unknown fields instead of ignoring

    user_id: int
    items: list[ItemSpec] = Field(min_length=1, max_length=50)
    notify_email: EmailStr | None = None
    coupon: str | None = Field(None, pattern=r"^[A-Z0-9]{4,12}$")

    @field_validator("items")
    @classmethod
    def no_duplicate_skus(cls, v):
        skus = [i.sku for i in v]
        if len(skus) != len(set(skus)):
            raise ValueError("duplicate SKUs in one order")
        return v


class OrderOut(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)   # build from an ORM object

    id: int
    status: str
    total: Decimal
    created_at: datetime
    # deliberately no internal_notes, no cost_price

Three rules, and each answers a likely follow-up:

  1. Separate input and output models. If you reuse the ORM model as the response model, adding an internal column later silently exposes it in the API. Separate models make the public contract explicit — the same argument as Java DTOs vs JPA entities in Part 6B.

  2. extra="forbid" is usually right for input. The default silently ignores unknown fields, so a client with a typo (quanity) gets a 200 and no effect. Forbidding turns that into a 422 with a clear message.

  3. Validate at the edge, then work with typed objects. Once past the boundary, your service takes list[ItemSpec], not a dict. Nothing downstream re-checks.

Pydantic v1 vs v2, briefly, because it comes up: v2 moved the validation core to Rust and is roughly 5–20× faster. Renames worth knowing: @validator → @field_validator, class Config → model_config = ConfigDict(...), .dict() → .model_dump(), orm_mode → from_attributes.

6A.3 The dependency injection system MUST KNOW

This is FastAPI's most distinctive feature and the highest-value thing to understand well.

# a dependency is just a callable
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()

# dependencies can depend on dependencies
def get_session(settings: Settings = Depends(get_settings)):
    session = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield session                  # everything before yield = setup
    finally:
        session.close()                # after yield = teardown, always runs

def get_order_service(session: Session = Depends(get_session)) -> OrderService:
    return OrderService(OrderRepository(session), InventoryClient())

@router.post("/orders")
def create(payload: CreateOrderRequest,
           service: OrderService = Depends(get_order_service)):
    ...

The four properties that matter

1. yield dependencies give you setup and teardown. This is FastAPI's answer to Spring's @Transactional proxy — except it's an ordinary generator you can read, not a proxy generated at runtime. The teardown runs after the response is produced, even if the handler raised.

2. Dependencies are cached per request. If five things depend on get_session, the session is created once and shared for that request. Opt out with Depends(get_thing, use_cache=False).

3. They can be applied at any level:

@router.get("/admin", dependencies=[Depends(require_admin)])    # no value needed, just a check
router = APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(verify_api_key)])      # whole router
app = FastAPI(dependencies=[Depends(rate_limit)])               # whole app

dependencies=[...] is for dependencies you run for their side effect — auth, rate limiting — where you don't want the return value cluttering your signature.

4. They're overridable in tests. This is the payoff:

app.dependency_overrides[get_session] = lambda: fake_session

No monkeypatching, no import juggling. It's the same benefit constructor injection gives you in Spring: explicit dependencies are substitutable dependencies.

Class-based dependencies

class Paginator:
    def __init__(self, page: int = 1, size: int = Query(20, le=100)):
        self.offset = (page - 1) * size
        self.limit = size

@router.get("/orders")
def list_orders(p: Paginator = Depends()):     # Depends() with no argument infers the type
    ...

The constructor's parameters become query parameters, documented automatically. Good for reusable parameter groups.

6A.4 def vs async def — the most important FastAPI decision MUST KNOW

This is where most real FastAPI performance problems come from, and it's a favourite interview question.

You write FastAPI runs it Blocking is
async def on the event loop, in the main thread catastrophic — stalls every other request
def in a threadpool (40 threads by default) contained — only that thread blocks 
@app.get("/a")
async def bad():
    time.sleep(5)              # ❌ blocks the ENTIRE event loop for 5 seconds
    return {"ok": True}        #    every other request in the process waits

@app.get("/b")
async def good():
    await asyncio.sleep(5)     # ✅ yields; other requests proceed
    return {"ok": True}

@app.get("/c")
def also_fine():
    time.sleep(5)              # ✅ blocking, but in a worker thread
    return {"ok": True}

The rule to state: "Use async def only if everything inside it is awaitable. If I'm calling a blocking library — a sync database driver, requests, a CPU-bound computation — I either declare the route as a plain def so FastAPI runs it in the threadpool, or I keep it async and push the blocking call out with await asyncio.to_thread(...). The dangerous case is async def with a blocking call inside, because that's the one that looks fastest and is actually the slowest."

The most common real instance: using async def with synchronous SQLAlchemy. Every query blocks the loop. Either use plain def routes with the sync session, or go fully async with asyncpg + AsyncSession. Mixing is what kills throughput.

CPU-bound work belongs in neither. The threadpool doesn't help because of the GIL (Part 2 §2.5.7). Offload to a process pool or a task queue.

6A.5 Middleware, background tasks, and lifespan SHOULD KNOW

@app.middleware("http")
async def add_request_id(request: Request, call_next):
    rid = request.headers.get("X-Request-Id", str(uuid4()))
    request.state.request_id = rid
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["X-Request-Id"] = rid
    log.info("%s %s %s %.3fs", request.method, request.url.path,
             response.status_code, time.perf_counter() - start)
    return response

Middleware vs dependency — the decision: middleware runs for every request and can see the raw request and response, so it's right for request IDs, timing, CORS and compression. A dependency is per-endpoint and can return a typed value, so it's right for auth checks, pagination objects, and anything you want to override in tests. Match the mechanism's blast radius to the concern's.

@router.post("/signup", status_code=201)
def signup(payload: UserCreate, bg: BackgroundTasks, svc = Depends(get_user_service)):
    user = svc.create(payload)
    bg.add_task(send_welcome_email, user.email)      # runs after the response is sent
    return user

Be honest about BackgroundTasks: it runs in the same process, so it dies with a restart, has no retries, and doesn't scale independently. Fine for a best-effort email. For anything that must not be lost, use a real queue — Celery, Dramatiq, or a database-backed queue — and return 202 Accepted with a job ID.

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.pool = await create_pool()     # startup
    yield
    await app.state.pool.close()             # shutdown

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

lifespan replaced the deprecated @app.on_event("startup"). Use it for connection pools, warm caches, and background schedulers.

6A.6 Authentication MUST KNOW

oauth2 = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="/auth/token")

def current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2),
                 session: Session = Depends(get_session)) -> User:
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, settings.secret_key, algorithms=["HS256"])
    except jwt.ExpiredSignatureError:
        raise HTTPException(401, "token expired",
                            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"})
    except jwt.PyJWTError:
        raise HTTPException(401, "invalid token")
    user = session.get(User, int(payload["sub"]))
    if user is None or not user.active:
        raise HTTPException(401, "invalid token")     # generic — don't reveal which
    return user

def require_role(role: str):
    def checker(user: User = Depends(current_user)) -> User:
        if role not in user.roles:
            raise HTTPException(403, "insufficient permissions")
        return user
    return checker

@router.delete("/orders/{id}")
def cancel(id: int, user: User = Depends(require_role("admin"))):
    ...

require_role is a dependency factory — the same three-level nesting as a decorator with arguments (Part 2B §2B.4), for the same reason: the outer call captures the configuration and returns the actual dependency.

The point to volunteer: a role check is not enough. DELETE /orders/123 must also verify that order 123 belongs to this caller, or you have an IDOR vulnerability — authenticated, authorised by role, and still able to delete someone else's data. Object-level authorisation is the most commonly missed control in real APIs.

Using OAuth2PasswordBearer also gives you the Authorize button in /docs, which makes the interactive documentation actually usable.

6A.7 Error handling MUST KNOW

class AppError(Exception):
    status_code, code = 500, "INTERNAL_ERROR"

class NotFound(AppError):
    status_code, code = 404, "NOT_FOUND"

class ValidationError(AppError):
    status_code, code = 400, "VALIDATION_ERROR"


@app.exception_handler(AppError)
async def handle_app_error(request: Request, exc: AppError):
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=exc.status_code,
        content={"error": {"code": exc.code, "message": str(exc),
                           "request_id": request.state.request_id}},
    )

@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)
async def handle_validation(request: Request, exc: RequestValidationError):
    return JSONResponse(422, content={"error": {
        "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
        "message": "Invalid request",
        "details": [{"field": ".".join(map(str, e["loc"][1:])), "issue": e["msg"]}
                    for e in exc.errors()],
        "request_id": request.state.request_id,
    }})

@app.exception_handler(Exception)
async def handle_unexpected(request: Request, exc: Exception):
    log.exception("unhandled error on %s %s", request.method, request.url.path)
    return JSONResponse(500, content={"error": {
        "code": "INTERNAL_ERROR", "message": "Something went wrong",
        "request_id": request.state.request_id}})    # never leak the traceback

HTTPException vs a domain exception: HTTPException is convenient but couples your service layer to HTTP. Raise domain exceptions in the service and map them in one handler — then the same service works from a CLI, a worker or a test with no HTTP anywhere. Use HTTPException directly only in the router layer, where HTTP is already the subject.

6A.8 Project structure and configuration SHOULD KNOW

app/
  main.py              # FastAPI(), middleware, exception handlers, router includes
  core/
    config.py          # Settings (pydantic-settings)
    security.py        # hashing, tokens
    deps.py            # shared dependencies: get_session, current_user
  api/v1/
    orders.py          # APIRouter — routes only
    users.py
  services/            # business rules
  repositories/        # data access
  models/              # SQLAlchemy models
  schemas/             # Pydantic request/response models
  workers/             # background jobs
tests/

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str
    secret_key: str
    debug: bool = False
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env")

settings = Settings()          # fails loudly at startup if something is missing

Two habits worth stating: fail fast at startup rather than crashing on the first request that needs a missing setting, and keep production secrets in a secret manager, not a committed .env.

app.include_router(orders.router, prefix="/api/v1/orders", tags=["orders"])

APIRouter is the unit of modularity — prefix, tags, and router-level dependencies all live there rather than being repeated per endpoint.

6A.9 Testing MUST KNOW

@pytest.fixture
def client(fake_session):
    app.dependency_overrides[get_session] = lambda: fake_session
    app.dependency_overrides[current_user] = lambda: User(id=1, roles=["admin"])
    with TestClient(app) as c:
        yield c
    app.dependency_overrides.clear()

def test_create_order_returns_201(client):
    r = client.post("/api/v1/orders", json={"user_id": 1, "items": [{"sku": "A", "qty": 2}]})
    assert r.status_code == 201
    assert "password_hash" not in r.json()          # regression guard on field leakage

def test_rejects_unknown_field(client):
    r = client.post("/api/v1/orders", json={"user_id": 1, "items": [], "quanity": 3})
    assert r.status_code == 422

dependency_overrides is the whole testing story: swap the session, swap auth, swap the external client — no patching. Use httpx.AsyncClient with ASGITransport when you need to test async behaviour properly rather than through TestClient's sync wrapper.

And as in Part 6: mock external systems, use a real database (a container or a transaction rolled back per test) for repository tests. Mocked-SQL tests pass while the actual query is broken.

6A.10 Performance in production SHOULD KNOW

gunicorn app.main:app -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker -w 4

Workers vs async. Each worker is a separate process with its own event loop and its own GIL, so workers give you CPU parallelism and async gives you I/O concurrency within a worker. Rule of thumb: workers ≈ cores. More workers than cores just adds context switching.

Watch the connection pool. Four workers × a pool of 10 is 40 database connections, plus overflow. Size the pool against what the database can actually take, not against what looks generous.

The performance checklist: - Never block the event loop (§6A.4). This is the big one. - Use async database drivers if the routes are async def. - Cache expensive reads; delete the key on write rather than updating it (Part 5 §5.8). - Watch for N+1 in SQLAlchemy — selectinload/joinedload instead of a lazy relation touched in a loop. Exactly the same problem as JPA's, with the same fixes. - Return ORJSONResponse for large payloads; JSON serialisation is often the actual bottleneck. - Paginate everything that can grow.

6A.11 FastAPI vs Spring Boot — the comparison MUST KNOW

Both parts describe the same architecture. The interesting differences are about where the magic lives.

Concern FastAPI Spring Boot
Wiring Depends(...), explicit per endpoint Container-managed, classpath scanning
What configures the framework Your type hints, at runtime Annotations plus autoconfiguration
Validation Pydantic models Bean Validation annotations
Transactions A yield dependency or an explicit context manager — visible code @Transactional proxy — invisible, with self-invocation gotchas
Concurrency One event loop per worker process; GIL limits CPU Real threads; true parallelism; real locking problems
Blocking mistake Blocks all requests in that worker Blocks one thread out of the pool
ORM traps SQLAlchemy N+1, lazy loads JPA N+1, LazyInitializationException
Test isolation dependency_overrides @MockBean, or plain new with mocks
Docs OpenAPI generated from types, free springdoc, generated from annotations
Startup Milliseconds Seconds, plus JIT warm-up
Typical failure mode Someone puts a blocking call in an async def Someone can't explain why @Transactional did nothing

The answer to "which would you choose?" — "For a service that's mostly I/O, ships fast, and sits near data or ML work, FastAPI: the wiring is explicit, the type hints do double duty as validation and documentation, and iteration is quick. For a large system with many contributors, CPU-heavy work that needs real parallelism, or an organisation already on the JVM, Spring Boot: static types and compile-time checking pay for themselves in refactoring safety, and there's a mature answer for every operational problem. The architecture I'd write is the same in both — router, service, repository, validate at the edge, map domain errors once."

6A.12 Trade-off drills MUST KNOW

Q1. "Your FastAPI service handles 5 requests/second and the CPU is idle. What do you look at?"

Think first, then open

Idle CPU with low throughput means you're blocked, not busy. The first thing I'd check is whether a blocking call is sitting inside an async def route — a sync database driver, requests, time.sleep, or a CPU-bound library call. That stalls the whole event loop, so the worker serves one request at a time no matter how many are queued.

The check is quick: convert the route to plain def and see if throughput jumps. If it does, that confirms it, and then the proper fix is either an async driver or keeping the route sync so FastAPI uses the threadpool.

The other candidates: a connection pool too small (requests queueing on a connection), or a slow upstream you're calling sequentially where asyncio.gather would run them concurrently.

Q2. "Should the transaction live in a dependency or in the service?"

Think first, then open

The session's lifecycle belongs in a yield dependency — created per request, closed in the finally, that's exactly what the dependency system is for.

The transaction boundary belongs in the service, because that's where a business operation begins and ends. If I commit in the dependency's teardown, then every request commits whatever happened to be pending, including partial work from a request that failed halfway.

I'd have the service own commit/rollback around the unit of work, and the dependency own connection setup and cleanup. That's the same conclusion as Spring's "put @Transactional on the service, not the controller" — for the same reason.

Q3. "Why not just reuse your SQLAlchemy model as the response model?"

Think first, then open

Because the API contract would then be defined by your database schema. Two concrete failures follow.

Leakage: add an internal column — cost_price, fraud_score, password_hash — and it appears in the API the moment you deploy, with no code change that looks like an API change.

Coupling: you can't rename a column or restructure a table without breaking clients, so the schema becomes frozen by the public contract.

A separate Pydantic output model makes the contract explicit and gives you a place to write a test that asserts the JSON has no internal fields. The extra mapping code is the price of being able to change your database.

Q4. "BackgroundTasks or Celery for sending the welcome email?"

Think first, then open

It depends entirely on whether losing one is acceptable.

BackgroundTasks runs in the same process after the response. It's free, needs no infrastructure, and it's fine for best-effort work. But it dies with a restart or a crash, has no retries, no visibility, and it competes for the same event loop or threadpool as your requests.

A welcome email is usually survivable — I'd start with BackgroundTasks and be explicit that I'm accepting that risk. A payment confirmation, an invoice or anything a customer would complain about missing needs a real queue: durability, retries with backoff, a dead-letter queue, and workers that scale separately from the API.

The tell that you've outgrown it: the first time someone asks "did that email actually go out?"

Q5. "Your endpoint takes 400 ms and 380 ms of it is three sequential HTTP calls. Fix it."

Think first, then open

If the calls are independent, run them concurrently:

a, b, c = await asyncio.gather(fetch_a(), fetch_b(), fetch_c())

That takes the total from the sum to the max — roughly 380 ms down to whatever the slowest single call is.

Two things I'd add rather than stopping there. First, gather fails fast on the first exception; if a partial result is acceptable, return_exceptions=True and handle them individually. Second, each call needs a timeout — without one, a hung upstream holds your request open indefinitely, and under load that exhausts the worker.

If the calls are dependent, concurrency won't help and the real answer is caching, a batch endpoint, or denormalising so the data is already local.

Q6. "Middleware or dependency for API-key checking?"

Think first, then open

A dependency, at the router level: APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(verify_api_key)]).

Middleware runs for everything, including /health and /docs, so you'd immediately be writing path exclusions — and path-matching logic in middleware is where subtle auth bypasses come from. A router-level dependency is explicit about scope, and it's overridable in tests.

I'd use middleware for the genuinely universal concerns: request IDs, timing, CORS, compression. The principle either way is to match the mechanism's blast radius to the concern's.

6A.13 Question bank

Question Short answer The follow-up
How does FastAPI know what to parse? It reads your type hints at runtime "What breaks that?" → a decorator without functools.wraps
def vs async def route? Threadpool vs event loop "Which is worse for a blocking call?" → async def, it stalls everything
What does a yield dependency give you? Setup and guaranteed teardown per request "Compare to Spring" → same job as the @Transactional proxy, but visible
Are dependencies cached? Yes, per request; use_cache=False to opt out "Why does that matter?" → one session shared by the whole request
How do you test with a fake DB? app.dependency_overrides "Why is that better than patching?" → no import juggling, scoped cleanly
Why separate input/output schemas? Prevents field leakage; decouples contract from schema "How do you catch a leak?" → assert the field is absent in a test
extra="forbid"? Reject unknown fields instead of ignoring them "Why?" → a client typo would otherwise return 200 and do nothing
Pydantic v1 vs v2? Rust core, much faster; renamed APIs "Name two renames" → field_validator, model_dump
HTTPException or domain exception? Domain in the service, mapped once at the edge "Why?" → the service stays usable from a worker or CLI
Workers vs async? Processes for CPU, event loop for I/O "How many workers?" → about one per core
BackgroundTasks limits? Same process, no retries, dies on restart "When do you need a queue?" → when losing one matters
N+1 in SQLAlchemy? Lazy relation touched in a loop "Fix?" → selectinload / joinedload, or a projection
