6B
Part 6B

Backend Development with Java and Spring Boot

Same layering as Part 6. What changes is that Spring does more for you — so the questions become “do you know what the framework is doing on your behalf?”

Suggested time · 8 h

Part 6 built a backend in Python and FastAPI. The concepts don't change — layering, validation, dependency injection, transactions, error handling. What changes is that Spring does much more for you, which means the interview questions shift from "how would you build this?" to "do you understand what the framework is doing on your behalf?"

That's the theme to hold onto. Almost every Spring question is really asking whether you know what's happening behind the annotation.

6B.1 The layers — identical to Part 6 MUST KNOW

// ---------- Controller: HTTP only ----------
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService service;

    public OrderController(OrderService service) {   // constructor injection
        this.service = service;
    }

    @PostMapping
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    public OrderResponse create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
        return OrderResponse.from(service.placeOrder(request.userId(), request.items()));
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public OrderResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return OrderResponse.from(service.findById(id));
    }
}

// ---------- Service: business rules, no HTTP, no SQL ----------
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final InventoryClient inventory;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository orders, InventoryClient inventory) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.inventory = inventory;
    }

    @Transactional
    public Order placeOrder(Long userId, List<ItemSpec> items) {
        if (items.isEmpty()) throw new ValidationException("order must contain items");
        if (!inventory.reserve(items)) throw new OutOfStockException(items);
        return orders.save(new Order(userId, items));
    }
}

// ---------- Repository: data access only ----------
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
    List<Order> findByUserIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(Long userId);

    @Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.items where o.id = :id")
    Optional<Order> findByIdWithItems(@Param("id") Long id);
}

The rule is the same as Python: dependencies point downward only. The service must not know it's being called over HTTP; the repository must not know the business rules. That's what lets you unit-test the service with a mock repository and no database.

6B.2 Dependency injection — what Spring actually does MUST KNOW

The problem, exactly as in Part 6: an object that constructs its own dependencies can't be tested with a fake and can't have its wiring changed without editing it.

What Spring does: at startup it scans for @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller and @Configuration classes, builds one instance of each (the default scope is singleton), works out the dependency graph, and hands each object what it needs through its constructor.

Constructor injection is the right answer MUST KNOW

// ✅ constructor injection
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orders;               // can be final
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orders) { this.orders = orders; }
}

// ❌ field injection
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired private OrderRepository orders;          // can't be final
}

Four reasons, and being able to give them all is a strong signal:

  1. The field can be final — genuinely immutable after construction, and safe to share across threads.
  2. You cannot construct an invalid object. With field injection, new OrderService() gives you an instance with a null repository.
  3. Testable without Spring. new OrderService(mockRepo) in a plain JUnit test — no context to start, milliseconds instead of seconds.
  4. It makes bad design visible. A constructor with nine parameters is uncomfortable to look at, and it should be — that class is doing too much. Field injection hides the same problem behind nine tidy annotations.

Spring hasn't required @Autowired on a single constructor since 4.3, so the modern form is just a plain constructor. Lombok's @RequiredArgsConstructor generates it from the final fields.

The questions behind the annotations

"What's the default bean scope?" — Singleton: one instance for the whole application context. Which means your @Service must be stateless, because every request shares it. Instance fields holding request data is a genuine production bug, not a style issue. Other scopes: prototype, request, session.

"How does @Transactional work?" MUST KNOW Spring creates a proxy around your bean. Calls from outside go through the proxy, which opens a transaction, calls your method, then commits or rolls back. This one mechanism explains its two famous limitations:

@Service
public class OrderService {
    public void outer() {
        inner();                    // ❌ self-invocation — bypasses the proxy, NO transaction
    }
    @Transactional
    public void inner() { }

    @Transactional
    private void alsoBroken() { }   // ❌ private methods can't be proxied
}

Self-invocation and private methods don't get the proxy. If you can explain that in terms of proxying rather than reciting it as a rule, you've answered the question properly. The fix is to move the transactional method to another bean, or inject a self-reference.

"@Component vs @Service vs @Repository?" — Functionally near-identical; they're @Component with different semantic labels. @Repository does add one real behaviour: it translates vendor-specific persistence exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy, so your service isn't coupled to JDBC or JPA exception types.

6B.3 Validation at the boundary MUST KNOW

public record CreateOrderRequest(
        @NotNull Long userId,
        @NotEmpty @Size(max = 50) List<@Valid ItemSpec> items,
        @Email String notifyEmail,
        @Positive BigDecimal maxTotal) { }

@Valid on the controller parameter triggers it. A failure raises MethodArgumentNotValidException before your code runs, which you map to a 400 in one place (§6B.6).

Keep request/response DTOs separate from JPA entities. Same argument as Part 6: if the entity is your API contract, adding an internal column silently exposes it, and a client can potentially set fields you never intended. It also couples your public API to your schema, so you can't refactor one without breaking the other.

public record OrderResponse(Long id, String status, BigDecimal total, Instant createdAt) {
    public static OrderResponse from(Order o) {
        return new OrderResponse(o.getId(), o.getStatus().name(), o.getTotal(), o.getCreatedAt());
    }
}

Explicit mapping is a little more code and a lot more control. It's also the place where a test can catch a leak: assert that the JSON has no passwordHash field.

6B.4 JPA, and the N+1 problem MUST KNOW

@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class Order {

    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)            // ← LAZY, always, for ManyToOne
    @JoinColumn(name = "user_id")
    private User user;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
}

The N+1 query problem — the most likely JPA question MUST KNOW

List<Order> orders = orderRepository.findAll();      // 1 query
for (Order o : orders) {
    o.getUser().getName();                           // N more queries, one per order
}

101 queries for 100 orders. It's invisible in the code — the loop looks like plain field access — which is exactly why it reaches production.

How to spot it: turn on SQL logging (spring.jpa.show-sql, or better, datasource-proxy / an APM) and look for the same statement repeated with different parameters.

How to fix it, in order of preference:

// 1. Join fetch — one query
@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.user where o.status = :status")
List<Order> findWithUser(@Param("status") Status status);

// 2. Entity graph — declarative, reusable
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"user", "lines"})
List<Order> findByStatus(Status status);

// 3. Batch fetching — N+1 becomes 1 + (N/size)
// application.yml: spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size: 50

// 4. Don't load the entity at all — project only what you need
public interface OrderSummary { Long getId(); String getUserName(); }
List<OrderSummary> findByStatus(Status status);

Option 4 is the one people forget and often the best: if the endpoint returns five fields, loading full entity graphs is wasted work.

A caution about join fetch with a @OneToMany: joining a collection multiplies rows, so pagination becomes wrong — Hibernate will fetch everything and paginate in memory (it warns about this in the log). Use batch fetching or a two-query approach for paginated collection loads.

Other JPA points worth having ready SHOULD KNOW

  • FetchType.EAGER is a trap. @ManyToOne defaults to EAGER, which means every load drags in relations you may not need. Set LAZY explicitly and fetch deliberately.
  • LazyInitializationException happens when you touch a lazy relation after the persistence context has closed — typically in the controller or during serialisation. The fix is to fetch what you need inside the transaction, not to widen the transaction to cover the view.
  • Entity equals/hashCode — don't use a generated ID, because it's null before persisting, so the object's hash changes when it's saved and it gets lost in any HashSet. Use a business key, or getClass() plus a UUID assigned at construction.
  • save() vs dirty checking — inside a transaction, modifying a managed entity is enough; Hibernate flushes the change at commit. An explicit save() on an already-managed entity is a no-op that many developers write anyway.

6B.5 Transactions MUST KNOW

@Transactional
public void transfer(Long fromId, Long toId, BigDecimal amount) {
    Account from = accounts.findByIdForUpdate(fromId);   // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
    Account to   = accounts.findByIdForUpdate(toId);
    if (from.getBalance().compareTo(amount) < 0) throw new InsufficientFundsException();
    from.debit(amount);
    to.credit(amount);
}

The rollback rule that catches people: by default, Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error) and commits on checked exceptions. So a method that throws IOException will commit whatever it had already written. If you use checked exceptions, say @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class).

Propagation, at the level you'll be asked: REQUIRED (default — join the caller's transaction, or start one), REQUIRES_NEW (suspend the caller's and start a separate one — useful for audit rows that must survive a rollback), NEVER, SUPPORTS.

Keep transactions short, and never do I/O inside one. An HTTP call inside a transaction holds a database connection and any row locks for the duration of someone else's network latency. That is how a slow third party takes down your database connection pool.

Optimistic vs pessimistic locking:

@Version private Long version;      // optimistic: fails on conflict, retry
// vs @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) — blocks, correct under contention

Optimistic when conflicts are rare (better throughput, OptimisticLockException to handle). Pessimistic when they're common and correctness matters more than concurrency.

6B.6 Error handling MUST KNOW

Same design as Part 6: domain code raises domain exceptions and knows nothing about HTTP; one handler at the edge maps them.

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(NotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> notFound(NotFoundException ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        return build(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "NOT_FOUND", ex.getMessage(), req);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> invalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex,
                                            HttpServletRequest req) {
        List<FieldIssue> issues = ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
            .map(f -> new FieldIssue(f.getField(), f.getDefaultMessage()))
            .toList();
        return build(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "VALIDATION_ERROR", "Invalid request", req, issues);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> unexpected(Exception ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        log.error("Unhandled error on {} {}", req.getMethod(), req.getRequestURI(), ex);
        return build(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "INTERNAL_ERROR",
                     "Something went wrong", req);      // never leak the stack trace
    }
}

public record ApiError(String code, String message, String requestId,
                       Instant timestamp, List<FieldIssue> details) { }

Adding a new error type means adding a handler method, not editing every controller. The requestId is what turns a user's bug report into a log search — include it in the response and in every log line.

6B.7 Testing MUST KNOW

// Unit test — no Spring at all, milliseconds
class OrderServiceTest {
    private final OrderRepository orders = mock(OrderRepository.class);
    private final InventoryClient inventory = mock(InventoryClient.class);
    private final OrderService service = new OrderService(orders, inventory);

    @Test
    void rejectsEmptyOrder() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.placeOrder(1L, List.of()))
            .isInstanceOf(ValidationException.class);
    }
}

// Web slice — controller + JSON only, repository mocked
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockBean OrderService service;

    @Test
    void returns201AndNoInternalFields() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(post("/api/v1/orders").contentType(APPLICATION_JSON).content("{...}"))
           .andExpect(status().isCreated())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.passwordHash").doesNotExist());
    }
}

// Integration — real Postgres in a container
@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryIT {
    @Container static PostgreSQLContainer<?> db = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16");
}

The point to make about slices: @SpringBootTest starts the whole context and is slow, so it belongs at the top of the pyramid. Constructor injection is what lets the majority of tests be plain new with mocks and no framework at all — which is the practical payoff of §6B.2, and worth connecting explicitly.

Use a real database for repository tests via Testcontainers. Mocked-SQL tests pass happily while the actual query is broken, and H2 has different SQL semantics than Postgres — the class of bug it lets through is exactly the class you were testing for.

6B.8 Spring Boot vs FastAPI — the comparison SHOULD KNOW

Concern FastAPI (Part 6) Spring Boot
DI Depends(...), explicit per endpoint Container-managed, constructor injection
Validation Pydantic models Bean Validation annotations
ORM SQLAlchemy JPA / Hibernate, or JdbcTemplate
Transactions Explicit session + context manager @Transactional proxy
Async async def on one event loop Thread-per-request; WebFlux or virtual threads for async
Errors Exception handlers @RestControllerAdvice
Startup Milliseconds Seconds (JIT warm-up too)
Where the magic is Very little — you can see the wiring A lot — proxies, autoconfiguration, classpath scanning

The comparison to draw: "FastAPI is explicit — I can read the wiring in the file. Spring does far more for me, which means less boilerplate and a huge ecosystem, but the cost is that things happen through proxies and autoconfiguration that aren't visible at the call site. That's fine as long as you understand the mechanism; the failure mode is someone who knows the annotations but can't explain why @Transactional silently does nothing on a self-invoked method."

6B.9 Trade-off drills MUST KNOW

Q1. "Your @Transactional method isn't rolling back. Diagnose."

Think first, then open

Four candidates, in the order I'd check them:

  1. The exception is checked. Spring rolls back on unchecked only by default. rollbackFor = Exception.class fixes it.
  2. Self-invocation. Called from another method in the same bean, so the proxy is bypassed and there was never a transaction.
  3. The exception is caught inside the method and swallowed — nothing propagates to the proxy, so it commits.
  4. The method isn't public, or the class isn't a Spring-managed bean, so no proxy exists at all.

All four come back to the same mechanism: the transaction lives in the proxy, not in your method. Explaining it that way is better than listing rules.

Q2. "An endpoint got slow after you added a field to the response. Why?"

Think first, then open

Very likely N+1. The new field reads a lazy relation, so serialising a page of 50 results now fires 50 extra queries — one per row — and nothing in the diff looks like a query.

I'd confirm it in the SQL log by looking for the same statement repeated with different IDs, then fix it with a join fetch or an @EntityGraph on that query. If the endpoint only needs a few columns, a projection interface avoids loading the entities at all.

The related trap to mention: if the relation is a @OneToMany, join fetch breaks pagination because the join multiplies rows — batch fetching is safer there.

Q3. "Field injection or constructor injection? Defend it."

Think first, then open

Constructor, for four reasons: the fields can be final; you can't construct an object in an invalid state; you can unit-test with new and mocks without starting Spring; and a ten-parameter constructor makes an overloaded class visibly uncomfortable, which is useful feedback that field injection hides.

The only real argument for field injection is brevity, and @RequiredArgsConstructor removes even that. The one place it still shows up legitimately is test classes, where the framework constructs the instance for you.

Q4. "Should @Transactional go on the controller or the service?"

Think first, then open

The service. That's where a business operation begins and ends, and it's the unit that must be atomic.

On the controller it would cover request parsing and response serialisation, which means the database connection and any row locks are held while you serialise JSON — and it makes serialisation lazily trigger queries inside the transaction, which is the "open session in view" pattern that hides N+1 problems rather than fixing them.

It also breaks reuse: a scheduled job or message consumer calling the same service should get the same transactional behaviour, and it will only if the boundary is on the service.

Q5. "Do you need @Transactional(readOnly = true) on reads?"

Think first, then open

It's worth adding, and for a reason beyond the obvious.

Hibernate skips dirty checking for a read-only transaction, so it doesn't take snapshots of loaded entities — that's a real memory and CPU saving on queries returning many rows. The driver may also route the connection to a read replica.

But it is a hint, not a guarantee: it doesn't stop you writing at the JDBC level, and it isn't a security control. And a read that fits in a single query doesn't strictly need a transaction at all — the value shows up on multi-query reads where you want a consistent snapshot.

6B.10 Question bank

Question Short answer Follow-up
Why constructor injection? final fields, valid object, testable without Spring "How do you test then?" → new Service(mock)
Default bean scope? Singleton — one instance for the app "So what must be true?" → the bean must be stateless
How does @Transactional work? A proxy wraps the bean "Why does self-invocation fail?" → bypasses the proxy
Default rollback rule? Unchecked only "How do you change it?" → rollbackFor
What is N+1? One query per row from a lazy relation "How do you find it?" → SQL log, repeated statements
How do you fix N+1? join fetch, entity graph, batch size, or a projection "Why not join fetch a OneToMany?" → breaks pagination
Entity as your API DTO? No — leaks fields and couples schema to contract "How do you catch a leak?" → assert JSON in a web-slice test
@Component/@Service/@Repository? Same mechanism, different intent "Does @Repository do anything?" → exception translation
LazyInitializationException? Touching a lazy relation after the session closed "Fix?" → fetch inside the transaction, not open-session-in-view
H2 or Testcontainers for repo tests? Testcontainers — real Postgres semantics "Why?" → H2 differs, so bugs survive the test
Optimistic vs pessimistic locking? @Version retry vs FOR UPDATE block "Which for inventory?" → pessimistic if contention is real
← Previous6A · FastAPINext →7 · SQL
7
Part 7

SQL and Database Interviews

About ten problem shapes recur everywhere. Learn the shapes, not a hundred queries.

Suggested time · 8 h

SQL rounds are very predictable. There are about ten problem shapes and they recur everywhere. Learn the shapes, not a hundred queries.

7.1 Logical execution order MUST KNOW (understand this and SQL stops being confusing)

You write SELECT first, but the database evaluates in this order:

FROM / JOIN  ->  WHERE  ->  GROUP BY  ->  HAVING  ->  SELECT  ->  DISTINCT  ->  ORDER BY  ->  LIMIT

Three consequences that answer several classic interview questions:

  1. You can't use a SELECT alias in WHERE — WHERE runs before SELECT exists. You can use it in ORDER BY.
  2. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. Filter as early as possible — WHERE reduces the rows that ever get grouped.
  3. Window functions run after GROUP BY but before ORDER BY, which is why you can't filter on a window function in WHERE — you need a CTE or subquery.

7.2 Joins MUST KNOW

Join Returns
INNER JOIN Only rows matching in both tables
LEFT JOIN All left rows; NULLs where no right match
RIGHT JOIN Mirror of LEFT
FULL OUTER JOIN All rows from both sides
CROSS JOIN Cartesian product
Self join A table joined to itself (hierarchies, comparing rows) 
-- Users with no orders: the LEFT JOIN + IS NULL idiom
SELECT u.id, u.name
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

The trap interviewers set MUST KNOW

-- WRONG: the WHERE clause turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN
SELECT u.name, o.total
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';

-- RIGHT: put the condition in the ON clause
SELECT u.name, o.total
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id AND o.status = 'paid';

Why: ON decides which rows match; WHERE filters the result after the join. Filtering on a right-table column in WHERE discards the NULL rows the LEFT JOIN just produced. Explaining this cleanly is a reliable way to stand out.

Self join example — employees earning more than their manager:

SELECT e.name
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

7.3 Aggregation MUST KNOW

SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE active = TRUE           -- filter rows first
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5           -- then filter groups
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;

COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) vs COUNT(DISTINCT col) — COUNT(*) counts rows including those with NULLs; COUNT(col) skips NULLs; COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-NULL values. Frequently asked.

NULL rules to know: NULL = NULL is not true — it's unknown. Use IS NULL. Aggregates ignore NULLs, except COUNT(*). NOT IN (subquery containing a NULL) returns no rows at all — a genuinely nasty bug; use NOT EXISTS instead.

7.4 Subqueries, CTEs, EXISTS MUST KNOW

-- CTE: readable, composable, can be chained
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at) AS month, SUM(total) AS spend
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT month, AVG(spend)
FROM monthly
GROUP BY month;

CTE vs subquery: functionally similar; CTEs are far more readable, can be referenced multiple times, and support recursion. Historically some databases materialised CTEs as an optimisation fence; modern Postgres inlines them unless you write MATERIALIZED.

EXISTS vs IN:

SELECT * FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id AND o.total > 1000);

EXISTS short-circuits on the first match and is NULL-safe. IN builds the full list. For large correlated sets, EXISTS is usually the better choice — and NOT EXISTS avoids the NULL trap above.

7.5 Window functions MUST KNOW (the highest-value SQL skill)

WHAT — compute across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing them the way GROUP BY does.

SELECT
  name, department, salary,
  RANK()        OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
  DENSE_RANK()  OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rnk,
  ROW_NUMBER()  OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn,
  AVG(salary)   OVER (PARTITION BY department)                      AS dept_avg,
  LAG(salary)   OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY hired_at)    AS prev_hire_salary
FROM employees;
Function Gives
ROW_NUMBER() 1,2,3,4 — always unique, arbitrary tie-break
RANK() 1,2,2,4 — ties share a rank, then it skips
DENSE_RANK() 1,2,2,3 — ties share, no gap
LAG() / LEAD() Previous / next row's value
SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...) Running total
NTILE(4) Quartile buckets

Know the difference between the three ranking functions cold — it's asked verbatim.

7.6 The ten classic problems MUST KNOW

1. Second highest salary

-- Handles ties and returns NULL when there's no second value
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);

-- Nth highest, general form
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
OFFSET 1 LIMIT 1;

The follow-up is always "what if there are ties?" — DENSE_RANK() = 2 gives the second distinct salary; ROW_NUMBER() = 2 gives the second row. Ask which they want.

2. Find duplicates

SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM users
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

3. Delete duplicates, keep the earliest

DELETE FROM users
WHERE id NOT IN (
    SELECT MIN(id) FROM users GROUP BY email
);
-- or, cleaner:
DELETE FROM users u
USING users dup
WHERE u.email = dup.email AND u.id > dup.id;

4. Latest record per user MUST KNOW (asked constantly)

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

This ROW_NUMBER() … PARTITION BY … WHERE rn = 1 pattern solves "latest per group", "first per group", "most expensive per category". Memorise it. Postgres also has DISTINCT ON (user_id) as a shortcut.

5. Top N per group

Same as above with WHERE rn <= 3.

6. Running total

SELECT
  order_date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date
                    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM orders;

7. Month-over-month growth

WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at) AS month, SUM(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 2) AS pct_change
FROM monthly;

NULLIF(x, 0) to avoid division by zero — a nice detail to include.

8. Consecutive records (3 logins in a row)

SELECT DISTINCT l1.user_id
FROM logins l1
JOIN logins l2 ON l2.user_id = l1.user_id AND l2.day = l1.day + 1
JOIN logins l3 ON l3.user_id = l1.user_id AND l3.day = l1.day + 2;

9. Gaps and islands (consecutive streaks) SHOULD KNOW

WITH grouped AS (
    SELECT user_id, login_date,
           login_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date))::int AS grp
    FROM logins
)
SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS streak_start, COUNT(*) AS streak_length
FROM grouped
GROUP BY user_id, grp
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

The trick to explain: for consecutive dates, date − row_number is constant within a run. Grouping by that constant collapses each streak into one group. It looks like magic until you say that sentence.

10. Pivot with conditional aggregation

SELECT
  department,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'active')   AS active,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'inactive') AS inactive,
  SUM(CASE WHEN salary > 100000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS high_earners
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;

7.7 Indexes MUST KNOW

WHAT — a separate structure (usually a B-tree) mapping column values to row locations.

WHY — turns a full table scan, O(n), into roughly O(log n).

COST — disk space, and slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE because every index must be maintained. Don't index a write-heavy, rarely-queried column.

When an index gets used:

Query Uses index on email?
WHERE email = 'a@b.com' ✅
WHERE email LIKE 'a%' ✅ (prefix)
WHERE email LIKE '%b.com' ❌ (leading wildcard)
WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com' ❌ — unless you create a functional index on LOWER(email)
WHERE email IS NOT NULL maybe — depends on selectivity

The most common real bug: wrapping the indexed column in a function or doing arithmetic on it (WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026) makes the index unusable. Rewrite as a range: WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'.

Composite index and the leftmost-prefix rule MUST KNOW An index on (user_id, created_at) serves queries filtering on user_id, or on user_id AND created_at — but not on created_at alone. Order the columns by equality-filter first, then range/sort.

Covering index — if the index contains every column the query needs, the database never touches the table. Very fast; mention it as an optimisation for hot read paths.

How to diagnose: EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Look for Seq Scan on a large table where you expected Index Scan, and compare estimated vs actual row counts — a big gap means stale statistics.

The N+1 problem (comes up in ORM discussions): fetching 100 orders then looping to fetch each customer = 101 queries. Fix with a join or eager loading (selectinload / joinedload).

7.8 Transactions and isolation SHOULD KNOW

ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

Isolation level Prevents Still allows
Read Uncommitted — dirty reads
Read Committed (Postgres default) dirty reads non-repeatable reads, phantoms
Repeatable Read (MySQL default) + non-repeatable reads phantoms (in theory)
Serializable everything — (lowest concurrency)
  • Dirty read — you see another transaction's uncommitted data.
  • Non-repeatable read — you read the same row twice and get different values.
  • Phantom read — you re-run the same query and new rows have appeared.

Optimistic vs pessimistic locking: pessimistic takes a lock up front (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) — correct under contention, but it blocks. Optimistic uses a version column and retries on conflict — better when conflicts are rare. Knowing when to pick each is a good senior answer.

7.9 Normalisation vs denormalisation SHOULD KNOW

Form Requirement
1NF Atomic values, no repeating groups
2NF 1NF + no partial dependency on part of a composite key
3NF 2NF + no transitive dependency (non-key depending on non-key)

Normalise to eliminate update anomalies and redundancy — the default for transactional systems. Denormalise deliberately when read performance demands it, accepting that you now must keep copies in sync.

"I normalise by default because it makes correctness the database's job. I denormalise when a specific read path is measurably too slow and joining is the bottleneck — for example a precomputed order-count column on the user row, updated by a trigger or in the same transaction. The cost is that I now own consistency between the two."

SQL vs NoSQL, one paragraph: relational for structured data with relationships, transactions, and ad-hoc queries. Document stores for flexible schemas and denormalised read-heavy access. Key-value for caching and sessions. Wide-column for very high write throughput on known access patterns. The honest answer to "which would you use?" is usually "relational, unless the access pattern proves otherwise."

7.10 SQL question bank

Question Short answer Follow-up
WHERE vs HAVING Rows before grouping vs groups after "Which is more efficient?" → WHERE, fewer rows to group
UNION vs UNION ALL Dedupes (costly sort) vs keeps everything "Which by default?" → UNION ALL unless you need dedupe
DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP Row-by-row & rollbackable / fast reset / removes the table "Which fires triggers?" → DELETE
RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER Gaps / no gaps / always unique "Second highest with ties?" → DENSE_RANK
What is an index B-tree mapping values to rows "When does it hurt?" → write-heavy, low selectivity
Why is my query slow EXPLAIN; look for seq scans, bad joins, missing index, function on indexed column "What if the index exists but isn't used?" → selectivity, stale stats, type mismatch
Latest row per group ROW_NUMBER() PARTITION BY … WHERE rn=1 "Without window functions?" → correlated subquery on MAX
ACID Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable "Give an example needing all four" → money transfer
Primary vs unique key One per table, not null, clustered vs many, nullable "Can a FK reference a unique key?" → yes
N+1 queries One query per row in a loop "How do you spot it?" → query logs / APM showing repeated identical SQL

8
Part 8

Data Structures and Algorithms

Fifteen patterns and how to recognise them from the wording — so you can solve a problem you have never seen.

Suggested time · 30 h

The goal of this section is not to teach you 200 problems. It is to make you able to solve a problem you have never seen.

There are roughly 15 patterns. Almost every interview question is one of them, or two of them stacked. Learn to recognise the pattern from the wording, and the solution becomes mechanical.

8.0 The recognition table — memorise this page

When you read a problem, scan for these words. They are not hints from the problem-setter; they are structural facts about the problem that constrain the solution.

Words in the problem Pattern to consider first Why
"contiguous", "subarray", "substring", "window", "at most K", "longest/shortest ... such that" Sliding window Contiguity means you can extend and shrink a range instead of re-scanning
"two elements that sum to", "pair", "sorted array", "closest", "container" Two pointers Sortedness gives you a decision rule for which pointer to move
"frequency", "count", "duplicate", "seen before", "anagram", "group by" Hash map / set You need O(1) membership or counting
"sorted" + "find", "minimum possible X", "maximum possible X", "can we do it in ≤ X" Binary search (on array or on the answer) Monotonic predicate
"sum of range", "range query", "how many subarrays sum to K" Prefix sum (+ hash map) Range sums decompose into differences of prefixes
"matching brackets", "next greater/smaller", "undo", "previous element that..." Stack LIFO / monotonic structure
"first ... in order", "level by level", "shortest path in unweighted graph", "nearest" BFS + queue BFS explores in distance order
"all paths", "all combinations", "all permutations", "generate every" Backtracking Exhaustive search with pruning
"top K", "K largest/smallest", "median of a stream", "merge K sorted" Heap Need repeated min/max of changing data
"connected", "islands", "cycle", "dependency", "prerequisite", "order of tasks" Graph — DFS/BFS/topological sort It's a graph even when it doesn't say "graph"
"overlapping", "merge", "meeting rooms", "schedule", "[start, end]" Intervals (sort by start) Sorting makes overlap checking local
"maximum profit", "minimum cost", "number of ways", "can you reach", "choose or skip" Dynamic programming Overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure
"locally best works", "minimum number of X", "always pick the largest/earliest" Greedy — but prove it Exchange argument
"in-place", "O(1) extra space" Two pointers, index-as-hash-marker, cyclic sort Constraint eliminates hash maps
n ≤ 20 Exponential is intended — bitmask/backtracking 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶
n ≤ 10³ O(n²) is fine 10⁶ ops
n ≤ 10⁵ You need O(n log n) or O(n) O(n²) = 10¹⁰, too slow
n ≤ 10⁹ O(log n) or O(√n) — binary search or maths

Use it in the interview: say the recognition out loud. "The word 'contiguous' plus 'at most K distinct' makes me think sliding window — let me check whether the window property is monotonic." That single sentence is worth more than the code.

8.1 Complexity, said properly

Big-O is about growth rate as n → ∞, ignoring constants. O(2n) and O(n/2) are both O(n).

Complexity n = 10⁶ feels like Typical source
O(1) instant hash lookup, arithmetic
O(log n) instant binary search, balanced tree, heap push
O(n) fast single pass
O(n log n) acceptable sorting, heap over all elements
O(n²) too slow nested loops over the same array
O(2ⁿ), O(n!) only for n ≤ 20 / n ≤ 10 subsets, permutations

Space complexity counts extra space you allocate, not the input. Recursion counts: the call stack is O(depth).

How to state it in an interview:

"Time is O(n log n) — dominated by the sort. Space is O(n) for the hash map, plus O(log n) for the sort's stack, so O(n) overall."

Naming what dominates is the mark of someone who understands it rather than reciting it.

Amortised vs average vs worst: list.append is amortised O(1) (occasional resize). Dict lookup is average O(1), worst O(n) (collisions). Quicksort is average O(n log n), worst O(n²). Interviewers like the distinction.

8.2 Pattern: Hashing MUST KNOW

CONCEPT — trade space for time. A hash map turns "have I seen this?" from an O(n) scan into an O(1) probe.

RECOGNITION — count, frequency, duplicate, "seen", "exists", grouping, complement.

BRUTE FORCE → OPTIMAL, using Two Sum:

# Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
def two_sum_brute(nums, target):
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
            if nums[i] + nums[j] == target:
                return [i, j]
    return []

Why it's insufficient: for each element we re-scan the rest looking for target - nums[i]. That search is the waste.

The improvement idea: we're repeatedly asking "does value X exist in the part I've already seen?" That's exactly what a hash map answers in O(1).

# Optimal: O(n) time, O(n) space
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                       # value -> index
    for i, num in enumerate(nums):
        complement = target - num
        if complement in seen:
            return [seen[complement], i]
        seen[num] = i               # store AFTER checking, so we don't reuse i
    return []

EDGE CASES — empty array, no valid pair, duplicates ([3,3], target 6 — works because we check before storing), negative numbers, target equal to 2*num.

INTERVIEW EXPLANATION (say this):

"Brute force is a nested loop, O(n²). The inefficiency is that the inner loop re-searches for the complement each time. Since I only need existence, I can store what I've seen in a hash map and look the complement up in O(1). One pass, O(n) time, O(n) space. I check for the complement before inserting the current element, which handles the case where the two values are equal without pairing an index with itself."

FOLLOW-UPS

Q Answer
What if the array is sorted? Two pointers — O(n) time, O(1) space. Better than the hash map
Return all pairs, not one? Keep going; use a set of pairs to dedupe
Three sum? Sort, fix one element, two-pointer the rest → O(n²); skip duplicates to avoid repeated triples
What if it doesn't fit in memory? External: sort-based, or hash-partition by key across files

COMMON MISTAKES — inserting before checking (self-pairing); returning values instead of indices; forgetting duplicates.

Other must-know hashing problems: group anagrams (key = sorted string or a 26-length count tuple), longest consecutive sequence (set + only start streaks from numbers with no predecessor → O(n)), first non-repeating character, subarray sum equals K (hashing + prefix sum, §8.6).

8.3 Pattern: Two pointers MUST KNOW

CONCEPT — two indices moving through the data, where a comparison tells you unambiguously which one to move.

WHY IT WORKS — it requires a monotonic decision rule. In a sorted array, if a[lo] + a[hi] < target, then no hi' < hi can help — so moving lo is provably safe. That's why sortedness matters.

RECOGNITION — sorted input, pair/triplet, palindrome, "in-place", "O(1) space", removing/partitioning elements, container/area problems.

Three sub-shapes:

(a) Opposite ends

def two_sum_sorted(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        s = nums[lo] + nums[hi]
        if s == target:
            return [lo, hi]
        if s < target:
            lo += 1        # need a bigger sum
        else:
            hi -= 1        # need a smaller sum
    return []

(b) Same direction (read/write pointers) — the in-place idiom

def remove_duplicates(nums):          # sorted array, in place
    if not nums:
        return 0
    write = 1
    for read in range(1, len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != nums[write - 1]:
            nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return write                      # new logical length

This shape solves: remove duplicates, move zeroes, remove element, partition by a predicate. Learn it once, reuse it four times.

(c) Fast/slow (Floyd's cycle detection)

def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False

Why it works: if there's a cycle, the fast pointer gains one step per iteration on the slow one inside the loop, so it must eventually land on it. To find the cycle start: reset one pointer to head and advance both one step at a time — they meet at the entry.

Container With Most Water — the classic "why is it safe to move?" question:

def max_area(height):
    lo, hi, best = 0, len(height) - 1, 0
    while lo < hi:
        best = max(best, min(height[lo], height[hi]) * (hi - lo))
        if height[lo] < height[hi]:
            lo += 1        # moving the taller side can never help
        else:
            hi -= 1
    return best

The proof to say out loud: area is limited by the shorter line. Moving the taller pointer inward keeps the same limiting height but reduces the width, so it can only make things worse. Moving the shorter one is the only move that can improve the answer.

COMMON MISTAKES — while lo <= hi when you need distinct elements; forgetting to skip duplicates in 3Sum; using two pointers on unsorted data where the decision rule isn't valid.

8.4 Pattern: Sliding window MUST KNOW (highest ROI pattern in interviews)

CONCEPT — maintain a contiguous range [left, right] and a running summary of what's inside it. Expand right; shrink left when the window becomes invalid. Each element enters and leaves at most once → O(n).

RECOGNITION — "contiguous", "subarray", "substring", "window", "at most K", "exactly K", "longest/shortest/maximum with property P".

WHEN IT'S VALID — the property must be monotone: if a window is invalid, extending it further right can't make it valid again (so shrinking from the left is the right response). Check this before committing. Sliding window is not valid for "max subarray sum" with negative numbers (that's Kadane) because removing a left element can increase the sum.

Template A — variable window, longest

def longest_substring_without_repeat(s: str) -> int:
    last_seen = {}
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last_seen and last_seen[ch] >= left:
            left = last_seen[ch] + 1       # jump left past the duplicate
        last_seen[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

Template B — variable window with a counter (the general workhorse)

def longest_with_at_most_k_distinct(s: str, k: int) -> int:
    counts = defaultdict(int)
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        counts[ch] += 1
        while len(counts) > k:             # window invalid -> shrink
            counts[s[left]] -= 1
            if counts[s[left]] == 0:
                del counts[s[left]]
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

Memorise this shape. Change only the "invalid" condition and it solves a dozen problems.

Template C — fixed window

def max_sum_window(nums, k):
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for right in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[right] - nums[right - k]
        best = max(best, window)
    return best

Template D — shortest window (minimum window substring)

def min_window(s: str, t: str) -> str:
    need = Counter(t)
    missing = len(t)                       # count of chars still needed (with multiplicity)
    left = 0
    best = (float("inf"), 0, 0)

    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if need[ch] > 0:
            missing -= 1
        need[ch] -= 1

        while missing == 0:                # valid -> try to shrink
            if right - left + 1 < best[0]:
                best = (right - left + 1, left, right)
            need[s[left]] += 1
            if need[s[left]] > 0:
                missing += 1
            left += 1

    return "" if best[0] == float("inf") else s[best[1]:best[2] + 1]

The "exactly K" trick SHOULD KNOW — sliding window naturally handles "at most K". For "exactly K": exactly(K) = atMost(K) - atMost(K-1). This turns a hard problem into two easy ones. Worth knowing; it comes up.

COMPLEXITY — O(n) time even though there's a nested while, because left only ever moves forward, total ≤ n moves across the whole run. Say this explicitly — interviewers ask "isn't that O(n²)?" to see if you understand amortised analysis.

EDGE CASES — empty string, k = 0, window larger than the array, all identical characters.

PROBLEM SET (this pattern alone covers a lot): longest substring without repeating characters · longest repeating character replacement · minimum window substring · permutation in string · max consecutive ones III · fruit into baskets (= at most 2 distinct) · maximum average subarray.

8.5 Pattern: Prefix sum SHOULD KNOW→MUST KNOW

CONCEPT — precompute cumulative sums so any range sum is a subtraction: sum(i..j) = prefix[j+1] - prefix[i].

PROBLEM IT SOLVES — repeated range queries, and "count subarrays summing to K" where sliding window fails because of negative numbers.

def subarray_sum_equals_k(nums, k):
    counts = defaultdict(int)
    counts[0] = 1          # empty prefix — crucial for subarrays starting at index 0
    running = result = 0
    for n in nums:
        running += n
        result += counts[running - k]   # how many earlier prefixes make this window sum to k
        counts[running] += 1
    return result

The insight to state: a subarray (i, j] sums to k exactly when prefix[j] - prefix[i] == k, i.e. prefix[i] == prefix[j] - k. So while scanning, I ask how many earlier prefixes had that value — a hash map gives that in O(1).

Related: running totals, product-except-self (prefix × suffix products, no division), range sum immutable, 2D prefix sums NICE TO KNOW.

8.6 Pattern: Binary search MUST KNOW

Two distinct uses. Candidates know the first and miss the second.

Use 1 — search a sorted array

def binary_search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2        # avoids overflow in other languages; habit
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1

Use 2 — binary search on the answer MUST KNOW (this is the one that separates candidates)

RECOGNITION — "minimum possible maximum", "maximum possible minimum", "smallest capacity/speed/days such that it's feasible", "can we do X in ≤ T".

The idea: you're not searching an array. You're searching the range of possible answers, and you have a feasibility function can(x) that is monotonic — false, false, false, true, true, true. Binary search finds the boundary.

def ship_within_days(weights, days):
    def can(capacity):
        needed, current = 1, 0
        for w in weights:
            if current + w > capacity:
                needed += 1
                current = 0
            current += w
        return needed <= days

    lo, hi = max(weights), sum(weights)      # bounds of the answer space
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if can(mid):
            hi = mid          # feasible: try smaller
        else:
            lo = mid + 1      # infeasible: must go bigger
    return lo

Explain it as: "The answer is somewhere between the heaviest single package and the total weight. Feasibility is monotonic — if capacity C works, every capacity above C works. So I binary search the answer space, with an O(n) feasibility check, giving O(n log(sum))."

The lo < hi + hi = mid template above is the safe one for boundary-finding. Use it and you won't get infinite loops. The invariant: the answer is always in [lo, hi], and the range strictly shrinks each iteration.

Also know: bisect_left / bisect_right from the standard library, search in rotated sorted array, find first/last occurrence, find peak element, median of two sorted arrays (hard NICE TO KNOW).

COMMON MISTAKES — infinite loop from lo = mid instead of mid + 1; wrong < vs <=; forgetting the array must actually be sorted (or the predicate monotonic).

8.7 Pattern: Stack MUST KNOW

RECOGNITION — matching/nesting, "next greater/smaller element", "previous smaller", undo, expression evaluation, histogram/rectangle problems, iterative DFS.

def is_valid_parentheses(s):
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    stack = []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in pairs:
            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
                return False
        else:
            stack.append(ch)
    return not stack        # leftovers = unclosed

Monotonic stack MUST KNOW — the technique worth real practice

Keep the stack sorted (increasing or decreasing). Pop while the incoming element violates the order — the popped element has just found its answer.

def next_greater_element(nums):
    result = [-1] * len(nums)
    stack = []                        # holds indices, values decreasing
    for i, n in enumerate(nums):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < n:
            result[stack.pop()] = n   # n is the next greater for that index
        stack.append(i)
    return result

O(n): each index is pushed once and popped at most once.

Solves: next greater/smaller element, daily temperatures, largest rectangle in histogram, trapping rain water, stock span, remove K digits.

8.8 Linked lists SHOULD KNOW

Less common than they used to be, but still appear. Three things to know cold:

def reverse_list(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        curr.next, prev, curr = prev, curr, curr.next
    return prev

def find_middle(head):              # slow/fast
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
    return slow

def merge_sorted(a, b):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()       # dummy node avoids special-casing the head
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else:
            tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b
    return dummy.next

The dummy-node trick removes almost all the edge-case pain in linked list problems. Mention it by name.

Also: detect cycle + find its start, remove Nth from end (two pointers gap N), reorder list (find middle → reverse second half → interleave).

8.9 Trees MUST KNOW

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

Traversals — know all four

def inorder(node):                  # left, root, right -> SORTED for a BST
    if not node: return []
    return inorder(node.left) + [node.val] + inorder(node.right)

def preorder(node):                 # root first -> serialisation, copying
    ...
def postorder(node):                # children first -> deletion, computing from below
    ...

def level_order(root):              # BFS
    if not root: return []
    out, q = [], deque([root])
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):     # freeze the level size before mutating q
            node = q.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:  q.append(node.left)
            if node.right: q.append(node.right)
        out.append(level)
    return out

The for _ in range(len(q)) line is the whole trick for level-by-level BFS. Get it right and you can answer every "by level" variation: zigzag, right side view, level averages, minimum depth.

The recursive template for tree problems

def solve(node):
    if not node:
        return base_case            # 1. base case
    left  = solve(node.left)        # 2. recurse
    right = solve(node.right)
    return combine(node, left, right)   # 3. combine

Almost every tree question is: max depth, diameter, balanced check, sum of paths, invert, same tree, subtree — all this shape with a different combine.

def max_depth(root):
    return 0 if not root else 1 + max(max_depth(root.left), max_depth(root.right))

def is_valid_bst(node, low=float("-inf"), high=float("inf")):
    if not node:
        return True
    if not (low < node.val < high):
        return False
    return (is_valid_bst(node.left, low, node.val) and
            is_valid_bst(node.right, node.val, high))

The classic BST mistake: only comparing a node to its immediate children. A node deep in the left subtree can still be larger than the root. You must pass down the range.

Lowest common ancestor:

def lca(root, p, q):
    if not root or root is p or root is q:
        return root
    left, right = lca(root.left, p, q), lca(root.right, p, q)
    if left and right:
        return root          # p and q split here -> this is the LCA
    return left or right

Complexity note: balanced tree operations are O(log n); a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) BST is O(n). That's why AVL/Red-Black trees exist. Traversals are O(n) time, O(h) space for the call stack.

8.10 Heaps / priority queues MUST KNOW

RECOGNITION — "top K", "K closest", "median of a stream", "merge K sorted", "schedule by priority".

import heapq

def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return [n for n, _ in counts.most_common(k)]        # fine to use

def k_largest(nums, k):                                  # explicit version
    heap = []
    for n in nums:
        heapq.heappush(heap, n)
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)      # min-heap of size k: pop the smallest
    return heap

def merge_k_sorted(lists):
    heap = [(lst[0], i, 0) for i, lst in enumerate(lists) if lst]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    out = []
    while heap:
        val, li, idx = heapq.heappop(heap)
        out.append(val)
        if idx + 1 < len(lists[li]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[li][idx + 1], li, idx + 1))
    return out

Why a min-heap of size K gives the K largest: the heap's root is the smallest of the K best so far. Anything smaller than it can't belong in the answer, so we evict the root. O(n log k), and O(k) space — better than sorting when k ≪ n.

Two-heap pattern (median of a stream) SHOULD KNOW — max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper; keep sizes balanced within one. Median is the top of the larger heap, or the average of both tops.

8.11 Graphs MUST KNOW

First skill: recognise a graph when it isn't called one. Grids, word ladders, course prerequisites, friend networks, task dependencies, flight routes — all graphs.

graph = defaultdict(list)
for u, v in edges:
    graph[u].append(v)
    graph[v].append(u)      # omit for a directed graph

DFS

def dfs(node, visited):
    if node in visited:
        return
    visited.add(node)
    for nbr in graph[node]:
        dfs(nbr, visited)

BFS — use for shortest path in an unweighted graph

def bfs_shortest(start, target):
    q = deque([(start, 0)])
    visited = {start}
    while q:
        node, dist = q.popleft()
        if node == target:
            return dist
        for nbr in graph[node]:
            if nbr not in visited:
                visited.add(nbr)          # mark on ENQUEUE, not dequeue
                q.append((nbr, dist + 1))
    return -1

Marking visited on enqueue is the fix for the most common graph bug — otherwise a node can be queued many times before it's processed, and the complexity blows up.

Grid traversal (islands / flood fill)

def num_islands(grid):
    if not grid: return 0
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    count = 0

    def sink(r, c):
        if not (0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols) or grid[r][c] != "1":
            return
        grid[r][c] = "0"                    # mark visited in place
        for dr, dc in ((1,0), (-1,0), (0,1), (0,-1)):
            sink(r + dr, c + dc)

    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == "1":
                count += 1
                sink(r, c)
    return count

The ((1,0), (-1,0), (0,1), (0,-1)) direction tuple is an idiom — use it everywhere in grid problems.

Topological sort MUST KNOW (Kahn's algorithm)

RECOGNITION — "prerequisites", "build order", "dependencies", "can all tasks be finished".

def course_order(n, prerequisites):
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    indegree = [0] * n
    for course, prereq in prerequisites:
        graph[prereq].append(course)
        indegree[course] += 1

    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indegree[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for nbr in graph[node]:
            indegree[nbr] -= 1
            if indegree[nbr] == 0:
                q.append(nbr)

    return order if len(order) == n else []   # short = there's a cycle

The cycle-detection insight: if the output is shorter than n, some nodes never reached in-degree 0, which means they're in a cycle. That's the answer to "how do you detect a circular dependency" — same algorithm, no extra work.

Complexity for graph traversals: O(V + E) time, O(V) space.

Also worth knowing SHOULD KNOW: Union-Find (connected components, cycle detection in undirected graphs, Kruskal's MST) — the path-compression + union-by-rank version is short and impressive. Dijkstra (weighted shortest path, heap-based, O((V+E) log V)) — know when it applies (non-negative weights) even if you don't memorise it.

8.12 Backtracking SHOULD KNOW→MUST KNOW

CONCEPT — build a candidate incrementally; when it can't lead to a solution, undo the last choice and try another.

RECOGNITION — "all combinations", "all permutations", "all subsets", "generate every valid X", "N-Queens", "sudoku", "word search". Small n (≤ 20).

The universal template

def backtrack(path, choices):
    if is_solution(path):
        results.append(path[:])        # COPY — path is mutated
        return
    for choice in choices:
        if not is_valid(choice, path):
            continue
        path.append(choice)            # 1. choose
        backtrack(path, next_choices)  # 2. explore
        path.pop()                     # 3. un-choose
    return

def subsets(nums):
    res, path = [], []
    def dfs(start):
        res.append(path[:])
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            path.append(nums[i])
            dfs(i + 1)
            path.pop()
    dfs(0)
    return res

def permutations(nums):
    res = []
    def dfs(remaining, path):
        if not remaining:
            res.append(path)
            return
        for i in range(len(remaining)):
            dfs(remaining[:i] + remaining[i+1:], path + [remaining[i]])
    dfs(nums, [])
    return res

COMMON MISTAKES — appending path instead of path[:] (every result ends up identical/empty); forgetting to pop(); not sorting first when you need to skip duplicates (if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue).

Complexity: subsets O(n·2ⁿ), permutations O(n·n!). Say the pruning matters more than the bound.

Problems: subsets, subsets II, permutations, combination sum, letter combinations of a phone number, word search, N-Queens, palindrome partitioning.

8.13 Intervals SHOULD KNOW

RECOGNITION — [start, end] pairs, "overlapping", "merge", "meeting rooms", "schedule".

The universal first move: sort by start. After that, overlap checking is local.

def merge_intervals(intervals):
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    merged = [intervals[0]]
    for start, end in intervals[1:]:
        if start <= merged[-1][1]:                    # overlaps
            merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end)   # max! not just end
        else:
            merged.append([start, end])
    return merged

def min_meeting_rooms(intervals):
    starts = sorted(i[0] for i in intervals)
    ends   = sorted(i[1] for i in intervals)
    rooms = best = 0
    s = e = 0
    while s < len(starts):
        if starts[s] < ends[e]:
            rooms += 1; s += 1
        else:
            rooms -= 1; e += 1
        best = max(best, rooms)
    return best

Meeting rooms explained: I don't care which meeting is in which room, only how many are concurrent. So I sort start times and end times separately and sweep — every start increments the count, every end decrements it, and the peak is the answer.

COMMON MISTAKE — merged[-1][1] = end instead of max(...). Fails when one interval fully contains another.

Problems: merge intervals, insert interval, non-overlapping intervals (greedy: sort by end), meeting rooms I & II.

8.14 Greedy SHOULD KNOW

CONCEPT — make the locally best choice at each step and never reconsider.

The danger: greedy is only correct if the problem has the greedy choice property. Coin change with arbitrary denominations breaks greedy; with Indian/US coins it works. In an interview, always say whether you can justify it.

def can_jump(nums):
    reach = 0
    for i, n in enumerate(nums):
        if i > reach:
            return False
        reach = max(reach, i + n)
    return True

def max_profit(prices):              # buy/sell once — this is Kadane in disguise
    best, lowest = 0, float("inf")
    for p in prices:
        lowest = min(lowest, p)
        best = max(best, p - lowest)
    return best

How to justify greedy in an interview (the exchange argument):

"Suppose an optimal solution differs from my greedy choice at the first step. I can swap in the greedy choice without making the solution worse — so there's an optimal solution that agrees with greedy. By induction, greedy is optimal."

You don't need a formal proof, but showing you know a proof is required earns real credit.

Problems: jump game, best time to buy/sell stock, gas station, non-overlapping intervals, task scheduler.

8.15 Dynamic programming MUST KNOW (start here if you're scared of DP)

WHEN DP APPLIES — two conditions, both required: 1. Overlapping subproblems — the same subproblem is solved many times. 2. Optimal substructure — the optimal answer is built from optimal answers to subproblems.

RECOGNITION — "maximum/minimum X", "number of ways", "can you reach", "longest/shortest", and a choice at each step (take it or skip it).

The four questions that produce any DP solution

  1. What is the state? What minimal information describes a subproblem? (usually an index, sometimes index + remaining capacity)
  2. What is the recurrence? How does state i relate to earlier states?
  3. What is the base case?
  4. What order do I fill it in?

Answer those four out loud in the interview and you've done the hard part.

Path 1 — memoisation (top-down): write the recursion, then cache it

from functools import lru_cache

def climb_stairs(n):
    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
    def ways(i):
        if i <= 2:
            return i
        return ways(i - 1) + ways(i - 2)
    return ways(n)

This is the easiest way to get to a working DP under pressure. Write the naive recursion first — it's usually obvious — then add one decorator. Say: "That's O(2ⁿ) because subproblems repeat; memoising collapses it to O(n)."

Path 2 — tabulation (bottom-up)

def climb_stairs(n):
    if n <= 2: return n
    a, b = 1, 2
    for _ in range(3, n + 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return b            # O(n) time, O(1) space — rolling variables

Space optimisation — if dp[i] only depends on dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], you don't need the array. Mentioning this is a strong-hire signal.

The five DP problems that cover most interviews

1. Climbing stairs / Fibonacci — the "1D, depends on last two" shape.

2. House robber — the "take it or skip it" shape:

def rob(nums):
    prev = curr = 0
    for n in nums:
        prev, curr = curr, max(curr, prev + n)   # skip vs take
    return curr

3. Coin change — the "unbounded knapsack / minimum" shape:

def coin_change(coins, amount):
    dp = [float("inf")] * (amount + 1)
    dp[0] = 0
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if c <= a:
                dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != float("inf") else -1

State = "minimum coins to make amount a". Recurrence = for each coin, one coin plus the best way to make a - c. O(amount × len(coins)).

4. Longest increasing subsequence — the "compare against all previous" shape:

def length_of_lis(nums):
    dp = [1] * len(nums)                # O(n^2)
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        for j in range(i):
            if nums[j] < nums[i]:
                dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1)
    return max(dp, default=0)

Follow-up: O(n log n) with bisect on a "tails" array. Know that it exists; know it doesn't reconstruct the actual subsequence trivially.

5. Grid paths / edit distance — the 2D shape:

def unique_paths(m, n):
    dp = [[1] * n for _ in range(m)]
    for r in range(1, m):
        for c in range(1, n):
            dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]
    return dp[-1][-1]

Also know: Kadane's algorithm (maximum subarray) — arguably the single most-asked DP:

def max_subarray(nums):
    best = curr = nums[0]
    for n in nums[1:]:
        curr = max(n, curr + n)     # start fresh, or extend
        best = max(best, curr)
    return best

"At each element I make one decision: extend the previous subarray, or start a new one here. I start fresh whenever the running sum has gone negative, because a negative prefix can only hurt."

COMMON MISTAKES — wrong base case; state that doesn't capture everything needed; iterating in an order where dependencies aren't computed yet; forgetting that lru_cache needs hashable (so no list arguments — convert to tuple).

8.16 The curated problem set

This is the minimum effective set: ~45 problems that between them teach every pattern above. Do these properly — writing the code, timing yourself, explaining out loud — rather than 300 problems shallowly.

Tier 1 — do these first (20 problems, ~2 weeks)

# Problem Pattern Difficulty
1 Two Sum Hashing Easy
2 Valid Anagram Hashing Easy
3 Group Anagrams Hashing Medium
4 Contains Duplicate Hashing Easy
5 Valid Palindrome Two pointers Easy
6 3Sum Two pointers + sort Medium

10 Longest Repeating Character Replacement Sliding window Medium

14 Search in Rotated Sorted Array Binary search Medium

16 Merge Two Sorted Lists Linked list Easy
17 Linked List Cycle Fast/slow pointers Easy

Tier 2 — the interview core (15 problems)

# Problem Pattern Difficulty
21 Minimum Window Substring Sliding window Hard

23 Product of Array Except Self Prefix/suffix Medium
24 Koko Eating Bananas / Ship Within D Days Binary search on answer Medium

Tier 3 — depth and follow-ups (10 problems)

# Problem Pattern Difficulty
36 Maximum Subarray (Kadane) DP Medium

LRU Cache deserves a note — it's a design problem disguised as DSA and it's asked constantly at product companies. The answer is a hash map (O(1) lookup) plus a doubly linked list (O(1) move-to-front and eviction). In Python you can also do it with OrderedDict and move_to_end — but be ready to explain the underlying structure, because "I used OrderedDict" alone doesn't demonstrate understanding.

How to work a problem (the routine)

  1. 20 minutes attempting it yourself. No hints.
  2. If stuck: look only at the pattern hint, not the solution. Try 10 more minutes.
  3. If still stuck: read the solution, then close it and write it from scratch.
  4. Write down, in one line, what clue in the problem should have told you the pattern. This list is the most valuable thing you'll build.
  5. Redo it 3 days later, and again 10 days later. Spaced repetition, not volume.

Do not move to the next problem until you can explain the current one out loud in 90 seconds, including complexity and one edge case.

8.17 What to do when you're completely stuck in the interview

In order:

  1. Say you're stuck — "I don't immediately see the optimal approach, let me work through a small example." This buys goodwill and time.
  2. Do a concrete example by hand. Write out [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] and solve it manually. The pattern often falls out.
  3. State the brute force and code it. A working O(n²) beats a broken O(n).
  4. Name the waste. "The inefficiency is that I'm re-computing the sum of the window each time." Naming the waste tells you the tool: repeated lookup → hash map; repeated range sum → prefix sum; repeated min → heap; repeated re-scan of a contiguous range → sliding window.
  5. Ask for a nudge. "Am I on the right track thinking about this as a graph problem?" Asking one targeted question is not a failure — it's how engineers work.

The waste-to-tool mapping in step 4 is the single most portable thing in this entire section. If you remember one paragraph from Part 8, make it that one.

8.18 DSA cheat card

Need Reach for
