Part 9

System Design

Requirement → Constraint → Bottleneck → Design decision → Trade-off. Framework first, then eight case studies.

Suggested time · 10 h

The goal is not to memorise architectures. It is to reason:

Requirement → Constraint → Bottleneck → Design decision → Trade-off

An interviewer can tell within two minutes whether you're reciting a diagram or thinking. Recite the framework; derive the diagram.

9.1 The vocabulary, defined so you can use it MUST KNOW

Term Definition The number that matters
Scalability Handling more load by adding resources Requests/sec, users
Availability % of time the system serves requests 99.9% = 8.7 h/yr down; 99.99% = 52 min/yr
Reliability Produces correct results, doesn't lose data Error rate, data loss
Latency Time for one request p50 / p95 / p99
Throughput Requests handled per unit time RPS, QPS
Consistency All readers see the same data Strong vs eventual
Durability Committed data survives failures Replication factor
Fault tolerance Keeps working when a component dies No single point of failure

Vertical vs horizontal scaling: bigger machine (simple, has a ceiling, single point of failure) vs more machines (needs statelessness and a load balancer, scales further, adds coordination complexity). The move to horizontal is why statelessness matters.

CAP theorem, stated correctly: during a network partition you must choose between consistency and availability. It is not "pick two of three" — you never get to give up partition tolerance in a distributed system. - CP — refuse writes until the partition heals. Banking, inventory. - AP — accept writes, reconcile later. Feeds, likes, DNS, shopping carts.

Say "for the payment path I want CP; for the activity feed AP is fine" and you've demonstrated the concept better than a definition would.

9.2 The building blocks MUST KNOW

Component What it solves Cost / trade-off
Load balancer Distributes traffic, health checks, enables horizontal scaling Another hop; must itself be redundant
Reverse proxy (Nginx) TLS termination, static files, routing, compression Config complexity
CDN Serves static assets from the network edge Cache invalidation; cost
Cache (Redis) Cuts DB load and latency for hot data Staleness, invalidation, another failure mode
Read replicas Scale reads Replication lag → stale reads
Sharding Scale writes and storage past one machine Cross-shard joins/transactions become hard; rebalancing
Message queue Decouple producers from consumers; absorb spikes; retries Eventual consistency; ordering and duplicate handling
Object storage (S3) Cheap durable blobs (images, video, backups) Higher latency than a local disk
Search index (Elasticsearch) Full-text and faceted search A second copy of the data to keep in sync
Rate limiter Protects against abuse and overload Can reject legitimate bursts

Replication vs sharding — get this distinction right: - Replication = copies of the same data. Scales reads, gives redundancy. - Sharding/partitioning = splitting different data across machines. Scales writes and storage. - You usually do both: shard, and replicate each shard.

Sharding keys: by hash (even distribution, but range queries hit every shard), by range (good range scans, risk of hot shards), by geography/tenant (natural isolation). The classic failure is a hot key — celebrity user, popular product.

9.3 The framework — memorise this MUST KNOW

13 steps, but really 5 phases. Spend the time proportionally: don't draw boxes for 30 minutes and skip requirements.

Phase 1 — Understand (5–8 min of a 45-min interview)

  1. Clarify requirements. Who uses it? What's in scope? What's explicitly out of scope?
  2. Functional requirements. "Users can shorten a URL and be redirected." List 3–5. Get agreement.
  3. Non-functional requirements. Availability target, latency target, consistency needs, read/write ratio, durability.
  4. Estimate scale. Order of magnitude only.

Phase 2 — Interface (3–5 min)

  1. Design the API. 3–4 endpoints with request/response shapes. This forces you to pin down the data model.

Phase 3 — Design (15 min)

  1. High-level architecture. Client → LB → service → data stores. Draw it and walk the request path.
  2. Data model. Tables/collections, keys, indexes. Say what the primary access patterns are.
  3. Caching. What, where, TTL, invalidation.

Phase 4 — Scale (10 min)

  1. Scaling. Where does it break first, and what do you do about it?
  2. Reliability. What happens when each component dies?
  3. Security. AuthN/authZ, rate limiting, input validation, data at rest.

Phase 5 — Reflect (5 min)

  1. Bottlenecks. Name the one that would bite first at 10× traffic.
  2. Trade-offs. State what you gave up and why.

Mnemonic: Requirements, API, Architecture, Data, Cache, Scale, Failure, Trade-offs — "Really Awesome Architects Draw Clean Scalable Fault-tolerant Things." Whatever helps; the point is not to skip Requirements.

Back-of-envelope numbers worth knowing

Quantity Value
1 day ~86,400 s (~10⁵)
1 million/day ~12 requests/sec
1 billion/day ~12,000 requests/sec
Read from memory ~100 ns
SSD random read ~100 µs
Same-datacentre round trip ~0.5 ms
Cross-continent round trip ~150 ms
One commodity server ~1,000–10,000 RPS for simple work
A row of typical metadata ~100 bytes–1 KB

Peak traffic is roughly 2–3× average. Say so when you estimate.

9.4 Case study 1 — URL shortener (the canonical warm-up)

Requirements - Functional: shorten a long URL; redirect a short code to the original; optional custom alias; optional expiry; click analytics. - Non-functional: redirect latency < 100 ms; read-heavy (~100:1); highly available (a dead redirect breaks everyone's links); links are effectively permanent.

Scale estimate - 100 M new URLs/month ≈ 40 writes/sec; at 100:1 that's ~4,000 reads/sec, peak ~10,000. - Storage: 100 M/month × 500 bytes × 12 months × 5 years ≈ 3 TB. Fits comfortably on a sharded database.

API

POST /api/v1/urls        {"long_url": "...", "alias": "...", "expires_at": "..."} -> 201 {"short_url": "..."}
GET  /{code}             -> 302 redirect
GET  /api/v1/urls/{code}/stats -> 200 {clicks, created_at, ...}

Key design decision — how to generate the code. This is the interview.

Approach Pros Cons
Hash the URL (MD5), take 7 chars Deterministic, dedupes Collisions must be detected and retried
Random 7-char base62 Simple, unguessable Must check for collisions
Auto-increment ID → base62 No collisions ever, short codes Sequential = guessable/enumerable; the counter is a bottleneck
Distributed counter (ticket server / Snowflake / range allocation) No collisions, scales Extra component

The answer to give: "I'd use base62 encoding of a globally unique ID. Base62 with 7 characters gives 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion codes, which is plenty. The problem with a single auto-increment counter is that it's a write bottleneck and a single point of failure, so I'd hand out ID ranges to each application server — server A gets 1–10,000, server B gets 10,001–20,000 — from a coordination service. Each server then allocates locally with no coordination. The trade-off is gaps in the sequence when a server dies, which doesn't matter here."

Data model

urls(code PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at)
clicks(id, code, ts, referrer, country)   -- append-only, or a stream

Architecture

Client -> CDN/LB -> Redirect Service (stateless, many instances)
                        |-> Redis cache (code -> long_url)
                        |-> Database (sharded by code hash)
                        \-> Kafka -> analytics consumer -> OLAP store

Caching: the read path is a single key lookup — perfect for Redis. Cache with a long TTL because URLs are immutable once created. Expect a very high hit rate since access follows a power law (a few links get most traffic).

Failure scenarios - Redis down → fall through to the database; make sure the DB can take the load, or use a local in-process cache as a second layer. - Database shard down → replicas promote; redirects for that shard degrade. - Analytics pipeline down → redirects must still work. Click logging is fire-and-forget through a queue; never block the redirect on it.

Bottleneck at 10×: read throughput. Answer: more cache, more read replicas, and push popular redirects to the CDN edge.

Trade-offs to state: 301 (permanent, browser caches it, so you lose analytics on repeat visits) vs 302 (temporary, every click hits your server, analytics work). Choose 302 here and say why — this is the single best detail to volunteer in this question.

9.5 Case study 2 — Rate limiter

Requirements: limit each API key to N requests per window; low latency; works across many app servers; fail open or closed (decide and say which).

Algorithms

Algorithm How Trade-off
Fixed window counter Count per key per minute bucket Simple; allows a 2× burst at the boundary
Sliding window log Store timestamps in a sorted set, trim old Exact; memory-heavy
Sliding window counter Weighted blend of current and previous window Good accuracy, low memory — usual choice
Token bucket Tokens refill at a rate; each request takes one Allows controlled bursts; the standard for APIs
Leaky bucket Fixed-rate outflow queue Smooths traffic; no bursts

Implementation: Redis, one key per (api_key, window), INCR + EXPIRE executed in a Lua script so the check-and-increment is atomic. Without atomicity, concurrent requests race past the limit.

Where it lives: at the API gateway/reverse proxy, before your application, so rejected traffic never costs you application resources.

Failure mode question they will ask: "What if Redis is down?" → Decide deliberately: fail open (allow traffic; availability over protection) for a public read API; fail closed for anything expensive or abusable. Having a stance and a reason is what's being scored.

9.6 Case study 3 — Chat application

Requirements: 1:1 and group messages; delivery within ~100 ms; message history; online presence; delivered/read receipts; offline delivery.

The central decision — transport.

"Polling is simple but wasteful and adds latency. Long polling is better but still churns connections. WebSockets give a persistent bidirectional connection, which is what a chat app actually needs. The cost is that connections are stateful — each server holds thousands of open sockets, so I need sticky routing or a way to find which server holds a given user's connection."

Architecture

Client <--WebSocket--> Gateway servers (hold connections)
                            |
                    Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka  (routes a message to the gateway holding the recipient)
                            |
                    Message service -> Cassandra (messages)  +  Redis (presence, TTL heartbeats)
                            |
                    Push notification service (for offline users)

Data model: partition messages by conversation_id, cluster by timestamp DESC — that matches the access pattern "load the last 50 messages in this conversation". A wide-column store like Cassandra suits this: very high write volume, no joins, known access pattern.

Presence: a Redis key per user with a short TTL, refreshed by heartbeats. Absence of a heartbeat = offline. Don't try to make presence perfectly consistent; it's inherently approximate.

Offline delivery: if the recipient has no live connection, persist and send a push notification. On reconnect, the client asks for everything since its last received message ID.

Ordering: use a server-assigned sequence number per conversation, not client clocks — clients disagree about time.

Group chat fan-out: for small groups, write to each member's inbox (fan-out on write, fast reads). For very large groups, store once and read on demand (fan-out on read). Same trade-off as the news feed below.

9.7 Case study 4 — Social media feed

The one decision that matters: fan-out on write vs fan-out on read.

Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull)
On post Write into every follower's feed list Store the post once
On read Read your precomputed list — fast Query everyone you follow and merge — slow
Good for Normal users Celebrities with millions of followers
Problem A celebrity post = millions of writes Slow reads for everyone

The answer that gets you hired: a hybrid. "Fan-out on write for ordinary accounts, so the common read is a single fast lookup. For accounts above a follower threshold, don't fan out — store the post once and merge it into the feed at read time. So a user's feed is 'my precomputed list, merged with recent posts from the handful of celebrities I follow'. That bounds the write amplification without making every read expensive."

Storage: Redis sorted set per user for the feed (score = timestamp), capped at ~1,000 entries; posts themselves in a durable store; media in object storage behind a CDN.

Ranking: start with reverse-chronological and say that a scoring model (recency, affinity, engagement) is the natural next step, computed offline and cached. Don't design the ML system unless asked.

9.8 Case study 5 — File upload and storage

Key insight to lead with: don't proxy the file through your application server.

"For large files I'd have the client request a pre-signed URL from my API and upload directly to object storage. That keeps big payloads off my application servers entirely — otherwise upload bandwidth and memory become my bottleneck and my API servers spend their time as a very expensive file relay."

The flow

1. POST /uploads/init  -> returns {upload_id, presigned_url}
2. Client PUTs the file directly to S3 (multipart for large files)
3. S3 event -> queue -> worker: virus scan, thumbnail, transcode, metadata
4. POST /uploads/{id}/complete  -> mark ready

Details worth mentioning: multipart upload with resumability for large or flaky connections; deduplication by content hash; a status field (pending → processing → ready → failed); serving through a CDN with signed URLs for private files; lifecycle rules to move cold objects to cheaper storage tiers.

9.9 Case study 6 — Notification system

Requirements: send email / SMS / push; multiple triggers; user preferences and opt-out; retries; no duplicates; don't lose notifications; handle provider outages.

Producers -> Notification API -> Queue (Kafka/SQS)
                                    |
                              Workers (per channel)
                                    |-> Template service
                                    |-> Preference/opt-out check
                                    \-> Provider (SES / Twilio / FCM)  -> retry w/ backoff -> DLQ

The points that score: - Idempotency — an event_id deduplicated at the worker, because queues give at-least-once delivery, so duplicates will happen. - Retries with exponential backoff + jitter, then a dead-letter queue plus an alert. Don't retry forever. - Rate limiting per user so a bug doesn't send someone 500 emails. - Priority queues — an OTP must not queue behind a marketing blast. - Provider failover — a second provider configured, with a circuit breaker so you stop hammering a dead one.

9.10 Case study 7 — E-commerce checkout (the consistency question)

The interesting part is inventory, and it's where CAP becomes concrete.

"Two customers buying the last item is a correctness problem, not a performance one, so this part of the system must be CP. I'd handle it with a conditional update — UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty >= 1 — and treat zero affected rows as out-of-stock. That's atomic in the database, so it can't oversell. The alternative is a reservation with a TTL: reserve on 'add to cart', release if checkout isn't completed in 15 minutes, which is what most real stores do because it gives the customer a fair window."

Payment: never mark the order paid based on the client's word. Use the payment provider's webhook, verify its signature, and make the handler idempotent because providers retry webhooks. Then use the outbox pattern — write the order and an outbox row in one transaction, and a separate process publishes from the outbox — so you can't commit the order but lose the "order placed" event.

Mentioning the outbox pattern by name in a design round is a very strong signal.

9.11 Case study 8 — Job queue / task scheduler

Requirements: submit a job, run it once, retry on failure, schedule for later, observe status.

Core mechanics: a durable store (queue or a table with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), workers that lease a job with a visibility timeout, heartbeats so a crashed worker's job is redelivered, and idempotent job handlers because at-least-once delivery means jobs will occasionally run twice.

That last sentence is the whole point of the question. Exactly-once delivery is not achievable end to end; what you build is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handlers, which is effectively once.

9.12 How to sound senior in a design round

Weak Strong
"I'd use Kafka." "I'd put a queue between the API and the workers so a traffic spike doesn't take down the database — Kafka if I need replay and ordering, SQS if I just need durable work distribution."
"Add a cache." "The read/write ratio is about 100:1 and the data is immutable once written, so caching is very effective here. I'd cache by code with a long TTL and accept a cold-start penalty on miss."
"It's scalable." "This scales reads to roughly 10× by adding replicas. The first thing to break after that is the write path on the primary, and that's where I'd shard."
"Use NoSQL, it's faster." "The access pattern is a single key lookup with no joins and a very high write rate, which fits a wide-column store. I'd give up ad-hoc querying, and I'd need a separate analytics path."
Silence, then drawing boxes "Before I draw anything — is search in scope? What availability target are we designing for?"

Three habits: 1. Always state the bottleneck before the solution. "The database write path is the constraint here, so…" 2. Always name what you gave up. Every design decision costs something. Naming it is the difference between a candidate and an engineer. 3. Don't over-engineer. If the scale is 1,000 users, say "a single Postgres instance with a read replica handles this comfortably; I'd only shard when we're actually near the limit." Interviewers deliberately test whether you'll add Kafka to a to-do app.

10
Part 10

Project Interview Preparation

The round you have the most control over — and the one that decides more offers than people expect.

Suggested time · 3 h

This round decides more offers than people expect. The DSA round proves you can code; the project round proves you can engineer. It's also the round you have the most control over, because you know the material and they don't.

10.1 The reusable structure MUST KNOW

Problem → Architecture → Decisions → Implementation → Challenge → Solution → Result → Improvements

Prepare this once per project, in writing, and rehearse it out loud. Two minutes for the opening version, expandable to ten when they dig.

The two-minute opening (memorise the shape, not the words)

"It's a live algorithmic trading system for NSE equities. The problem was that I was manually watching charts and placing orders, which meant I missed entries and made emotional decisions. The architecture is a Python FastAPI backend that ingests live market data, evaluates a composite signal from MACD, RSI and Bollinger Bands, sizes positions using ATR, and places orders through a broker API — with a React dashboard on top for monitoring. The key decision was building a paper-trade mode first that runs the identical code path with order placement stubbed, so I could validate the strategy without risking capital. The hardest part was handling partial fills and reconciling my internal position state with the broker's, because the two could diverge after a network failure. I solved it by treating the broker as the source of truth and reconciling on every poll rather than trusting my local state. The result is a system that runs unattended through a trading session. What I'd change is moving from polling to a websocket feed, and adding a proper backtest harness before the live path."

Notice: no jargon padding, a concrete problem, one real technical difficulty, and an honest improvement. That's the template.

10.2 The questions, and what's actually being tested MUST KNOW

Question What they're testing How to answer
"Tell me about your project." Communication, scoping Two minutes, the structure above. Then stop and let them steer
"What problem does it solve?" Do you build for a reason or for a resume? Concrete pain, concrete user (even if that user is you)
"Why this architecture?" Do you make decisions or copy tutorials? Name the alternative you rejected and why
"Why this database?" Same Access patterns → data model → engine
"What was your contribution?" Honesty, ownership Be specific and truthful. "I did the backend and data pipeline; a teammate did X"
"What was the hardest problem?" Depth. This is the highest-signal question. A technical difficulty, not "learning React"
"How did you debug it?" Method vs flailing Reproduce → isolate → hypothesise → verify → fix → prevent
"What performance problems did you hit?" Do you measure? Symptom → measurement → cause → fix → number
"How would you scale it?" Systems thinking Identify the current bottleneck first
"How did you handle errors?" Production mindset Retries, timeouts, fallbacks, structured logging
"How did you secure it?" Do you think about it at all? AuthN/authZ, validation, secrets, TLS
"How did you test it?" Rigour Something honest — even "I tested the pricing logic in isolation because it was the risky part" beats pretending
"What would you change?" Self-awareness Name a real weakness and what you'd do instead
"What did you learn?" Growth A specific insight, not "teamwork"

10.3 Preparing "the hardest problem" MUST KNOW

This is the answer to over-prepare, because it's where interviewers spend their follow-ups. It must have four parts:

  1. The symptom — what was observably wrong. ("Orders were occasionally placed twice.")
  2. The investigation — how you narrowed it down. ("I added a request ID to every log line and found two entries for the same signal, 900 ms apart, from the same retry path.")
  3. The root cause — the actual mechanism. ("My HTTP client retried on timeout, but the broker had already accepted the first request — the response was lost, not the request.")
  4. The fix and what it cost — ("I added a client-generated order tag and checked the open-orders list before retrying. It costs an extra API call per retry, which is fine because retries are rare.")

Bad hardest-problem answers: "setting up the environment", "learning the framework", "a merge conflict", "CORS errors". They signal you haven't hit a real engineering problem yet. If you truly haven't, pick the most interesting decision instead and be honest: "The hardest part wasn't a bug, it was deciding how to model X — here's the trade-off I wrestled with."

10.4 Preparing for the attack

Interviewers deliberately find the weakest technical decision in your project and push. Pre-empt it: list your project's three weakest points yourself, and prepare an honest answer for each.

Likely attack Weak response Strong response
"You used SQLite — that won't work with concurrent writers." "It worked fine for me." "Correct — SQLite serialises writers, which is fine for a single-laptop scoring app but would break the moment I had two writers. I chose it because I needed zero-config file-based sync across laptops on a LAN. If I needed real concurrency I'd move to Postgres and change the connection layer — the repository interface is already isolated for that."
"Why no tests?" "I didn't have time." "I tested the parts where a bug is expensive — the position-sizing and signal logic — and left the UI untested. If this were shared with others, the first thing I'd add is integration tests around the order path, because that's where a mistake costs money."
"This wouldn't scale." "It scales fine." "At my current load it's not close to the limit. The first thing to break would be the polling loop — it's O(instruments) per tick, so around a few hundred symbols I'd need to move to a streaming feed."
"Isn't this just a tutorial project?" defensive "The scaffolding follows common patterns, but the parts I actually designed are X and Y — here's the decision I made in X that a tutorial wouldn't have."

The meta-rule: conceding a real limitation and explaining the condition under which you'd change it is the strongest possible answer. Defending an indefensible choice is the weakest.

10.5 Numbers make you credible

Vague claims read as invented. Attach a number to everything you can:

  • "It handles about 200 symbols per polling cycle in under 800 ms."
  • "The dashboard query was taking 4 seconds; adding an index on (user_id, created_at) brought it to 40 ms."
  • "The draw algorithm seeds a 64-competitor bracket in about 30 ms."
  • "It ran for six sessions without manual intervention."

You don't need impressive numbers. You need real ones. "It serves my one user reliably" is a fine answer honestly delivered.

10.6 The prep worksheet

Fill this in for your two strongest projects. Write it out — don't just think it.

PROJECT NAME:
One-line pitch:
Problem it solves (and for whom):
Stack, and why each piece:
Architecture in 4 boxes:
Data model — main tables and the primary access pattern:
Decision 1: chose ___ over ___ because ___ ; the cost was ___
Decision 2: chose ___ over ___ because ___ ; the cost was ___
Hardest technical problem: symptom / investigation / root cause / fix / cost
A performance issue: measurement before ___ after ___
Error handling: what fails, and what happens when it does
Security: authN ___ authZ ___ secrets ___ validation ___
Testing: what I tested and what I deliberately didn't
Three weakest points, and my honest answer for each:
What I'd do differently with another month:
What I learned that changed how I build things:

Do this for two projects and you can survive any project round, including the ones where they ask about a project you built two years ago.

11
Part 11

Engineering Fundamentals & Principles

Git, Docker, Linux, CI/CD, cloud — plus SOLID, coupling and the five design patterns worth knowing.

Suggested time · 6 h

Only what a Full Stack SDE is actually expected to know. This is not a DevOps course.

11.1 Git MUST KNOW

Daily commands — you should never hesitate on these:

git status                       # before everything
git add -p                       # stage selectively; forces you to review your own diff
git commit -m "fix: handle empty cart in checkout"
git switch -c feature/order-api  # (modern form of checkout -b)
git pull --rebase origin main    # keeps history linear
git push -u origin feature/order-api
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -20
git diff main...HEAD             # what my branch adds

Merge vs rebase MUST KNOW — asked constantly.

Merge Rebase
What it does Creates a merge commit joining two histories Replays your commits on top of the target branch
History Preserves exactly what happened, non-linear Linear, easier to read
Safety Safe on shared branches Rewrites commit hashes

The rule: rebase your local, unpushed work to keep history clean; merge when integrating into a shared branch. Never rebase a branch that other people have pulled — their history and yours diverge and everyone suffers. git pull --rebase for your own feature branch is fine and usually preferable to a pull that creates noise merge commits.

Undoing things — know which is which:

Command Effect
git restore <file> Discard uncommitted changes to a file
git reset --soft HEAD~1 Undo the commit, keep changes staged
git reset --mixed HEAD~1 Undo the commit, keep changes unstaged (default)
git reset --hard HEAD~1 Undo the commit and destroy the changes
git revert <sha> New commit that undoes an old one — the safe option on a shared branch
git stash / git stash pop Park work temporarily
git cherry-pick <sha> Copy one commit onto the current branch
git reflog Your safety net — find "lost" commits after a bad reset

revert vs reset is a good interview question: reset rewrites history (private branches), revert adds history (public branches).

Merge conflicts: Git marks <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>. Edit to the correct final state, delete the markers, git add, then git rebase --continue or git commit.

Branching strategy: trunk-based (short-lived branches merged to main daily, feature flags for incomplete work) is the modern default and what most product teams use. GitFlow (develop/release/hotfix branches) is heavier and mostly appears where there are versioned releases. Have an opinion and a reason.

Good PR habits worth mentioning: small and single-purpose, a description explaining why not what, self-review before requesting review, conventional commit messages, and don't mix refactoring with behaviour changes in one PR.

11.2 Docker SHOULD KNOW

PROBLEM IT SOLVES: "works on my machine". A container packages the application and its dependencies and runs the same everywhere.

Container vs VM: a VM virtualises hardware and runs a full guest OS (GBs, slow boot). A container shares the host kernel and isolates the process using namespaces and cgroups (MBs, starts in milliseconds). That one sentence answers the question.

FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependency files first — this layer is cached until they change
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

The layer-caching point MUST KNOW — copying requirements.txt and installing before copying the source means a code change doesn't reinvalidate the dependency install. Interviewers specifically look for this; it's the difference between a 3-second and a 3-minute rebuild.

Other things worth knowing: - Multi-stage builds — build in a fat image, copy only the artefact into a slim runtime image. Much smaller final image, no build tools in production. - .dockerignore — keep .git, node_modules, .venv out of the build context. - Don't run as root — USER appuser. - Never bake secrets into an image — layers are inspectable. Use environment variables or a secret manager. - Image vs container — an image is the template; a container is a running instance. Same relationship as class and object. - Volumes — containers are ephemeral; anything that must survive a restart goes in a volume or an external service.

# docker-compose.yml — local multi-service development
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://user:pass@db:5432/app
    depends_on: [db, redis]
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass }
  redis:
    image: redis:7
volumes: { pgdata: }

Note that services reach each other by service name (db, redis) on Compose's internal network — a common point of confusion.

11.3 CI/CD NICE TO KNOW→SHOULD KNOW

CI — every push runs lint, tests, and a build, so broken code is caught before review. CD — passing builds deploy automatically (continuous deployment) or are made deployable at one click (continuous delivery).

A realistic pipeline: lint → unit tests → build image → integration tests → push to registry → deploy to staging → smoke tests → deploy to production.

Deployment strategies: blue-green (two identical environments, flip traffic, instant rollback), canary (route 5% of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, ramp up), rolling (replace instances gradually). Know what each buys you.

Migrations: the thing that actually bites. Deploy schema changes backwards-compatible first — add the new nullable column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, then deploy code that reads the new column, then drop the old one. Saying this shows real deployment experience.

11.4 Linux basics SHOULD KNOW

ps aux | grep python          # processes
top / htop                    # live resource usage
kill -9 <pid>                 # SIGKILL (SIGTERM, kill -15, is the polite one)
lsof -i :8000                 # what's holding a port
netstat -tulpn                # listening sockets
df -h  /  du -sh *            # disk usage
tail -f app.log               # follow a log
grep -r "TODO" --include="*.py" .
chmod 755 script.sh           # rwx r-x r-x
export API_KEY=abc            # env var for this shell
cat file | grep x | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head    # the classic pipeline

Concepts: a process has its own memory; threads share it. Ports below 1024 need root. SIGTERM asks a process to shut down gracefully (flush, close connections); SIGKILL can't be caught — your app should handle SIGTERM so a container restart doesn't drop in-flight requests. Standard streams: stdin/stdout/stderr, and 2>&1 merges them.

11.5 Nginx, DNS, HTTPS NICE TO KNOW→SHOULD KNOW

Nginx as a reverse proxy — terminates TLS, serves static files, load balances, adds headers, rate limits:

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name api.example.com;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    }
}

Forward vs reverse proxy: a forward proxy sits in front of clients (corporate egress, VPN). A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and clients don't know it's there. Common interview clarifier.

DNS record types: A (name → IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias to another name), MX (mail), TXT (verification, SPF). TTL controls caching — lower it before a migration, not during.

HTTPS/TLS: the handshake authenticates the server via a certificate signed by a CA, agrees a symmetric session key using asymmetric crypto, then all traffic uses fast symmetric encryption. It gives confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication. Note that TLS protects data in transit only — data at rest needs separate encryption.

11.6 Cloud fundamentals NICE TO KNOW→SHOULD KNOW

Know what each service is for, not its configuration options.

Need AWS Concept
Virtual machine EC2 Compute you manage
Managed containers ECS / EKS / Fargate Run containers without managing hosts
Serverless functions Lambda Per-request compute; scales to zero; cold starts
Object storage S3 Cheap, durable blobs
Managed relational DB RDS / Aurora Postgres/MySQL with backups and failover
Managed NoSQL DynamoDB Key-value at scale
Cache ElastiCache Managed Redis
Queue / streaming SQS / Kinesis Decoupling, buffering
CDN CloudFront Edge caching
Load balancer ALB / NLB L7 / L4 distribution
Secrets Secrets Manager / Parameter Store Don't put secrets in env files in the repo
Identity IAM Roles and least-privilege policies

The two ideas that matter more than the service list: 1. Least privilege — a service gets exactly the permissions it needs, via a role, not long-lived access keys. 2. Managed over self-hosted — running your own Postgres means you own backups, failover, patching and monitoring. Take the managed service unless you have a specific reason.

Serverless vs containers: Lambda for spiky, event-driven, short work — you pay nothing at idle but accept cold starts and time limits. Containers for steady traffic, long-running processes, and full control.

Part 12 — Software Engineering Principles

Principles only matter in interviews if you can give a concrete example. Memorising the acronym alone is worse than not mentioning it.

12.1 SOLID SHOULD KNOW

Principle Meaning Concrete example
Single Responsibility A class has one reason to change OrderService shouldn't also format emails and generate PDFs — pull those into their own classes so a template change doesn't touch order logic
Open/Closed Open to extension, closed to modification Adding a new payment provider should mean adding a class that implements PaymentProvider, not adding an elif to a growing chain
Liskov Substitution A subclass must be usable wherever the base is The classic: Square inheriting Rectangle breaks code that sets width and height independently. That's why Square is-a Rectangle fails as a code relationship even though it's true in maths
Interface Segregation Many small interfaces beat one fat one A read-only consumer shouldn't be forced to depend on an interface with save() and delete()
Dependency Inversion Depend on abstractions, not concretions OrderService takes a Repository interface, not a concrete PostgresRepository — which is exactly what makes it testable

How to use these in an interview: never recite the list. When explaining a design decision, name the principle after the reasoning: "…so I injected the repository rather than constructing it inside the service — that's dependency inversion, and the practical payoff is that I can pass a fake in tests."

12.2 The short principles SHOULD KNOW

DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) — but the real rule is "don't duplicate knowledge". Two pieces of code that look the same but change for different reasons should stay separate. Premature abstraction is worse than duplication — this nuance is worth saying, because over-DRYing is a real junior failure mode.

KISS — the simplest thing that works. Complexity should be earned by a requirement.

YAGNI — don't build for a requirement you're imagining. The generic plugin system you built for a future that never arrived is pure cost.

Separation of concerns — each module handles one aspect. Why your React component shouldn't contain SQL.

Coupling and cohesion MUST KNOW — the pair that actually matters: - Coupling = how much modules depend on each other. Low is good. High coupling means one change ripples. - Cohesion = how related the things inside a module are. High is good. Low cohesion is a utils.py that does everything. - Goal: low coupling, high cohesion. If you remember one principle from this section, make it this one — it explains most architecture decisions on its own.

Composition over inheritance — see §2.4.6. Inheritance couples you to a parent's implementation; composition depends on a small interface you can swap.

12.3 Design patterns that are genuinely useful SHOULD KNOW

Skip the other twenty. These five you will actually use and be asked about.

Pattern Problem it solves Real use
Strategy Swap an algorithm at runtime without if/elif chains Payment providers, pricing rules, trading signal strategies
Factory Creating objects whose concrete type is decided at runtime Building a client based on config
Repository Abstract data access from business logic Everything in §6.1
Observer / Pub-Sub Notify many listeners without coupling to them Event buses, React state subscriptions, webhooks
Singleton One shared instance DB connection pool, config, logger — but it's global state, which hurts testability; dependency injection is usually the better answer 
# Strategy — the pattern to actually know
class PricingStrategy(Protocol):
    def price(self, order: Order) -> Decimal: ...

class StandardPricing:
    def price(self, order): return order.subtotal

class BulkDiscountPricing:
    def price(self, order):
        return order.subtotal * (Decimal("0.9") if order.qty > 100 else Decimal("1"))

class Checkout:
    def __init__(self, pricing: PricingStrategy):
        self.pricing = pricing          # swap behaviour without touching Checkout

The interview framing: "Adding a new pricing rule means adding a class, not editing a growing conditional in Checkout. That's open/closed in practice, and it means the existing pricing paths can't be broken by the new one."

12.4 Clean code, briefly SHOULD KNOW

The rules that survive contact with reality:

  • Names carry the weight. elapsed_ms beats t. A good name removes the need for a comment.
  • Functions do one thing. If you need "and" to describe it, split it.
  • Comment why, not what. The code says what. # broker returns 0 for market orders, so we fall back to LTP is worth writing.
  • Fail fast, fail loudly. Validate at the boundary; raise rather than silently returning None.
  • Delete dead code. Version control remembers it; your reader doesn't need to.
  • Consistency beats personal preference. Follow the codebase's existing style.
  • Make the change easy, then make the easy change. Refactor first, then add the feature — as two separate commits.
← Previous10 · ProjectsNext →13–14 · Answering
13
Part 13

Follow-Up Trees & Answering Like an Engineer

How interviewers drill down, six full follow-up trees, and weak vs strong answers side by side.

Suggested time · 4 h

The per-topic question banks live at the end of Parts 2–7 and 9. This part adds the thing those tables can't show: how an interviewer drills down, and what a strong answer looks like three levels in.

13.1 How interviewers drill

Every follow-up comes from one of six moves:

Your answer
   |-- SCALE:      "what happens at 10x?"
   |-- FAILURE:    "what if it goes down?"
   |-- ALTERNATIVE:"why not X instead?"
   |-- INTERNAL:   "how does that actually work?"
   |-- COST:       "what does that cost you?"
   \-- CONCRETE:   "show me where you've done this"

If you learn to anticipate these, you can pre-empt them: answer, then volunteer the cost. That single habit is the difference between "passed" and "strong hire".

13.2 Follow-up tree — "Why did you use Redis?" (backend / system design)

Level Question Strong answer
1 Why Redis? The data is read far more than written and changes rarely, so caching cuts database load and tail latency
2 What if Redis goes down? Cache-aside means requests fall through to the database — degraded, not broken. The risk is a thundering herd, so I'd want request coalescing or a short rebuild lock
3 What if the data goes stale? Depends on tolerance. TTL where eventually-correct is acceptable; explicit invalidation on write where it isn't
4 How do you invalidate? Delete the key on write rather than updating it — an update races with a concurrent read that could repopulate the old value
5 Traffic 10×? First measure whether it's CPU, memory or network bound. Then read replicas for read scaling, or Redis Cluster to shard by key
6 What breaks when you shard? Multi-key operations and transactions stop working across slots; you'd use hash tags to co-locate related keys

13.3 Follow-up tree — "Why did you choose PostgreSQL?" (SQL / design)

Level Question Strong answer
1 Why Postgres? The data is relational with real constraints, I need transactions, and the query patterns aren't all known upfront — ad-hoc SQL is worth a lot
2 Why not MongoDB? Flexible schema sounds attractive early, but my data has genuine relationships and I'd end up doing joins in application code. Schema-on-read pushes correctness into every caller
3 What happens when the table hits 100 M rows? Indexing and partitioning first — the tables are usually time-ordered so range partitioning by month works well and makes old-data pruning cheap
4 And when writes exceed one primary? That's when I'd shard, most likely by tenant or user ID. The cost is cross-shard queries and distributed transactions, which is why I'd delay it as long as possible
5 How do you scale reads before that? Read replicas — but that introduces replication lag, so read-your-own-writes has to go to the primary
6 How would you handle the lag? Route reads to the primary for a short window after a write for that user, or pass a "read from primary" hint through the request context

13.4 Follow-up tree — "Why did you use useMemo here?" (React)

Level Question Strong answer
1 Why memoise? The sort runs over a few thousand rows on every render and the input rarely changes
2 Did you measure it? Yes — Profiler showed it as the dominant cost in that commit. If it hadn't, I'd have removed it, since memoisation isn't free
3 What's the cost? A dependency comparison per render plus retained memory. Over-memoising also hides which computations are actually expensive
4 What if the dependency is an object? Then it's a new reference every render and the memo never hits. I'd depend on primitive fields, or memoise the object one level up
5 Is there a better fix? Often yes — moving state down or restructuring so the expensive subtree doesn't re-render at all removes the work rather than caching it

13.5 Follow-up tree — "Walk me through what happens when a user logs in" (full stack)

Level Question Strong answer
1 Describe the flow POST credentials over TLS → server looks up the user → constant-time bcrypt verify → issue tokens → client stores them → subsequent requests carry the access token
2 Where do you store the token? Access token in memory, refresh token in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie — so an XSS payload can't read the long-lived credential
3 How do you handle expiry? On a 401 the client silently calls the refresh endpoint once and retries the original request. Concurrent 401s should share a single in-flight refresh, or you get a stampede
4 How do you log someone out everywhere? Refresh tokens are stored server-side, so I delete them. Access tokens stay valid until expiry — which is why they're short-lived. If instant revocation is required, a denylist keyed by token ID
5 How do you stop brute-force attacks? Rate limit per account and per IP, exponential backoff, and a generic error message so the response doesn't reveal whether the account exists
6 What if the database is slow under bcrypt load? bcrypt is CPU-bound by design; I'd tune the cost factor to a measured target (around 100 ms), and scale login handling horizontally rather than weakening the hash

13.6 Follow-up tree — "How would you find and fix a slow endpoint?" (debugging)

Level Question Strong answer
1 Where do you start? Reproduce it and measure. I want to know whether it's slow always or only at p99, and whether it's the database, an external call, or CPU in my process
2 How do you measure? Request timing in logs, then a trace or timing around the suspicious segments. APM if available
3 Say it's the database EXPLAIN ANALYZE the query. Sequential scan on a large table, or a huge gap between estimated and actual rows, points at a missing index or stale statistics
4 You add the index and it's still slow Check whether it's used — a function wrapping the column or a type mismatch will prevent it. Also check whether it's actually N+1 queries rather than one slow query
5 It's N+1 Eager-load the relation or batch the fetch. The tell is many identical queries with different parameters in the log
6 Now it's fast for you but not in production Data volume and cache state differ. Check the production query plan directly, and whether the connection pool is saturated — queueing looks like slowness

This tree is worth rehearsing because "how do you debug something" comes up in nearly every round and most candidates answer it vaguely.

13.7 Rapid-fire bank (know all of these in one sentence)

Python: GIL · mutable default arg · generator vs list · decorator · is vs == · shallow vs deep copy · @classmethod vs @staticmethod · list vs tuple vs set · context manager · __str__ vs __repr__

JavaScript: closure · this binding rules · event loop / microtasks · var/let/const · Promise.all vs allSettled · debounce vs throttle · == vs === · prototype chain · event delegation · hoisting/TDZ

React: why keys · why it re-renders · useEffect purpose and misuse · useMemo vs useCallback · controlled vs uncontrolled · Context vs Redux · custom hooks · React.memo · error boundaries · rules of hooks and why

Backend/API: 401 vs 403 · idempotency · CORS · JWT storage and revocation · pagination styles · rate limiting · transactions and ACID · connection pooling · layered architecture · N+1

SQL: WHERE vs HAVING · join types and the LEFT JOIN + WHERE trap · RANK/DENSE_RANK/ROW_NUMBER · latest-per-group · indexes and when they don't apply · normalisation · isolation levels · EXISTS vs IN

DSA: the 15 recognition signals in §8.0 · complexity of every container operation · amortised vs average vs worst · when sliding window is invalid · when greedy is provably correct

System design: CAP in practice · vertical vs horizontal · replication vs sharding · cache-aside and invalidation · fan-out on write vs read · at-least-once + idempotency · availability nines

Part 14 — How to Answer Like a Real Engineer

The same technical knowledge, delivered two ways, produces two different hiring decisions. This is the delivery.

14.1 The three-part answer MUST KNOW

Claim → Reason → Trade-off. Every technical answer. No exceptions.

❌ "I would use Redis because Redis is fast."

✅ "I'd consider Redis here because the data is read frequently and changes rarely — caching it cuts database load and improves latency. The thing I'd need to decide is the TTL and invalidation strategy, because stale data would be a problem for this particular field."

The second answer isn't longer because it's padded. It's longer because it contains two more pieces of information: why the property of the data makes the tool appropriate, and what the decision costs.

14.2 Weak vs strong, side by side

Question Weak Strong
"Why NoSQL?" "It's faster and more scalable." "The access pattern is a single-key lookup with no joins and a very high write rate, which fits a wide-column store well. I'd be giving up ad-hoc queries and transactions, so anything reporting-shaped would need a separate path."
"How do you optimise a React app?" "Use useMemo and React.memo." "First I'd profile to find which component is actually re-rendering and why. Usually the fix is structural — moving state closer to where it's used, or passing subtrees as children — which removes the render entirely. Memoisation is what I'd reach for after that, when the structure is right and I've measured a real cost."
"How do you handle errors?" "I use try/except." "Domain code raises domain exceptions that know nothing about HTTP, and one handler at the edge maps them to status codes and a consistent error body. I log the stack trace server-side with a request ID and return only the ID to the client, so support can find it without leaking internals."
"Is your code tested?" "Not really, I ran out of time." "I tested the parts where a bug is expensive — the position-sizing logic — and skipped the UI. If this were shared, the first thing I'd add is an integration test around the order path, because that's where a mistake costs real money."
"Why did you use a dict here?" "It's faster." "I'm doing membership checks inside a loop. With a list that's O(n) per check, so the whole thing becomes O(n²); a set makes each check O(1) and the algorithm linear. I'm trading O(n) memory for that."
"How would you scale this?" "Add more servers." "The first thing to break would be the write path on the single primary — reads I can scale with replicas fairly far. So the ordering is: cache the hot reads, add replicas, and only shard when the write volume genuinely exceeds one machine, because sharding costs me cross-shard queries."
"What's a closure?" "A function inside a function." "A function together with the lexical scope it was created in, so it keeps access to those variables after the outer function returns. It's the mechanism behind useState keeping its value between renders, and behind debounce remembering its timer."

The pattern in every strong answer: it names a property of the situation that makes the choice correct, and it names what the choice costs. Generic praise for a technology ("it's fast", "it's scalable") is the tell of someone repeating what they read.

14.3 Phrases that make you sound experienced

Use these honestly — they're not tricks, they're how engineers actually talk:

  • "It depends on ___ — if ___ then , but if ___ then ."
  • "I'd want to measure that before optimising."
  • "The trade-off is ___."
  • "That works until , and then I'd need ."
  • "I'd start with the simplest thing that works and add complexity when the requirement forces it."
  • "I've hit this before — what happened was ___."
  • "I'm not sure. My instinct is ___, and here's how I'd check."
  • "Can I clarify something about the requirement first?"

14.4 Phrases that hurt you

  • "It's best practice." (Whose? Why? For what?)
  • "Everyone uses X." (Argument from popularity.)
  • "It's just faster." (Faster at what, compared to what?)
  • "That would never happen." (It will.)
  • "I'd just Google it." (Fine as a supplement, fatal as the whole answer.)
  • "I don't know." (...with nothing after it.)
  • Over-apologising after a mistake.
  • Filler confidence: "obviously", "simply", "of course" — especially when you're unsure.

14.5 The calibration habit

State your confidence. It costs nothing and it builds enormous trust:

"I'm confident about the first part — the GIL means threads won't speed up CPU-bound work. I'm less sure about the exact behaviour in 3.13's free-threaded build; I know it exists as an experimental option but I haven't used it."

Interviewers write this down as a positive. It tells them that when you do speak confidently, they can rely on it — which is the entire point of the exercise.

14.6 The single sentence to carry into every round

Answer the question, then volunteer the constraint under which your answer changes.

That's it. Apply it to a Python question, a React question, a SQL question, a design question. It converts a correct answer into an engineer's answer.

Part 17 — The One-Day Emergency Revision

Read this tomorrow morning and again tonight. Nothing else. It is deliberately dense — it's a reminder, not a lesson.

Python — the ten traps

Mutable default arg (=None) · class-level mutable shared across instances · += on strings is O(n²) → join · mutating a list while iterating · [lambda: i for i in ...] all capture the final i · shallow copy shares nested objects · is vs == · list.pop(0) is O(n) → deque · sort() returns None · 0.1+0.2 != 0.3.

Python — say these correctly

GIL: one thread runs bytecode at a time in CPython; threads help I/O, processes help CPU, it's released during I/O and in C extensions. Generator: lazy iterator from yield; O(1) memory; single use. Decorator: function wrapping a function; always functools.wraps. Complexity: list index O(1)/search O(n) · dict & set O(1) avg · deque O(1) both ends · heap O(log n) push/pop.

JavaScript — the five

var function-scoped, let/const block-scoped with a TDZ · closure = function + captured scope · this is set by the call site; arrows inherit it lexically · microtasks (promises) drain completely between macrotasks (setTimeout) · Promise.all fails fast, allSettled doesn't.

React — the six

Re-renders come from: own state, parent render, context value, key change · never mutate state; use the functional updater when the new value depends on the old · useEffect is for syncing with the outside world, not for derived data or event responses · infinite loops come from setting a state that's in your own deps, or deps recreated every render · keys must be stable IDs, not indices · memoise only for measured cost, React.memo boundaries, or dependency arrays.

SQL — the seven

Execution order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT · WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups · a right-table condition in WHERE turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN — put it in ON · ROW_NUMBER()/RANK()/DENSE_RANK() = unique / gaps / no gaps · latest per group = ROW_NUMBER() PARTITION BY … WHERE rn=1 · a function on an indexed column kills the index · composite index follows the leftmost prefix.

DSA — the recognition list

contiguous/at-most-K → sliding window · sorted + pair → two pointers · frequency/duplicate → hash map · minimum-possible-maximum → binary search on the answer · range sums → prefix sum · next greater / nesting → stack · shortest unweighted path → BFS · all combinations → backtracking · top K → heap · prerequisites → topological sort · overlapping [s,e] → sort by start · choice + overlapping subproblems → DP (memoise the recursion first).

Stuck? Name the waste. Repeated lookup → hash map. Repeated range sum → prefix sum. Repeated min → heap. Re-scanning a contiguous range → sliding window.

Big-O

n ≤ 20 exponential OK · n ≤ 10³ O(n²) OK · n ≤ 10⁵ need O(n log n) · n ≤ 10⁹ need O(log n).

API

401 = not authenticated, 403 = not permitted · 201 create, 204 delete, 409 conflict, 429 rate limited · idempotency = same effect on repeat; use an idempotency key for POST · CORS is browser-enforced and configured on the server; it does not secure your API · JWT is signed, not encrypted — no secrets inside · cursor pagination for large/changing data.

System design framework

Requirements → API → Architecture → Data → Cache → Scale → Failure → Trade-offs. Ask before drawing. Estimate order-of-magnitude. Name the bottleneck before the fix. Name what you gave up. Don't over-engineer. CAP: during a partition, choose C or A. Replication scales reads; sharding scales writes.

Git / Docker

revert for shared branches, reset for private ones · rebase local work, merge into shared · copy dependency files before source in a Dockerfile for layer caching · containers share the host kernel, VMs don't.

Your project — the shape

Problem → Architecture → Decisions → Implementation → Challenge → Solution → Result → Improvements. Two minutes. Have one real technical difficulty with symptom/investigation/root cause/fix, and three honest weak points with answers.

The communication rules

  1. Restate → clarify → brute force → optimise → code → test.
  2. Every answer: claim → reason → trade-off.
  3. Don't know? Adjacent knowledge, first principles, or an honest gap — never a bluff.
  4. Mistake? Notice it aloud, fix the line, name the bug class, move on.
  5. Answer the question, then volunteer the constraint under which your answer changes.

Tonight

Test the screen share. Charge everything. Have water, paper, a pen. Sleep. You know more than you think you do at 11pm.

18.1 Python cheat sheet

# Containers
lst = [1,2,3];  lst.append(x); lst.extend(it); lst.insert(i,x); lst.pop(); lst.pop(0)
lst.remove(x); lst.index(x); lst.count(x); lst.sort(key=..., reverse=True); lst.reverse()
d = {};  d.get(k, default); d.setdefault(k, []); d.pop(k, None); d.items(); d.keys(); d.values()
s = set(); s.add(x); s.discard(x); s | t; s & t; s - t; s ^ t

# Slicing
a[start:stop:step]; a[::-1]; a[-3:]; a[:n]

# Iteration
enumerate(it, start=1); zip(a, b); reversed(it); sorted(it, key=..., reverse=True)
any(it); all(it); sum(it); min(it, key=...); max(it, key=...)

# Comprehensions
[f(x) for x in it if p(x)];  {k: v for k, v in pairs};  {x for x in it};  (x for x in it)

# Strings
s.split(sep); s.strip(); "".join(parts); s.replace(a,b); s.startswith(p); s.lower()
s.isdigit(); s.isalpha(); s.isalnum(); f"{x:.2f}"; f"{x:>10}"; f"{n:,}"

Counter(it).most_common(k);  defaultdict(list);  deque(maxlen=n).appendleft(x)
import heapq; heapq.heappush(h,x); heapq.heappop(h); heapq.heapify(l); heapq.nlargest(k,it)

# Functions

lambda x: x*2

    return inner

# Classes

    attr = "class var"
    def __init__(self, x): super().__init__(); self.x = x
    @property
    def y(self): return self.x * 2
    @classmethod
    def make(cls, d): return cls(d["x"])
    @staticmethod
    def helper(): ...
    def __repr__(self): return f"C(x={self.x!r})"

# Generators / context managers / exceptions

    yield from other()
with open(p) as f: ...
from contextlib import contextmanager
try: ... except ValueError as e: raise NewError() from e
else: ... finally: ...

18.2 Python complexity cheat sheet

Operation list deque dict / set heap
index / access O(1) O(1) ends O(1) avg by key O(1) peek min
search in O(n) O(n) O(1) avg O(n)
append / push O(1)* O(1) O(1) avg O(log n)
insert front O(n) O(1) — —
pop end O(1) O(1) O(1) avg —
pop front / min O(n) O(1) — O(log n)
delete by value O(n) O(n) O(1) avg O(n)

* amortised. sorted() / .sort() = O(n log n), stable (Timsort). min/max/sum = O(n). Slicing a[i:j] = O(j−i). String concat in a loop = O(n²).

18.3 JavaScript cheat sheet

// Arrays
map filter reduce find findIndex some every includes flat flatMap
slice(non-mutating) splice(mutating) sort((a,b)=>a-b) [...arr].sort()

// Objects
const {a, b: alias, c = 1} = obj;        // destructuring w/ rename + default
const {x, ...rest} = obj;                 // rest
const merged = {...a, ...b};              // spread (b wins)
Object.keys/values/entries/assign/freeze
obj?.a?.b ?? fallback                     // optional chaining + nullish coalescing

// Async
await Promise.all([...])                  // parallel, fail fast
await Promise.allSettled([...])           // parallel, never rejects
for (const x of arr) { await f(x); }      // sequential on purpose
await Promise.all(arr.map(f))             // parallel

// this
f.call(o, a, b); f.apply(o, [a,b]); const g = f.bind(o);
// arrow functions: no own this/arguments; cannot be `new`ed

// Event loop order
sync -> ALL microtasks (promises) -> ONE macrotask (setTimeout) -> repeat

// Utilities
const debounce=(fn,d)=>{let t;return(...a)=>{clearTimeout(t);t=setTimeout(()=>fn(...a),d)}}
structuredClone(obj)                      // deep copy

18.4 React cheat sheet

const [s, setS] = useState(init);         // useState(() => expensive()) for lazy init
setS(prev => prev + 1);                   // functional update when depending on prev

useEffect(() => { ...; return cleanup; }, [deps]);   // sync with the outside world
const v = useMemo(() => compute(a), [a]);            // cache a value
const cb = useCallback(() => f(a), [a]);             // cache a function identity
const ref = useRef(null);                             // persists, no re-render
const ctx = useContext(MyContext);
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, init);

React.memo(Component)                                 // shallow prop compare
React.lazy(() => import("./X")) + <Suspense fallback>
Symptom Likely cause Fix
Infinite render loop Effect sets state in its own deps; deps recreated each render Fix deps; depend on primitives
Stale value in a callback Closure captured an old render's value Functional updater, or a ref
List state attached to the wrong item Index keys Stable IDs
Child re-renders constantly New object/function prop each render useCallback/useMemo + React.memo
Whole page re-renders on one keystroke State too high in the tree Move state down
Everything re-renders on context change Provider value recreated each render useMemo the value; split contexts

Re-render triggers: own state · parent render · context value · key change.

18.5 SQL cheat sheet

-- Execution order
FROM/JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT

-- Latest per group  (memorise)
WITH r AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) rn
           FROM orders)
SELECT * FROM r WHERE rn = 1;

-- Rows with no match
SELECT u.* FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id=u.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- Nth highest
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC OFFSET n-1 LIMIT 1;

-- Duplicates
SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- Running total
SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

-- Previous row
LAG(x)  OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY d)
LEAD(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY d)

-- Conditional aggregation (pivot)
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status='active'), SUM(CASE WHEN c THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

-- Safe division
NULLIF(denominator, 0)

Index rules: used for =, ranges, prefix LIKE 'a%', and ORDER BY matching the index. Not used when the column is wrapped in a function, on leading-wildcard LIKE, or on a low-selectivity column. Composite indexes follow the leftmost prefix.

Ranking: ROW_NUMBER 1,2,3,4 · RANK 1,2,2,4 · DENSE_RANK 1,2,2,3.

18.6 DSA pattern cheat sheet

Signal in the problem Pattern Template
contiguous, substring, at most K Sliding window expand right, shrink left while invalid
sorted + pair/triplet, in-place, O(1) space Two pointers lo/hi, or read/write, or slow/fast
frequency, duplicate, seen, complement Hash map/set seen = {} in one pass
range sum, count subarrays summing to K Prefix sum + hash counts[0]=1, res += counts[run-k]
min possible max, feasibility, sorted search Binary search while lo<hi: mid; if can(mid): hi=mid else lo=mid+1
next greater, nesting, previous smaller Monotonic stack pop while incoming violates order
shortest path unweighted, level by level BFS + deque mark visited on enqueue
connectivity, islands, all reachable DFS recurse + visited set, or mark in place
prerequisites, ordering, cycle detection Topological sort in-degree + queue; short output = cycle
top K, stream median, merge K Heap min-heap of size K for K largest
all subsets/permutations/combinations Backtracking choose → explore → un-choose; append path[:]
[start, end] overlapping Intervals sort by start; max(end) when merging
choose or skip + overlapping subproblems DP state → recurrence → base → order
locally optimal, minimum count Greedy justify with an exchange argument

Stuck → name the waste: repeated lookup → hash · repeated range sum → prefix · repeated min → heap · re-scanning a range → window · recomputing subproblems → memoise.

18.7 Big-O cheat sheet

Algorithm Time Space
Binary search O(log n) O(1)
Linear scan O(n) O(1)
Sorting (Timsort/merge) O(n log n) O(n)
Quicksort O(n log n) avg, O(n²) worst O(log n)
Heapify O(n) O(1)
Heap push/pop O(log n) —
BFS / DFS O(V+E) O(V)
Topological sort O(V+E) O(V)
Dijkstra (heap) O((V+E) log V) O(V)
Subsets O(n·2ⁿ) O(n)
Permutations O(n·n!) O(n)
Tree traversal O(n) O(h)
Balanced BST ops O(log n) —

Input-size guide: 10⁹→O(log n) · 10⁷→O(n) · 10⁵→O(n log n) · 10³→O(n²) · 20→O(2ⁿ) · 10→O(n!).

18.8 HTTP / API cheat sheet

Code Meaning Code Meaning
200 OK 403 Forbidden (authenticated, not allowed)
201 Created (+Location) 404 Not Found
202 Accepted (async) 409 Conflict
204 No Content (DELETE) 422 Unprocessable
304 Not Modified (ETag) 429 Too Many Requests (+Retry-After)
400 Bad Request 500 Server Error
401 Unauthorized (not authenticated) 503 Unavailable
Method Safe Idempotent
GET ✅ ✅
POST ❌ ❌
PUT ❌ ✅
PATCH ❌ usually ❌
DELETE ❌ ✅

Cookie flags: HttpOnly (no JS access) · Secure (HTTPS only) · SameSite (CSRF) · Max-Age. JWT: header.payload.signature — signed, not encrypted. Short-lived access + revocable refresh. CORS: browser-enforced; server sends Access-Control-Allow-*; preflight OPTIONS for non-simple requests; * is invalid with credentials. Pagination: offset (simple, slow deep) · cursor (fast, consistent, no random access). Cache: Cache-Control: max-age · ETag/If-None-Match → 304 · cache-aside + delete-on-write.

18.9 System design cheat sheet

Framework: Requirements → API → Architecture → Data → Cache → Scale → Failure → Trade-offs.

Numbers: 1 M/day ≈ 12 rps · 1 B/day ≈ 12,000 rps · memory read 100 ns · SSD read 100 µs · same-DC RTT 0.5 ms · cross-continent RTT 150 ms · peak ≈ 2–3× average.

Availability: 99% = 3.65 d/yr · 99.9% = 8.8 h/yr · 99.99% = 52 min/yr · 99.999% = 5 min/yr.

Problem Reach for
Too many reads Cache, read replicas, CDN
Too many writes Shard, batch, queue, write-behind
Slow queries Index, denormalise, precompute
Spiky traffic Queue + autoscaling
Slow third party Async + retry with backoff + circuit breaker
Large files Pre-signed URLs direct to object storage
Search Dedicated search index
Abuse Rate limiter at the gateway
Hot key Consistent hashing, key splitting, local cache
Duplicate processing Idempotency keys (at-least-once is the default)

CAP: during a partition choose C or A. Replication scales reads; sharding scales writes. Fan-out on write for normal users, on read for celebrities.

18.10 Git cheat sheet

git status; git add -p; git commit -m "msg"; git push -u origin branch
git switch -c feature/x            # new branch
git pull --rebase origin main      # linear history
git log --oneline --graph -20
git diff main...HEAD

git restore <file>                 # discard working changes
git reset --soft HEAD~1            # undo commit, keep staged
git reset --hard HEAD~1            # undo commit, DESTROY changes
git revert <sha>                   # safe undo on shared branches
git stash / git stash pop
git cherry-pick <sha>
git reflog                         # recover "lost" commits

Rebase private, merge shared. Reset private, revert shared.

18.11 Docker cheat sheet

docker build -t app:latest .
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --env-file .env --name api app:latest
docker ps -a; docker logs -f api; docker exec -it api bash
docker stop api; docker rm api; docker image prune -a
docker compose up -d --build; docker compose logs -f; docker compose down -v

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .            # deps BEFORE source = cached layer
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
USER appuser                       # don't run as root
CMD ["uvicorn","app.main:app","--host","0.0.0.0","--port","8000"]

Image = template, container = running instance. Containers share the host kernel; VMs don't. Data that must survive goes in a volume. Never bake secrets into an image.
